ety: Abbreviation of membrane theory.

s.def: A generalized theory of eleven-dimensional supergravity that attempts to unify the five superstring theories

ety: The noun is a contraction of madam, and represents a regional pronunciation of that word in the United Kingdom. The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: A form of address for a woman: contraction of madam.
ex: "You're very, very kind to me, ma'am," said Oliver.
Very pleased to meet you, Mem. I'm Mr. McCunn from Glasgow.

s.def: A polite and formal way to address a woman.
ex: Ma'am, will you be attending the dinner this evening?

s.def: A respectful term of address to a woman of higher rank or position.
ex: – Sergeant, have the platoon in formation and ready for inspection at 0800. – Aye aye, ma'am.

s.def: A title for a married woman.
ex: That is Ma'am Smith, the matriarch of the Smith families.

s.def: A female schoolteacher; a schoolmarm.
To address (a woman) as "ma'am".

ety: Borrowed from French macabre, whose etymology is uncertain. Possibly from the term danse macabre, most commonly believed to be from corruption of the biblical name Maccabees; compare Latin Chorea Machabaeorum. Another theory derives the French term (through Spanish macabro) from Arabic مَقَابِر (maqābir, “cemeteries”), plural of مَقْبَرَة (maqbara) or مَقْبُرَة (maqbura).

s.def: Obsessed with death or the gruesome.
Ghastly, shocking, terrifying.
Representing or personifying death.

ety: Named after Scottish engineer John Loudon McAdam (1756–1836), who invented the process of macadamization. Used for describing road surfaces originally constructed using the McAdam method, but now sometimes used for any road or street.

s.def: The surface of a road consisting of layers of crushed stone (usually tar-coated for modern traffic).
Any road or street.
To cover or surface with macadam.
The hard-shelled edible seed of the macadamia tree.

ety: From macadam + -ize, after Scottish engineer John Loudon McAdam who pioneered this method of road construction around 1820.

s.def: To cover (a road) with macadam (small, broken stones) so as to form a smooth, hard, convex surface.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French macaque, from Portuguese macaco, of uncertain origin (see macaco for more). Doublet of macaco.

s.def: Any of a group of Old World monkeys of the genus Macaca.
ex: They are able to recall past images and apply them to current problem solving. In other words, macaques employ memory in order to survive.

ety: Borrowed from French macaron. Doublet of macaroon.

s.def: Any of various confections made with almond and egg white, traditionally made in France.

ety: From Italian maccaroni (plural of maccarone (archaic variant of maccheroni (“fool”))), of uncertain origin. Variously derived from late Byzantine Greek μακαρία (makaría, “food made from barley”), from Ancient Greek μάκαρ (mákar, “blessed; favored by the gods”), or from maccare (archaic variant of ammaccare (“to bruise; to crush”)), from Latin maccāre of the same meaning. Compare Sicilian maccarruni (“a single piece of macaroni”). * As a fop, apparently from the British Macaroni Club rather than…

s.def: A type of pasta in the form of short tubes, typically boiled and served in soup, with a sauce, or in melted cheese; a dish of this.
ex: Take half a pound of small pipe-macaroni.

s.def: Pasta, particularly thicker noodles, spaghetti.
Synonym of gnocchi (“Italian dumpling made of potato or semolina”).
ex: Maccaróni, a kind of meat made of round peeces of paste, boyled in water and put into a dish with butter, spice and grated-cheese vpon them.

s.def: A dandy or fop, particularly in the 18th century a young Englishman who had travelled in Europe and subsequently dressed and spoke in an ostentatiously affected Continental manner.
ex: ... the Maccaroni Club (which is composed of all the travelled young men who wear long curls and spying-glasses) ...
Lady Falkener's daughter is to be married to a young rich Mr. Crewe, a Macarone...
'Sure never were seen two such beautiful Ponies; Other Horses are Clowns—and these macaronies

s.def: A 19th-century quarter-silver dollar coin, typically a full 2-real coin or a quarter clipping of an 8-real coin from Central or South America.
ex: The silver coins are dollars (6s. 8d.), half dollars, and quarter dollars, or maccaronies as they are here popularly called.

s.def: Ellipsis of macaroni penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus).
ex: 15 penguins were hatched and reared in the Edinburgh Zoo—seven kings, four gentoos, three maccaronis, and one ringed.

s.def: Synonym of Italian (“a person from Italy or of Italian ethnicity”).
ex: Surely I shall always be able, go where I will, among frogs or maccaronis, to procure sucre noir, or inchiostro nero.

s.def: Synonym of lizard canary.
ex: Lizards are known among Scotchmen as ‘macaronies’.

s.def: A mix of languages in macaronic verse.
ex: ... political songs in Latin or in a maccaroni of Latin and English ...

s.def: Ellipsis of macaroni tool.
ex: Now take the maccaroni and cut away the wood on either side of the vein...

ety: From French macaron. Doublet of macaron.

s.def: A soft biscuit or cookie prepared with almond or coconut dough.
Alternative spelling of macaron.
A coarse, rude, low fellow.
ex: Like a big wife, at sight of lothed meat, Ready to travail; so I sigh and sweat, To hear this macaroon talk on in vain.

ety: From Portuguese macau, of unknown origin. English sources point to Nheengatu makawana, which is only attested from the 20th century onwards.

s.def: Any of various parrots of the genera Ara, Anodorhynchus, Cyanopsitta, Orthopsittaca, Primolius and Diopsittaca of Central and South America, including the largest parrots and characterized by long sabre-shaped tails, curved powerful bills, and usually brilliant plumage.

ety: From Middle English mace, borrowed from Old French mace, mache, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea, matia, (compare Italian mazza, Spanish maza), probably from Proto-West Germanic *mattjō (“cutting tool, hoe”).

s.def: A ceremonial form of this weapon.
A spice obtained from the outer layer of the kernel of the fruit of the nutmeg.
A heavy fighting club.

A long baton used by some drum majors to keep time and lead a marching band. If this baton is referred to as a mace, by convention it has a ceremonial often decorative head, which, if of metal, usually is hollow and sometimes intricately worked.
An officer who carries a mace as a token of authority.
A knobbed mallet used by curriers to make leather supple when dressing it.
ex: In the foreground one man uses the "head knife” to work over the skin on the beam, while another softens a skin with the currier's mace.

s.def: A flail.
A billiard cue.
To hit someone or something with a mace.
Tear gas or pepper spray, especially for personal use.
Alternative form of macédoine.
ex: Try the whole filet mignon, roast duckling, green lasagna, choucroute garni, Cornish hens, and the macedonia of fruit made each day.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μακεδονία (Makedonía, “Macedonia”), from μακεδονία (makedonía, “highland”), from μακεδνός (makednós, “high, tall”). Doublet of macedoine.

s.def: A geographic region in Southeastern Europe in the Balkans which includes the Republic of North Macedonia, the region of Macedonia in Greece, the Pirin region of Bulgaria, and small parts of Albania and Serbia.
An ancient Greek kingdom in Southeastern Europe in the Balkans, located to the north of Thessaly, comprising the Greek city of Thessaloniki and its surroundings.
A geographic region and former administrative region of Greece, comprising the regions of West Macedonia, Central Macedonia and the East Macedonia part of the region of East Macedonia and Thrace.
modern geographical region
Former name of North Macedonia: a country in Southeastern Europe in the Balkans.
A geographic region in southwestern Bulgaria; in full, Pirin Macedonia or Bulgarian Macedonia.
A former constituent republic of Yugoslavia.
A former province of the Roman Empire.

ety: From Middle English Macedonyen, partly from Macedonia and partly from Latin Macedonius, + -an; equivalent to Macedonia + -an.

s.def: Of or pertaining to Macedonia or its people or language.
A person from Macedonia (in any sense).
A South Slavic language, the standard language of the Republic of North Macedonia.
The tongue of the Ancient Macedonians, spoken in Macedon during the 1st millennium BC. (see Ancient Macedonian)
The Greek dialect in Macedonia, region of Greece.

ety: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin mācerātus, perfect passive participle of mācerō (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from Proto-Indo-European *mag-, *mak- (“to knead”), whence make. Cognate with French macérer.

s.def: To soften (something) or separate it into pieces by (or as if by) soaking it in a heated or unheated liquid.
To reduce solids to small pieces (in a macerator).
ex: Near-synonyms: comminute, crush, pulverize

s.def: To make lean; to cause to waste away.
To subdue the appetite by poor or scanty diet; to mortify.
To mortify the flesh in general.
past participle of macerate
A macerated substance.

ety: Latin mācerātiō.

s.def: The act or process of macerating.
ex: […] proposed that the small size of the teeth […] implied that most of the maceration of the food occurred after swallowing.

ety: After physicist Ernst Mach.

s.def: The ratio of the speed of a body to that of sound in the surrounding medium.

ety: Borrowed from French mâche.

s.def: Valerianella locusta, a small dicot annual plant of the family Caprifoliaceae often cultivated as a salad green or herb.

ety: From Spanish machete, diminutive of macho (“sledgehammer”), from Latin mattea, possibly from mactare (“slaughter in sacrifice”); cognate with Old French machier, French massue, English mace.

s.def: A sword-like tool used for cutting large plants with a chopping motion, or used as a weapon.
ex: Near-synonyms: (all sometimes or regionally synonymous) bolo, golok, panga, parang, sundang

s.def: A small stringed instrument from Madeira, Portugal, having a double bulged body, traditionally of wood, with a small rib and four metallic strings, sometimes attached by wooden pegs.
To cut or chop with a machete.
ex: After some hours of intense work, we had macheted a path through the jungle to the bank of the river.

ety: Etymology tree English Machiavellian Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English Machiavellianism From Machiavellian + -ism.

s.def: ruthless, duplicitous behavior
The political philosophy of Machiavelli, especially the realist doctrine which emphasizes the maintenance of the state above ethical concerns.
ex: "Machiavellianism is a radical type of political realism that is applied to both domestic and international affairs."
Let us turn, finally, to the war itself, and ask ourselves if it can be understood as the victory of decency over Machiavellianism.

s.def: A political maneuver that exemplifies the philosophy. Unsavory government politics.
A psychological construct centered on interpersonal manipulation, lack of empathy, cold affect, and indifference to morality.

ety: From Late Latin machicol(amentum) (“machicolation”) + -ation (suffix indicating an action or process). Machicolamentum may be derived from Old French macher (“to chew; to crush”) (modern French mâcher) + col (“neck”) + Latin -mentum (suffix indicating an instrument or medium, or the result of something). The English word is cognate with Middle English machecolled (“having machicolations”), machecolling (“act of constructing machicolation; the openings making up the machicolation”), Middle Frenc…

s.def: An opening between corbels that support a projecting parapet, or in the floor of a gallery or the roof of a portal, of a fortified building from which missiles can be shot or heated items dropped upon assailants attacking the base of the walls.
A projecting parapet with a series of such openings.

ety: First attested in 1537; borrowed from Latin machinātus, perfect active participle of machinor (“to invent, devise; to scheme, plot”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from māchina (“machine, contrivance, device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. See also machine.

s.def: To devise a plot or secret plan; to conspire.
ex: Had she already managed to machinate a cushy job for her husband?

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-der.? Ancient Greek μηχᾰνή (mēkhănḗ) Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́)bor. Latin māchinabor. Middle French machinebor. English machine Borrowed from Middle French machine, from Latin māchina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́), cognate with Attic Greek μηχᾰνή (mēkhănḗ, “a machine, engine, contrivance, device”), from which comes mechanical. Displaced native Old English searu.

s.def: A device that directs and controls energy, often in the form of movement or electricity, to produce a certain effect.
A person or organisation that seemingly acts like a machine, being particularly efficient, single-minded, or unemotional.
ex: Bruce Campbell was a "demon-killing machine" because he made quick work of killing demons.
The government has become a money-making machine.

s.def: A vehicle operated mechanically, such as an automobile or an airplane.
ex: As the aviator turned his machine to reconnoitre in the new direction, he was surprised to see the hostile aeroplane between him and his objective.

s.def: An answering machine or, by extension, voice mail.
ex: I called you earlier, but all I got was the machine.

s.def: A computer.
ex: Game developers assume they're pushing the limits of the machine.
He refuses to turn off his Linux machine.

s.def: Especially, the group that controls a political or similar organization; a combination of persons acting together for a common purpose, with the agencies which they use.
ex: The whole machine of government, civil and religious, ought never to bear upon the people with a weight so oppressive

s.def: Supernatural agency in a poem, or a superhuman being introduced to perform some exploit.
ex: I am apt to think, that the changing of the Trojan fleet into water-nymphs, which is the most violent machine in the whole Æneid[…]

s.def: The system of special interest groups that supports a political party, especially in urban areas.
ex: He was thrust into a political maelstrom for which he was ill-prepared, and yet he was, most notably, the Chicago machine's political savior.

s.def: Penis.
A contrivance in the Ancient Greek theatre for indicating a change of scene, by means of which a god might cross the stage or deliver a divine message; the deus ex machina.
A type of fully automatic firearm that fires bullets in rapid succession by a single action of the trigger and is capable of sustained fire.
ex: I'm gonna get you, baby / Like a machine gun, I'm gonna… Tak-Tak-Tak-Tak-Tak

s.def: The set of instructions that a particular computer is designed to execute; generated from an assembly language by an assembler, or from a high-level language by a compiler or interpreter.
ex: Though machine language is efficient for computers, it is inefficient for programmers.

s.def: A tool, typically a power-driven machine and typically stationary, used especially for machining (removing hard material via cutting, grinding, or other subtractive processes) and (more broadly) for any mix of subtractive, forming/stamping, or additive work.
The act of translating something from one language to another by means of a machine, especially a computer.
The production of instructions in a computer language that are equal in meaning to that in another language.

ety: From machine + -ery. Compare French machinerie.

s.def: The machines constituting a production apparatus, in a plant etc., collectively.
The working parts of a machine as a group.
The collective parts of something which allow it to function.
ex: All of the machinery of the law was brought to bear on the investigation.

s.def: The literary devices used in a work, notably for dramatic effect.

ety: From French machiniste, from machine (“machine, mechanical device”), from Latin māchina, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

s.def: A constructor of machines and engines; someone knowledgeable about machines.
A person skilled in the use of machine tools for fashioning metal parts or tools out of metal.
A person who operates machinery.
A person employed to shift scenery in a theater.

ety: From Mach + -meter.

s.def: An instrument that measures the speed of an aircraft relative to that of sound and displays it in Mach numbers.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish macho (“male”), from Latin masculus. Doublet of male.

s.def: Masculine in an overly assertive or aggressive way. Very masculine.
ex: macho culture

s.def: A macho person; a man who is masculine in an overly assertive or aggressive way.
ex: You can tell a macho, he has a funky walk / His western shirts and leather, always look so boss

s.def: A very masculine man.
Machismo
ex: […] about how the military is anti-gay and uses intimidation and peer pressure. How it promotes a sense of false macho and patriotism.

s.def: The striped mullet of California (Mugil cephalus, syn. Mugil mexicanus).
A male llama.

ety: From Middle English mackerell, macrell, macrelle, makarell, makerel, makerell, makerelle, makrel, makrell, makyrelle, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown.

s.def: edible fish
Certain smaller edible fish, principally true mackerel and Spanish mackerel in family Scombridae, often speckled,
ex: […] you may buy land now as cheap as stinking mackerel.
I am living fast, to see the Time, when a Book that misses its Tide, shall be neglected, as the Moon by Day, or like Mackarel a Week after the Season.
He sometimes pinches the maids till their arms are as many colours as a mackerel’s back.

s.def: A true mackerel, any fish of tribe Scombrini (Scomber spp., Rastrelliger spp.)
Certain other similar small fish in families Carangidae, Gempylidae, and Hexagrammidae.
A regular pattern, similar to fish scales, of undulating small clouds with sky visible between them.
ex: a mackerel sky
MACKEREL CLOUDS.- Mackerel scales and mares' tails / Make lofty ships carry low sails.
Mackerel clouds in sky, Expect more wet than dry. A mackerel sky, Not twenty-four hours dry.

s.def: A pimp; also, a bawd.
ex: NETTING MACKEREL: THE PIMP DETAIL
Hundreds of ‘night birds’ and their ‘mackerels’ and other vice-pushers were sent packing.
You can't 'work' in a legal brothel without mackerel.

ety: From Charles Macintosh (1766–1843), who patented a type of rubberized cloth in 1823. Former trademark. The letter k is a later addition.

s.def: A waterproof long coat made of rubberized cloth.
Any waterproof coat or raincoat.
Waterproof rubberized cloth.

ety: From the earlier form macle, from macule, which see for more.

s.def: Obsolete form of macule.
Obsolete form of macule.
To assemble in a makeshift manner; to cobble together.
To speak like or act like rapper Macklemore, particularly in a way perceived as naive or cringeworthy.
ex: A number of followers thanked him for his decision, with one fan writing, “He mackled less, for our sake.”

ety: Borrowed from French macle, which in turn derives either from Latin macula (from Italic) or from Latin mascula (from Germanic). See mascle for more.

s.def: Chiastolite; so called from the tessellated appearance of a cross-section.
A crystal having a similar tessellated appearance.
A twin crystal.
Alternative spelling of macramé.
Alternative spelling of macramé.

ety: 1865, borrowed from French macramé, from Italian macramè, from Ottoman Turkish مقرمه (makrame), from Arabic مِقْرَمَة (miqrama, “ornamental fringe, embroidered veil”), from مِقْرَم (miqram, “bedspread”), from قَرَمَ (qarama, “to gnaw”), from Proto-Semitic *q-r-m.

s.def: A form of decorative textile made by knotting and weaving.
ex: Robby is contemplating macramé.

s.def: An extension to an assembly language in which macroinstructions, containing a series of instructions, may be written.
A system for defining and processing macros.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós Proto-Hellenic *makrós Ancient Greek μᾰκρός (măkrós)der. French macro-der. English macro- From French, from Latin, from Ancient Greek μακρο- (makro-), combinging form of μακρός (makrós, “long”). By surface analysis, macr- + -o-.

s.def: large
ex: macronucleus

s.def: long
ex: macrobiotics

s.def: inclusive
ex: macroinstruction

s.def: intensely, extremely, or exceptional
great in scope or scale, to analyse at a high level, or existing in such a frame of reference
ex: macrosociology, macroanatomy, macrobenthos

s.def: large in quantity
ex: macronutrient, macrodose

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós Proto-Hellenic *makrós Ancient Greek μᾰκρός (măkrós)der. French macro-der. English macro- English burst English macroburst From macro- + burst.

s.def: A strong downdraft, of over 2.5 miles in diameter, that can cause damaging winds.

ety: From macro- + -cephaly.

s.def: A condition in which the head is abnormally large.
The excessive concentration of population and development in a single centre, to the detriment of other areas.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós Proto-Hellenic *makrós Ancient Greek μᾰκρός (măkrós)der. French macro-der. English macro- English climate English macroclimate From macro- + climate.

s.def: The climate of a relatively large geographic area.

ety: From Middle French macrocosme (from Old French macrocosme) and Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”).

s.def: A complex structure, such as a society, considered as a single entity that contains numerous similar, smaller-scale structures.
The universe.

ety: From macro- (“large scale”) + economics. The first published use of the term was by the Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch (1895–1973) in 1933.

s.def: The study of the entire economy in terms of the total amount of goods and services produced, total income earned, the level of employment of productive resources, and the general behavior of prices.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós Proto-Hellenic *makrós Ancient Greek μᾰκρός (măkrós)der. French macro-der. English macro- Latin mōlēs Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Proto-Italic *-kelos Latin -cula New Latin mōlēculalbor. French moléculebor. English molecule English macromolecule From macro- + molecule.

s.def: A very large molecule, especially used in reference to large biological polymers (e.g. nucleic acids and proteins).
ex: Beadle discovered that genes carried instructions to build proteins—complex, multidimensional macromolecules that were the workhorses of the cell.

ety: From macropod + -ian.

s.def: A macropod.

ety: From Middle English macula (“spot on the skin or in the eye”), borrowed from Latin macula (“spot, stain”). Doublet of macchia and macule.

s.def: An oval yellow spot near the center of the retina of the human eye, histologically defined as having two or more layers of ganglion cells, responsible for detailed central vision.
A small chamber of the inner ear of certain vertebrates filled with endolymph and containing an otolith.
A spot, as on the skin, or on the surface of the sun or of some other luminous orb.
A rather large spot or blotch of color.
In planetary geology, an unusually dark area on the surface of a planet or moon.

ety: First attested during the last quarter of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English maculaten (“to spoil, polute”), borrowed from Latin maculātus, perfect passive participle of maculō (“to spot”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: To spot; to stain; to blur.
ex: they wolde nat maculate the honour of their people with suche a reproche
There was a fresh smell in the air. Sidewalks began to be maculated with spreading areas of dryness

s.def: past participle of maculate
ex: That the honour of verteous gentil men, be nocht maculat vitht the vice ande inciuilite of vicius pretendit gentil men.

s.def: Marked with spots or maculae; blotched.
Defiled, impure.

ety: From Middle English macule, from Middle French macule and its etymon Classical Latin macula. Doublet of macchia, macula and, with a suffix, maquis.

s.def: A spot.
A blur or an appearance of a double impression, as when the paper slips a little during printing.
To blur or be blurred; especially to blur or double an impression from type.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Germanic *ga- Proto-West Germanic *ga- Old English ġe- Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- Proto-Indo-European *moyth₂-éye-tider. Proto-Germanic *maidijanąder. Old English *mǣdan Old English ġemǣdan, ġemǣded Middle English mad English mad From Middle English mad, madde, madd, medd, from Old English ġemǣd, ġemǣded (“enraged”), past participle of ġemǣdan, *mǣdan (“to make insane or foolish”), from Proto-Ger…

s.def: Insane; crazy; mentally deranged.
ex: You want to spend a thousand pounds on a pair of shoes? Are you mad?
He's got this mad idea that he's irresistible to women.
I have heard my grandsire say full oft, / Extremity of griefs would make men mad.

s.def: Angry; annoyed.
ex: Are you mad at me?

s.def: Used litotically to indicate satisfaction or approval.
ex: Wow, you really made this pie from scratch? I'm not mad at it.
I'm not mad at this little house, though.
But I mean, once the flow was there, nobody was mad at it.

s.def: Bizarre; incredible.
ex: It's mad that I got that job back a day after being fired.

s.def: Extremely foolish or unwise; irrational; imprudent.
Wildly confused or excited.
ex: to be mad with terror, lust, or hatred
It is the land of graven images, and they are mad upon their idols.

s.def: Extremely enthusiastic about; crazy about; infatuated with; overcome with desire for.
ex: Aren't you just mad for that red dress?
My wife is soccer-mad.
She's mad on the baking these days.

s.def: Abnormally ferocious or furious; or, rabid, affected with rabies.
Intensifier, signifying abundance or high quality of a thing; very, much, excellent or many.
ex: I gotta give you mad props for scoring us those tickets. Their lead guitarist has mad skills. There are always mad girls at those parties.

s.def: Having impaired polarity.
Synonym of bovine spongiform encephalopathy.
Honey that is toxic or psychoactive due to chemicals in plants or the environment.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French Madagascar, from Madageiscar, popularly reputed as a corrupted transliteration of Mogadishu by Marco Polo's misreading of Arabic. The maps of particular interest are that of al-Idrisi in the 12th century, who produced the Tabula Rogeriana, the most advanced world map at the time. The actual misconstrued term was Arabic جَزِيرَة المَالَائِيّ (jazīrat al-mālāʔiyy, “The Island of Mālāī”) listed alongside Arabic جَزِيرَة القَمَر (jazīrat al-qamar, “The Island of the Moon…

s.def: An island and country off the east coast of Africa. Official name: Republic of Madagascar. Capital: Antananarivo.

ety: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (“my”) + dame (“lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. Doublet of Madonna.

s.def: A polite form of address for a woman or lady.
ex: Mrs Grey wondered if the outfit she was trying on made her look fat. The sales assistant just said, “It suits you, madam”.
Later, Mrs Grey was sitting in her favourite tea shop. “Would madam like the usual cream cakes and patisserie with her tea?” the waitress asked.

s.def: To convert (a road) into a main or primary road.
Ellipsis of mainline (“to inject (a drug) directly into a vein”).
To mainly play a specific character or side, or with specific equipment, during a game.
ex: He mains the same character as me in that game.
What race do you main and what is your favourite race to beat?
For new players, I recommend maining the dagger and using the axe as a backup weapon.

s.def: The most important building of a group of buildings (e.g. in a school/university).

ety: The US state is from French Maine, named by its French explorers after the province in France with the same name. From Old French Cemaine, from Latin *Cenomania, from the name of the Gaulish Cenomani tribe of Gallia Celtica. The word was rebracketed as ce (“this”) + Maine, and the ce- was lost by the 12th century.

s.def: US State
A state of the United States; probably named for the province in France. Capital: Augusta. Largest city: Portland.
A town in New York.
A town in Outagamie County, Wisconsin; named for the state.
A former province of Pays de la Loire, France. Capital: Le Mans.
A river in Maine, United States, flowing 5.5 miles from Pocomoonshine Lake in Princeton into Crawford Lake in Crawford.
University of Maine.

ety: From main + frame.

s.def: A large, powerful computer able to manage very many simultaneous tasks and communicate with very many connected terminals; used by large, complex organizations (such as banks and supermarkets) where continuously sustained operation is vital.
A computer chassis that hosts and interconnects modules that perform various tasks.
The main frame of a vehicle etc., more commonly main frame.

ety: From Middle English mayne londe; equivalent to main + land. Compare Scots mayn-land, magan-land, madin-land (“mainland”), Faroese meginland (“mainland”), Icelandic meginland (“mainland”).

s.def: The continent; the principal land, as distinguished from islands or a peninsula.
ex: You may have not realised when I was using the term mainland Europe, I was excluding the British Isles.

s.def: The principal island of a group.
Great Britain.

ety: From mainland + China.

s.def: The People's Republic of China, viewed as the general geographical region administered by the PRC in the aftermath of the Chinese Civil War (as opposed to Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan which are coastal and insular areas)
ex: Tsuen Wan is a working-class area near Hong Kong’s border with the Chinese mainland, miles from the city’s gleaming financial district.

s.def: Also used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see mainland, China.

ety: From main + mast.

s.def: The tallest mast of a sailing ship that has more than one mast; particularly a full-rigged ship.
ex: The try-works are planted between the foremast and mainmast, the most roomy part of the deck.

s.def: The second-foremost mast of a non-sailing ship with more than one mast.

ety: From main + spring. For figurative sense, compare spring (“source, origin”).

s.def: The principal spring of a clockwork mechanism, which drives it by uncoiling.
ex: He was wise, for he had seen a long succession of mechanical toys arrive to boast and swagger, and by-and-by break their mainsprings and pass away.

s.def: The most important reason for, or element of, something.
ex: My daughter is the mainspring of my life.
But in the England of Shakespeare’s history plays, the mainspring of the system has broken down.

ety: From Middle English main stai, equivalent to main + stay (“rope”).

s.def: A chief support.
ex: Agriculture is the mainstay of this country’s economy.
Oil is the mainstay of Nigeria's economy.
Conventional radiography has a major role in, and remains the mainstay of, initial evaluation and follow-up of rheumatologic disease.

s.def: Someone or something that can be depended on to make a regular contribution.
ex: The marina was a mainstay of the neighborhood, and Mr. O’Rourke was known for staging salsa and merengue concerts.

s.def: A stabilising rope from high on the mainmast to the base of the foremast.

ety: From main + stream. Cognate with Icelandic meginstraumur (“a main current, mainstream”).

s.def: Used or accepted broadly rather than by small portions of population, market, scientific community, etc.
ex: They often carry stories you won't find in the mainstream media.
As unsubstantiated claims receive significant backing, skeptics and defenders of mainstream science enter the fray.
If Ms. Le Pen looks more mainstream now, it’s because the mainstream looks more like her.

s.def: The principal current in a flow, such as a river or flow of air
That which is common; the norm.
ex: ideas outside of the mainstream
"Railways seldom slavishly followed styles to be seen in the mainstream of contemporary architecture," HE [Historic England] explains.

s.def: To popularize, to normalize, to render mainstream.
ex: Acknowledging the role X plays in mainstreaming the worst constituencies makes for awkward conversations with those who continue to use it.

s.def: To become mainstream.

s.def: To educate (a disabled student) together with non-disabled students.

ety: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manūteneō, manūtenēre (“I support”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”, ablative of manus) + tenēre (“to hold”).

s.def: To keep up; to preserve; to uphold (a state, condition etc.).
ex: maintain contact
maintain order
maintain a relationship

s.def: To declare or affirm (a clause) to be true; to assert.
ex: Pullman traditionalists will no doubt maintain that the full-service-at-every-seat principle is popular with their clientele; [...].

s.def: To keep in good condition and working order.
To support (someone), to back up or assist (someone) in an action.
To keep composed; to keep one's head up; to stay confident, strong, self-assured; to avoid being a victim; to keep oneself from falling apart.
ex: No matter what, you gotta maintain.

ety: Etymology tree English maintain Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English maintainable From maintain + -able.

s.def: Able to be maintained
The act of doing maintenance.

ety: From Middle English mayntenaunce, from Old French maintenance, from maintenir, from Latin manus tenēre (“to hold in the hand”). By surface analysis, maintain + -ance. Note that maintain has undergone a sound and spelling change, hence is spelt with -tain-, rather than the -ten- still found in maintenance.

s.def: keeping a machine or system in service — see also care
Actions performed to keep some machine or system functioning or in service.
A tort and (in some jurisdictions) an offence committed when a third party who does not have a bona fide interest in a lawsuit provides help or acquires an interest to a litigant's lawsuit.
Alimony, a periodical payment or a lump sum made or ordered to be made to a spouse after a divorce.
Child support.
Money required or spent to provide for the needs of a person or a family.
The natural process which keeps an organism alive.
Ellipsis of maintenance medicine.
Software updates that fix bugs and improve stability rather than adding new features.
ex: a maintenance release; a maintenance version

ety: Borrowed from German Mainz, from Latin Mogontiacum, from a Celtic language.

s.def: A city, the state capital of Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, on the River Rhine.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno *mahis, *mahisi, from Proto-Arawak *marikɨ. Cognate with Lokono marisi, Wayuu maiki.

s.def: Corn; a type of grain of the species Zea mays.

ety: From majesty + -ic, 1600s.

s.def: Having qualities of splendor or royalty.
ex: The gymnast performed a majestic vault.

ety: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.

s.def: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.
ex: the majesty of the Great Pyramids

ety: Borrowed from Arabic مَجْلِس (majlis).

s.def: A council, assembly, or public meeting, in some Muslim countries or territories.

ety: From Italian maiolica, named after the Island of Mallorca (formerly known as Maiòlica), which was once a commerce center for work produced in Valencia, Spain. Doublet of Mallorca and Majorca.

s.def: Earthenware decorated with coloured lead silicate glazes applied directly to an unglazed body, a process invented in Victorian England.
ex: The Italian Vase [top, left, p.8] is Majolica, […] The Ewer [bottom, middle, p.8] is a Palissy vase.
[…] the coloured glaze decorated wares which we now call majolica, but which Minton referred to as Palissy wares.

ex: Enamel - A vitrifiable substance; opaque, generally Stanniferous majolica […]
[…] the use of the word majolica will be restricted to its original meaning of lustred stanniferous glazed pottery.
The word Majolica, or Maiolica […] was applied to all Stanniferous faience of Italy and Spain.

s.def: Of full legal age, having attained majority.
ex: major children

s.def: music: of a scale
The principal subject or course of a student working toward a degree at a college or university.
ex: Midway through his second year of college, he still hadn't chosen a major.

s.def: military rank
Greater in dignity, rank, importance, significance, or interest.
Greater in number, quantity, or extent.
ex: the major part of the assembly

The five major religions are Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism, and Buddhism.

ex: In short, when I've a smattering of elemental strategy-- [...] You'll say a better major-general has never sat agee.

s.def: One of the diatonic scales; a group of notes or musical pitches in a particular pattern, used to make melodies. The pattern for a major scale is: tone - tone - semitone - tone - tone - tone - semitone.
ex: {c' d' e' f' g' a' b' c}

ety: From Italian maggiordomo and Spanish mayordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).

s.def: The head servant or official in a royal Spanish or Italian household; later, any head servant in a wealthy household in a foreign country; a leading servant or butler.
A manager of a hacienda, ranch or estate.
ex: She called upon a Missouri cousin named Edward Hardy Clark, who became the indispensable majordomo of the Hearst estate.

ety: Short for drum majorette, equivalent to major + -ette. Doublet of marjoret.

s.def: A female dancer who twirls and performs stunts with a lightweight baton, whether as a solo, in a group of majorettes, or in the company of a marching band.

ety: From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.

s.def: More than half (50%) of some group.
ex: The majority agreed that the new proposal was the best.
Those opposing the building plans were in the majority, so the building project was canceled.

s.def: Any share or fraction that is bigger than any one of its counterpart shares or fractions (of the same whole).

In a parliament or legislature, the difference in seats between the ruling party and the opposition; (UK) in an election, the difference in votes between the winning candidate and the second-place candidate, or between the winning candidate and all of the other candidates combined.
ex: The ruling party had a narrow three-seat majority in the legislature.
The winner with 53% had a 6% majority over the loser with 47%.

s.def: Legal adulthood, age of majority.
ex: By the time I reached my majority, I had already been around the world twice.

s.def: The office held by a member of the armed forces in the rank of major.
ex: On receiving the news of his promotion, Charles Snodgrass said he was delighted to be entering his majority.
He was a captain before he went to the front, and following the Argonne battles he got his majority and the command of the divisional machine-guns.

s.def: Ancestors; ancestry.
ex: Of evil parents an evil generation, a posterity not unlike their majority; of mischievous progenitors, a venomous and destructive progeny.

ety: Borrowed from French majuscule, from Latin majuscula (littera).

s.def: A capital letter, especially one used in ancient manuscripts.
Capital letters.
ex: Many of these strips are palimpsest and bear earlier writing in majuscule and old minuscule.

ety: From Middle English macen, machiæ, macian, macke, mak, make, maken, makiȝe, from Old English macian (“to build, make, work”), from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to build, make, work”), from *mak (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ-, *meh₂ḱ- (“to knead”) or *meg- (“to be comfortable, pleasant”). s.def: To create.
ex: We made a bird feeder for our yard.

He makes deodorants.

s.def: To behave, to act.
ex: To make like a deer caught in the headlights.

He made as if to punch him, but they both laughed and shook hands.

s.def: To tend; to contribute; to have effect; with for or against.

s.def: To add up to, have a sum of.
ex: Two and four make six.

s.def: To interpret.
ex: I don’t know what to make of it.
They couldn't make anything of the inscription.
What time do you make it?

s.def: To cause to be.
ex: The blisters on my foot made it a problem to walk without a cane.
Caesar made rich men of his supporters back in Rome.
The citizens made their objections clear.

s.def: To cause to appear to be; to represent as.
ex: Homer makes Aphrodite the daughter of Zeus, unlike Hesiod who depicted her as born from the sea foam.
1709–1710, Thomas Baker, Reflections on Learning He is not that goose and Ass that Valla would make him.

s.def: To cause (to do something); to compel (to do something).
ex: You're making her cry.
I was made to feel like a criminal.

s.def: To force to do.
ex: The teacher made the student study harder.
Don’t let them make you suffer.

der: beauty won't make the pot boil

s.def: To decide.
ex: You need to make a decision whether or not to go.

s.def: To succeed in (something); especially, to succeed in making a living.
ex: He quit his regular job and tried to make a go of it as an artist.
They made a go of the new business.
They had to sell farm; after three consecutive crop failures, they just couldn’t make a go of it.

w: make a mountain out of a molehill

s.def: To treat a problem as greater than it is; to blow something out of proportion; to exaggerate the importance of something trivial.
ex: If you’re stuck in traffic, try not to make a mountain out of a molehill worrying about it too much. You could be making it much worse.
She wondered why he, who did not usually trouble over trifles, made such a mountain of this molehill.

s.def: To survive, get by (with), or use whatever is available (due to lack of resources).
ex: There is barely enough money, so we will have to make do with what we have.

s.def: To put into action.
ex: Make the movie do! (Put on the movie!)
Brandon’s makin’ the grill do so we can get to eatin’.

s.def: To use for one's purpose something worn, defective, or intended for another purpose.
ex: It is not the same hide but we make it do. You work harder to make it into good leather and harder to make it into good shoes, and we get by.

der: make it do or do without

ety: Unknown. Perhaps originally referred to the ends of rope meeting, signifying continuity and therefore security and stability. Perhaps shifting later to refer to the attempt at making money last from one pay period to the next (i.e. the ends), thereby leaving no gap or break in the availability of funds. Compare French joindre les deux bouts (literally “join the two ends”) with the same meaning. The form make both ends meet is attested from the 17th century, and was the more common form until th…

s.def: To have enough money to cover expenses; to get by financially; to get through the pay period (sufficient to meet the next payday).
ex: Although most of the poor and displaced in Khartoum struggle to make ends meet, a very small number not only find work, but form small co-operatives.
'Cause it's a bitter sweet symphony that's life / Trying to make ends meet, you're a slave to money then you die
Investigators discover that Captain Ospina was forced to take a second job, moonlighting in a bar, in order to make ends meet for his family.

ety: From Middle English maken frendes, equivalent to make + friends.

s.def: To form friendships with others.
ex: He hasn't made friends easily at his new school.

s.def: To befriend.
ex: He made friends with his new neighbour.
I tried to be a friend to Jane but we never really made friends. She was never a friend to me.
Sara and I made friends right away.

ety: Recorded 1737. Preserves the older meaning of fun, from Middle English fon, fonne (“foolish, simple, silly”), fun (c. 1700) meaning "a cheat, trick, hoax", from a verb fun meaning "to cheat, trick" (1680s).

s.def: To tease, ridicule or make jokes about, generally in a pejorative manner.
ex: Please stop making fun of your sister and just help her!

ety: Calque of Old Occitan far amor, Middle French faire l'amour.

I feel like makin' love to you / That's the time / I feel like makin' dreams come true

After all, the chief charm is in the fact of being made love to. You are making love to me, aren't you?
‘Ever since I was sixteen men have been making love to me.’

Harry said, "It's too bad, but of course we couldn't attempt to smuggle him. The old man has made his bed and he must lie in it."
He had made his own bed, chosen his own course in life, taking the path of easy money over hard work and initiative.

s.def: To end hostilities; to reach a peace agreement; to initiate or resume a cordial relationship after a period of animosity.
ex: Both countries can rebuild now that they have made peace with each other.

s.def: To settle a dispute or disagreement.
ex: The committee made peace and agreed to go with the new plan.

s.def: To accept something, especially if it is considered unfavourable.
ex: I've finally made peace with the fact that having diabetes means no more sugar.

s.def: To rearrange or organize existing people, objects, furniture, belongings, etc., to create space for new objects.
ex: I moved the books off my desk to make room for my labtop.

I was in your arms Thinking I belonged there I figured it made sense Building me a fence

s.def: Used to express interest or desire in something; to be pleasing or beneficial; to work, be operative, or be advantageous to.

s.def: To be in the realm of the ordinary, to be not particularly developed.
ex: If you want to grow spinal erectors that don’t make sense, you have to do a lot of bent-over compound lifts.

ex: He was a great storyteller and could make up a story on the spot.

s.def: To apply cosmetics.

s.def: To constitute, to compose.

s.def: To build, to complete.

s.def: To decide; to reach a conclusion.

s.def: To use, usually productively and/or for a specific purpose.

A person who applies makeup and prosthetics for theatrical, television, film, fashion, magazines and similar productions.

ex: They used the ledge and a few branches for a makeshift shelter.

ety: From the name of Mrs. Malaprop, a character in the play The Rivals (1775) by Richard Brinsley Sheridan + -ism. ety: From mandate + -ary.

ety: First attested in 1521; borrowed from Latin mandātum (“a charge, order, command, commission, injunction”), substantivized from the neuter forms of mandātus, perfect passive participle of mandō (“to commit to one's charge, order, command, commission, literally to put into one's hands”) (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from manus (“hand”) + -dere (“to put”). Sense 3 in Canadian English is likely a semantic loan from French mandat.

s.def: An official or authoritative command; an order or injunction; a commission; a judicial precept; an authorization.
The order or authority to do something, as granted to a politician by the electorate.
ex: John Tyler and James K. Polk both regarded the election results as a mandate for the annexation of Texas.

s.def: A period during which a government is in power.
An order by the League of Nations to a member nation to establish a government responsible for a conquered territory, as the colonies of Germany after World War I.
To (officially) require someone to do something or act in a certain way, to give them the authority to do so; to command.
ex: A delegate conference was called, and garages invited to mandate their representatives to vote for or against continuance.

s.def: To make mandatory.
ex: Federal law mandates that at least one nongroup insurer in your state must provide coverage to everyone, regardless of health issues.
As the Superintendent of Austin, TX, schools I have mandated that our kids must be masked when they start school on Tuesday.

s.def: To administer or assign a territory to a nation under a mandate.
To repeat, rehearse sermons or speeches aloud.

He rose and walked his study, ‘mandating’ his opening sentences with appropriate gestures.
I had only from that evening at six till Sabbath to mandate my two discourses.

ety: From Late Latin mandatorius (“of or belonging to a mandator”), from mandātor (“one who commands”), equivalent to mandate + -ory; see mandate.

ety: From Middle English mandrake, mandroke, an alteration of mandragora with the ending -dragora reinterpreted as related to dragon and replaced with native drake, from Old English mandragora, from Medieval Latin mandragorās, from Ancient Greek μανδραγόρας (mandragóras).

s.def: The shape of the edge of a leaf.
ex: Red Whortleberry leaves have a crenate margin.

s.def: To add a margin to; to furnish with a margin.

ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, equivalent to margin + -al.

s.def: Of, relating to, or located at or near a margin or edge; also figurative usages of location and margin (edge).
ex: The marginal area at the edge of the salt-marsh has its own plants.
In recent years there has been an increase in violence against marginal groups.

s.def: Determined by a small margin; having a salient characteristic determined by a small margin.
ex: His writing ability was marginal at best.
Having reviewed the test, there are two students below the required standard and three more who are marginal.
The pilots lacked experience flying in marginal weather conditions.

s.def: Marginalized.
Pertaining to changes resulting from a unit increase in production or consumption of a good.
Something or somebody that is marginal.
ex: […] discusses those who belong to the discipline's dominant cults, the mainliners, and their relations with the marginals and mavericks.

s.def: A constituency won with a small margin.

ety: From New Latin marginālia (cf. margināle (neuter singular (adjective / noun)), from Medieval Latin neuter plural of marginālis (“on the periphery”), from Latin margō (“border, edge”). By surface analysis, marginal + -ia. Compare margin.

s.def: Notes in the margin of a document.
ex: We know what the composer was thinking as he wrote the piece because we can read his handwritten marginalia on the manuscript.

ety: Borrowed from Latin marginātus, perfect passive participle of marginō (“to margin”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: With a well marked edge or margin.
To provide with margins.
ex: undulating lines marginated with pale, one on each side, Maxillæ nearly straight, their base narrow

ety: From French marguerite. Doublet of Margaret (and various forms, q.v.), margarita, margarite, and Margherita, and related to margarine.

s.def: An oxeye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare).
A shrub with daisy-like flowers, Argyranthemum frutescens
The China aster.

ety: Transliteration of Georgian მარგველაშვილი (margvelašvili).

s.def: A transliteration of the Georgian surname მარგველაშვილი (margvelašvili).
ex: Giorgi Margvelashvili, president of Georgia

ety: Borrowed from Western Mari мари (mari, “Mari language term for the Mari”).

s.def: language
A Finno-Ugric language spoken by the Mari people.
Meadow Mari; Eastern Mari.

ety: After the Marianas Islands.

s.def: A submarine trench in the North Pacific Ocean, noted for having the deepest known point on Earth.

ety: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew מִרְיָם (miryɔm)bor. Aramaic מריםbor. Koine Greek Μᾰρῐ́ᾱ (Mărĭ́ā)bor. Latin Marīa Old French Mariebor. Middle English Marie Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰĺ̥h₃-to-mder. Proto-Germanic *gulþą Proto-West Germanic *golþ Old English gold Middle English gold Middle English golde Middle English marigolde English marigold From Middle English marigolde, marygoldye, from Mary (referring to the Virgin Mary) + Middle English golde (“marigold”).

s.def: Any of the Old World plants, of the genus Calendula, with orange, yellow or reddish flowers.
ex: A piece of marigold or bay leaf was imbedded in the metal, and over it a carbuncle or chrysolite was placed.

s.def: Any of the New World plants, of the genus Tagetes, with orange, yellow or reddish flowers.
ex: Native Americans introduced whites and slaves to several edible greens including marigold, milkweed, and pokeweed (Whit 2007).

s.def: A million pounds sterling.
Alternative form of Marigold (rubber glove for cleaning).
Having the color of marigolds, a bright yellowish-orange hue.

ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish marihuana, from mariguana. First attested in 1874 in the publications of Hubert Howe Bancroft. Altered by influence of a folk etymology involving the proper name María Juana (“Mary Jane”).

s.def: The inflorescence of the Cannabis sativa plant, smoked or ingested for euphoric effect.
ex: After smoking a bowl of that fine marijuana, they ate some brownies.
You could smell tea, weed, I mean marijuana, floating in the air, together with the chili beans and beer.
Sunday is 420 day, when lovers of marijuana get together to celebrate their fondness for weed.

s.def: The hemp plant itself, Cannabis sativa.

ety: From Portuguese marimba, via a Bantu source, perhaps Kimbundu marimba (“xylophone”).

s.def: A percussion instrument with African origins, similar to a xylophone with resonators, but much lower in range and darker in timbre.
ex: The default ringtone for your iPhone is a marimba sound, but if you'd like to change it, start at the Home screen, then tap on the Settings icon.

ety: From Latin marinus (“of the sea, marine”), by way of Italian marina and Spanish marina.

s.def: A harbour for small boats.
ex: It's a peaceful marina with not too many boats and yachts.
The marina was a mainstay of the neighborhood, and Mr. O’Rourke was known for staging salsa and merengue concerts.

ety: First attested in 1645; adapted from either French mariner or the earlier attested Italian marinare (“to pickle, marinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Late Latin marina (“brine, salt water”), short for aqua marina (“sea water”), from Latin marinus (“marine, of the sea”), from Latin mare (“the sea”) from Proto-Indo-European *móri (“the sea”).

s.def: To allow a sauce or flavoring mixture to absorb into something; to steep or soak something in a marinade to flavor or prepare it for cooking.
ex: You'll get a better flavour from the chicken if you marinate it first.
After the chicken has marinated for two hours, discard the remaining marinade.

s.def: To allow a substance to be absobed into the hair or scalp.
ex: oblucy: "vinegar... to marinate the scalp... oil... to lubricate the scalp..."
Let your scalp marinate while you shave.
Wrap a dry towel around the wet towel, and let your child's hair marinate for an hour.

s.def: Of a substance, to absorb into the hair or scalp.
ex: a rejuvenating oil you use to saturate your hair and let it marinate from 15 minutes to 2 hours

s.def: Especially of a haircut, to settle in and for one to get used to it.
ex: It's not a bad haircut! You just got to let it marinate!

s.def: Of ideas or feelings, to mentally develop over time.
Marinated.

ety: Recorded since c.1420 as Middle English marin, borrowed from Middle French marin, from Old French, from Latin marinus (“of the sea”), itself from mare (“sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri (“body of water, lake”) (cognate with Old English mere (“sea, lake, pool, pond”), Dutch meer, German Meer, all from Proto-Germanic *mari). The modern pronunciation is presumably due to the influence of modern French marine, feminine singular of marin.

s.def: of or pertaining to the sea
Belonging to or characteristic of the sea; existing or found in the sea; formed or produced by the sea.
Relating to or connected with the sea (in operation, scope, etc.), especially as pertains to shipping, a navy, or naval forces.
Used or adapted for use at sea.
Inhabiting the high seas; oceanic; pelagic. (distinguished from maritime or littoral)
Belonging to or situated at the seaside; maritime.
Of or concerning underwater conditions, either saltwater or freshwater ones, and the equipment used therein.
ex: This grease is suitable for marine use.

s.def: A soldier, normally a member of a marine corps, trained to serve on board or from a ship.
ex: He was a marine in World War II.

s.def: A marine corps.
ex: He fought with the Marines in World War II.

s.def: A painting representing some marine subject.
The branch of biology dealing with organisms that live in the sea.

ety: From Middle English mariner, maryner, from Anglo-Norman mariner, marinier, from Old French marinier, maronnier, from marin and Medieval Latin marinellus and marinarius (“sailor”), from marīnus (“marine”), from mare (“sea”) + -īnus (“-ine: forming adjectives”). Eclipsed Middle English marinel, marynell (“mariner, sailor”) from Old French marinel from the same sources. Equivalent to marine + -er.

s.def: Synonym of sailor, particularly one on a maritime vessel.
ex: My mariners, / Souls that have toil'd, and wrought, and thought with me—

ety: Borrowed from French marionnette. The word had originally meant a small statue of the Virgin Mary, then also a puppet of her used in religious theatrical presentations, finally generalised to any puppet.

s.def: A puppet, usually made of wood, which is animated by the pulling of strings.
ex: If you think we are worked by strings, Like a Japanese marionette, You don't understand these things: It is simply Court etiquette.

s.def: The buffel duck.
To control (somebody) as if they were a puppet; to manipulate.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

s.def: Pertaining to marriage.
ex: marital affairs
marital bliss
marital issues

s.def: Pertaining to a husband.
The rape of one's own spouse.
One of several discrete options describing a person's relationship with a significant other, such as single, married, divorced, widowed, civil union, domestic partnership, etc.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French maritime, from Latin maritimus.

s.def: Relating to or connected with the sea or its uses (as navigation, commerce, etc.).
ex: maritime law
maritime insurance
maritime risks

s.def: Bordering on the sea; living near the seacoast; coastal.
ex: the maritime states; a maritime people

s.def: Inhabiting the seashore; living coastwise; littoral. (distinguished from marine)
ex: a maritime bird or animal

s.def: Of or relating to a sailor or seaman; nautical.

ety: Borrowed from Ukrainian Маріу́поль (Mariúpolʹ), from Russian Мариу́поль (Mariúpolʹ), from Greek Μαριούπολη (Marioúpoli), from being named after the Virgin Mary, Empress Maria Feodorovna, the Crimean Greek city of Mariampol, from Μαρία (María) + πόλη (póli).

s.def: city
A city in Mariupol Raion, Donetsk Oblast, in eastern Ukraine, on the shore of the Sea of Azov, of the Black Sea.
ex: No incidents during passage across the Sea of Azov. At 1800 the formation continued passage to Mariupol as scheduled.

ety: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiōrana.

s.def: A herb of the mint family, Origanum majorana, having aromatic leaves.
ex: Among the ancients, especially the Romans, marjoram was known to have an aphrodisiac value.

s.def: The leaves of this plant, especially dried, used in flavouring food.

ety: From Middle English mark, merk, merke, from Old English mearc (“mark, sign, line of division; standard; boundary, limit, term, border; defined area, district, province”), from Proto-West Germanic *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary; boundary marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary, border”). Compare march. Cognates * Dutch mark, merk (“mark, brand”) * German Mark (“mark; borderland”), Marke (“mark, brand”) * Swedish mark (“mark, land, territory”) * Icelandic mark (“…

s.def: Score, grade, or related judgement.
ex: A mark for tardiness or for absence is considered by most pupils a disgrace, and strenuous efforts are made to avoid such a mark.

s.def: A half pound, a former English and Scottish currency equivalent to 13 shillings and fourpence and notionally equivalent to a mark of sterling silver.
ex: He had been made a royal counsellor, drawing a substantial annual salary of a hundred marks.

s.def: Boundary, land within a boundary.
ex: There dwells Théoden son of Thengel, King of the Mark of Rohan.

s.def: Characteristic, sign, indication for measurement; visible impression.
ex: Then she put before her face her poor crushed hands, which bore on their whiteness the red mark of the Count's terrible grip[…].

s.def: Target or indicator.
ex: A skilfull archer ought first to know the marke he aimeth at, and then apply his hand, his bow, his string, his arrow and his motion accordingly.

s.def: Attention.
ex: His last comment is particularly worthy of mark.

s.def: The female genitals.
ex: A mark saies my Lady. Let the mark haue a prick in't, to meate at, if it may be.

s.def: A catch of the ball directly from a kick of 10 metres or more without having been touched in transit, resulting in a free kick.
Limit or standard of action or fact.
ex: to be within the mark
to come up to the mark

s.def: To leave a mark (often an undesirable or unwanted one) on (something).
ex: See where this pencil has marked the paper.
The floor was marked with wine and blood.
Those Wheels returning ne’er shall mark the Plain;

s.def: Listen to me; used before or after a statement one wishes to emphasize, especially a prediction.

ety: From mark (“sign, characteristic, visible impression”) + -ed. Less common disyllabic pronunciation (/ˈmɑː.kɪd/) is likely an analogy derived from markedness (explaining its restriction to sense 2).

s.def: Having a visible or identifying mark.
Clearly evident; noticeable; conspicuous.
ex: The eighth century BC saw a marked increase in the general wealth of Cyprus.
In ancient times, the Romans imported truffles, credited with marked aphrodisiac virtue, from Libya as well as Greece.
The drop in merchandise and mineral receipts again reflects the fall in steel output, most marked in the North-East; […].

s.def: Distinguished by a positive feature.
ex: "Young" is the marked element of the old/young pair, since the usual way of asking someone's age is "How old are you?".

s.def: Singled out; suspicious; treated with hostility; the object of vengeance.
ex: A marked man.

s.def: In police livery, as opposed to unmarked. (of a police vehicle)
simple past and past participle of mark

ety: Etymology tree English mark Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English marker From mark + -er.

s.def: Someone or something that creates marks, particularly
ex: Don't use the permanent marker on the whiteboard.

s.def: Someone or something used to mark a position or amount, particularly
ex: Board member Phillip Carlson […] said he considers [the election of] Brading to be a marker for the distance the gay and lesbian community has come.

s.def: A personal favor owed to someone, whether written or not.
ex: We may not be able to do this alone. Maybe it’s time to call in some of our markers.

s.def: A player employed by a private club to compete against members.
ex: I played seven sets of doubles with Mitchell (the second best player in Ceylon) and David, the native marker.

s.def: A point, unit of scoring in a game or competition.
Someone who assigns marks on tests, examinations, etc.; a grader.
ex: So, in his end of term report, what marks would Brown award himself for his time at TfL? "8½," he replies. Why? "I'm a hard marker! […]

s.def: The ink marks or residue of a felt-tipped pen.
ex: Susie got marker all over the walls.

s.def: A formal certification that a company was the first to approach a competition authority to reveal the existence of a cartel, generally entitling it to greater leniency during the cartel's dissolution and punishment.
A player on defense used to mark one or more offensive players.
To mark or write on (something) using a marker
ex: On one page someone has markered: "Remember, you are your own best thing."

s.def: A pen, often with a thick tip made of felt.

ety: From Middle English market, from late Old English market (“market”) and Anglo-Norman markiet (Old French marchié); all ultimately from Latin mercātus (“trade, market”), from mercor (“to trade, deal in, buy”), itself derived from merx (“wares, merchandise”). Doublet of mart. Cognate with West Frisian merk (“market”), Dutch markt, German Markt, Danish and Norwegian marked (“market”), Faroese and Icelandic markaður (“market”), Swedish marknad (“market”).

s.def: A relatively spacious outdoor or covered site where traders set up stalls, either temporarily or permanently or semi-permanently, and buyers browse the merchandise.
ex: This site on North Street used to be the market, until it was redeveloped.

s.def: A group of potential or current customers for one's product.
ex: We believe that the market for the new widget will be the older homeowner.
Senior citizens are our core market at present, and we can't afford to alienate them as we explore other markets.
There is a third thing to be considered: how a market can be created for produce, or how production can be limited to the capacities of the market.

s.def: To make (products or services) available for sale and promote them.
ex: We plan to market an ecology model by next quarter.

s.def: A gathering of people for the purchase and sale of merchandise, often periodic at a set time.
ex: The right to hold a weekly market was an invaluable privilege not given to all towns in the Middle Ages.
There's a market every Thursday and Saturday in the town square.
The market is a process, actuated by the interplay of the actions of the various individuals cooperating under the division of labor.

s.def: Any physical store selling groceries, such as a grocery store or convenience store.
ex: Stop by the market on your way home and pick up some milk.

s.def: A geographical area or region where a certain commercial demand exists.
ex: Foreign markets were lost as our currency rose versus their valuta.

s.def: A formally organized, sometimes monopolistic, system of trading in specified goods or effects.
ex: The stock market ceased to be monopolized by the paper-shuffling national stock exchanges with the advent of Internet markets.

s.def: The sum total traded in a process of individuals trading for certain commodities.
The price for which a thing is sold in a market; hence, value or worth; market value.
ex: Q: What's the market on such a thing, nowadays? A: Oh, no less than forty, I should reckon.
What is a man If his chief good and market of his time Be but to sleep and feed?

s.def: To promote for or as if for sale.
An economy in which goods and services are exchanged in a market, as opposed to a state-controlled economy.

ety: Etymology tree English market Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English marketable From market + -able.

s.def: Capable of being marketed.
ex: The quality and scarcity ensured that the product was eminently marketable.

s.def: Saleable (of goods) or employable (of people).
Able to be converted into cash quickly, but at a price that is determined by the market in that commodity

ety: By surface analysis, market + -ing.

s.def: present participle and gerund of market
The promotion, distribution and selling of a product or service; the work of a marketer; includes market research and advertising.
ex: a bachelor's degree in marketing

s.def: Buying and/or selling in a market (street market or market fair).
ex: [Wife to husband:] I'm going out to do my marketing – keep out of the kitchen, while I'm gone.

ety: From Middle English marking, merking, merkunge, from Old English mearcung, from Proto-West Germanic *markungu, equivalent to mark + -ing.

s.def: The action of marking.
ex: The Seasiders equalised soon after when Gary Taylor-Fletcher made the most of slack marking to slot home.

s.def: A mark.
The characteristic colouration and patterning of an animal.
A symbol or set of letters used to identify the type or identity of an object.
ex: The markings on the plane identified it as belonging to law enforcement.

s.def: Any configuration of a Petri net with a number of marks or tokens distributed across it.
present participle and gerund of mark
A discrete-time stochastic process containing a Markov property.

ety: Etymology tree English mark English -s- Proto-Indo-European *mon- Proto-Germanic *mann- Proto-West Germanic *mann Old English mann Middle English man English man English marksman From mark + -s- + man.

s.def: A man or person skilled at hitting targets, as with a firearm, bow, or thrown object.
Goalscorer.

ety: Deverbal from mark up.

s.def: An increase in price.
ex: There will be a markup on those products next week; better buy them now.

s.def: The percentage or amount by which a seller hikes up their buy-in price when determining their selling price.
ex: You don’t make much money selling gas because the markup is so low.

s.def: The notation that is used to indicate the meaning of the elements in an electronic document, or to dictate how text should be displayed.
ex: For example, a filename of “home.html” would be appropriate for an ASCII/text file containing HTML markup.
You can display the icon on any site you offer your software for download using the following markup[…]

s.def: The process by which proposed legislation is debated and amended.

ety: From Middle English marle, from Old French marle, from Late Latin margila, diminutive of marga (“marl”). Doublet of marla.

s.def: A mixed earthy substance, consisting of carbonate of lime, clay, and possibly sand, in very variable proportions, and accordingly designated as calcareous, clayey, or sandy.
ex: ... uneasie steps / Over the burning Marle, not like those steps / On Heavens Azure...
Important marl and marine-shell deposits are worked in Michigan, Virginia, and Florida.
The surroundings were unearthly. It was not a fish setting—only bare rock, no trees, pungent sagebrush, and marl dust floating when a truck passed.

s.def: To cover (the ground) with marl (noun sense).
To cover, as part of a rope, with marline, marking a peculiar hitch at each turn to prevent unwinding.
A species of bandicoot, Perameles myosurus, of southern Western Australia.

ety: From Middle English merlin, from Middle Low German marling, from Middle Dutch marlijn (“cord”), from marlen (“secure, fasten”), frequentative of maren (“to moor”), from Proto-Germanic *mairōną (“to moor, fasten to”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-.

s.def: A light all-purpose cord commonly used to bind the end of a larger rope, to prevent fraying.
Twine used similarly.
To wind marline around.
ex: to marline a rope

s.def: Alternative spelling of marlinspike.

ety: From marl + -ite.

s.def: A wind-resistant variety of marl.
ex: Marlites […]are not disintegrated by exposure to the atmosphere, at least in six years.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (“quince jam”), from marmelo (“quince”), from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον (melímēlon), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). A false folk etymology claims that this comes from the French phrase “Marie est malade” (“Mary is ill”), referring to Mary, Queen of Scots, falling ill and being given marmalade to feel better.

s.def: A kind of jam made with citrus fruit, distinguished by being made slightly bitter by the addition of the peel and by partial caramelisation during manufacture. Most commonly made with Seville oranges, and usually qualified by the name of the fruit when made with other types of fruit.
ex: lime marmalade
thick cut marmalade

s.def: Quince jam.
A cat having orange- or ginger-colored fur.
ex: We breed our marmalades for a modern taste. Gingers can be tiger-striped, splotched, or all one shade in a choice of spicy colors; […]

s.def: To spread marmalade on.

ety: The name Marmara ultimately derives from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”), referring to the island’s famous marble deposits.

s.def: An island of Turkey in the Sea of Marmara.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French marmouset (“a gargoyle; a small child”), probably from marmouser (“to mumble”), of imitative origin.

s.def: Any small monkey, now specifically a Central and South American monkey of the genera Callithrix, Mico, Cebuella, and Callibella, with claws instead of nails, and a rather primitive layout.
A hideous figure; a grotesque.
An unappealing or foolish man.

ety: From Middle French marmotte, from Old French marmotte; further etymology uncertain, possibly from a Gallo-Romance base *marm- (“to mumble; to murmur”) (referring to the sound made by the marmot when eating; possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *mur- (whence murmur) and ultimately imitative; compare also French marmot and marmonner) + Middle French -otte (diminutive suffix). Akin to French marmotte, Italian marmotta, Engadin Romansh murmont, Old High German *murmento (dialectal German Murment…

s.def: Any of several large ground-dwelling rodents of the genera Marmota and Cynomys in the squirrel family.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Maron, from Ancient Greek Μάρων (Márōn), from Classical Syriac ܡܪܘܢ (mārūn). Compare Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܡܪܐ (mar, “lord, master”).

s.def: Syriac saint, whose followers moved to Mount Lebanon from northern Syria, establishing the Maronite Church.

ety: From Maron + -ite.

s.def: Of or pertaining to Saint Maron or the Maronite Church.
A member of the Maronite Church.
A Syriac Eastern Catholic particular church (sui juris), founded by St Maron, in full communion with the Holy See and the rest of the Catholic Church.

ety: From French marron (“feral; fugitive”, adjective), from Spanish cimarrón (“fugitive, wild, feral”); see that entry for more.

s.def: An escaped black slave of the Caribbean and the Americas or a descendant of such a person.
A castaway; a person who has been marooned (abandoned).
Associated with Maroon culture, communities or peoples.
To abandon in a remote, desolate place, as on a desert island.
A rich dark red, somewhat brownish, color.
Of a dark red or reddish-brown color.
A rocket-propelled firework or skyrocket, often one used as a signal (for example, to summon the crew of a lifeboat or warn of an air raid).
An idiot; a fool.
ex: At least, I would not be sleeping that night. Why did I have that espresso? What a maroon!

ety: From marquise, from French marquise. Ultimately from same root as march (“border country”), margin (“edge”). Ultimately cognate with marque.

s.def: A projecting canopy over an entrance, especially one with a sign that displays the name of the establishment or other information of it.
A large tent with open sides, used for outdoors entertainment.
Lights that turn on and off in sequence, or scrolling text, as these are common elements on a marquee.
An illuminated panel that appears above the screen/playfield of an arcade game, typically displaying the game's title and manufacturer.
A banner on a web page displaying text that scrolls horizontally.
In graphical editing software, a special selection tool, used to highlight a portion of an image.
ex: Rectangular Marquee Tool

s.def: Most famous; preeminent.
ex: Without adoubt, Brees was a marquee player.
Even after a marquee player is traded, he can have a lasting impact on the franchise for which he made his mark.
Fashion Week is a marquee event providing a consolidated platform for the display of high-quality designer fashion.

s.def: To select (an object or region) with the marquee selection tool.
To display text prominently at the top, as in a video.
ex: The text was marqueed at the end of the presentation.

s.def: a group of volcanic islands in French Polynesia

ety: See marquis for etymology. Note also that marquess is very unusual in the English language in that it ends in -ess but is a masculine term. The title is granted only to males (the female equivalent is marchioness).

s.def: A title of nobility for a man ranking beneath a duke and above an earl (count).
Synonym of marchioness, a female marquess.
ex: Anne Boleyn was created Marquess of Pembroke in 1532

ety: From Middle French marqueterie.

s.def: A decorative technique in which veneers of wood, ivory, metal etc. are inlaid into a wooden surface to form intricate designs.
ex: strawen marquetry

s.def: An example of this work.

ety: From Middle English markis, from Old French markis, marchis, from Late Latin marchensis, from Old High German marcha and Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”). Meaning is “lord of the march”, in sense of march (“border country”).

s.def: A nobleman in England, France, and Germany, of a rank next below that of duke, but above a count. Originally, the marquis was an officer whose duty was to guard the marches or frontiers of the kingdom. The office has ceased, and the name is now a mere title conferred by letters patent or letters cl…
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the Asian genus Bassarona (or Euthalia).

ety: From marquis + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it), on the pattern of Middle French marquisat, Italian marchesato.

s.def: The territory held by a marquis, margrave or marchioness.
The state or rank of a marquis.
ex: he has Mary Boleyn's word for it that the marquisate has bought Henry only the right to caress her sister's inner thigh.

ety: Borrowed from French marquise.

s.def: A marchioness, especially one who is French.

ety: From Mary + Magdalene; from Middle English Marie Magdaleyn, Marie Magdeleyne, Marye Maudelen, Marye Maudeleyne, Marie Mawdeleyn, Mary Maudelen, Mary Mawdelayn, from Old French Marie Madelaine and Latin Marīa Magdalēna.

ety: From Mary + -land. Named after Henrietta Maria of France, the wife of Charles I of England.

ety: From French masculinité, from Old French, equivalent to masculine + -ity. Earlier in same sense was masculineness.

ety: From Middle English mash, from Old English mǣsċ, māsċ, māx, from Proto-Germanic *maiskaz, *maiskō (“mixture, mash”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyǵ-, *meyḱ- (“to mix”). ety: Borrowed from Middle French masque (“a covering to hide or protect the face”), from Italian maschera (“mask, disguise”), from (a byform of, see it for more) Medieval Latin masca, mascha, a borrowing of Proto-West Germanic *maskā, from which English mesh and mask (“mesh”) (below at Etymology 2) are inherited.
