ety: From master + piece, a calque of Dutch meesterstuk or German Meisterstück (“masterpiece”). Piecewise doublet of maestropiece and masterstick. Compare also journeyman's piece.

ety: Of Latin origin, via or reinforced by Old French matriarche, from Latin māter (“mother”) + -archa, -arches, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχός (arkhós, “chief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”). By surface analysis, matri- + -arch.

ety: Via French from Latin maximum.

ex: This is the fundamental principle of good legislation. It is the art of conducting a nation to the maximum of happiness and the minimum of misery

s.def: The greatest value of a set or other mathematical structure, especially the global maximum or a local maximum of a function.
An upper bound of a set which is also an element of that set.
The largest value of a batch or sample or the upper bound of a probability distribution.
A 147 break; the highest possible break.
A score of 180 with three darts.
A scoring shot for 6 runs.
maximum security
ex: I just got out of maximum where I did 4 months for an arguent I had in the serving area.

s.def: To the highest degree.
ex: Use the proper dose for the maximum effect.
Each Piccadilly Line train consists of seven cars, the construction of the stations below ground making this the maximum length.

ety: From Middle English magen, mauen, mawe, mawen, mayen, maȝen, mouin, mow, mowen, moȝen, mugen, from Old English magan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”). Cognates Cognate with Scots mey (“may”), Yola ma, maa, mai, mey, mye (“may”), North Frisian mai, mei, mooge (“like to, would”), West Frisian meie (“may; to like”), Alemannic German möge (“may; can”), Bavarian megn (“to…

s.def: To be strong; to have power (over).
To be able; can.
ex: But many times[…]we give way to passions we may resist and will not.

s.def: To be able to go.
To have permission to, be allowed. Used in granting permission and in questions to make polite requests.
ex: you may smoke outside
may I sit there?
May we request that patrons kindly take their seats.

s.def: Granting the admissibility of a supposition, in a way that can be semantically either subjunctive or indicative.
ex: he may be lying
Schrödinger's cat may or may not be in the box.
A female crocodile may lay up to forty eggs. [Typical occurrence.]

s.def: Expressing a wish (with present subjunctive effect).
ex: may you win; may the weather be sunny; long may your reign last
Let us pray that peace may soon return to our war-torn homeland.
May I never miss the thrill of being near you

s.def: Used in modesty, courtesy, or concession, or to soften a question or remark.
ex: How old may Phillis be, you ask, / Whose Beauty thus all Hearts engages.

s.def: The hawthorn bush or its blossoms.
ex: The fire from Lindfield was coming down the grassy hillside to the right between the hedges of may.

s.def: To gather may, or flowers in general.
ex: In valleys green and still / Where lovers wander maying

s.def: To celebrate May Day.

s.def: The fifth month of the Gregorian calendar, following April and preceding June.
ex: Holonyms: calendar year; year
All in the merry month of May, / When green leaves they was springing, / This young man on his death-bed lay, / For the love of Barbara Allen.

s.def: abbreviation of the month above
A female given name, usually pet name for Mary and Margaret, reinforced by the month and plant meaning.
A surname from Middle English.
A number of places in the United States:
Labour Day, the first day of May, a worldwide workers' holiday.
The first day of May, a festival celebrating the beginning of the spring season; originally, and still among neopagans, a fertility celebration.

w: may the Force be with you
ety: From the Star Wars film franchise, in which "the Force" is an omnipresent energy that can influence events and may be harnessed by gifted individuals.

s.def: Used to wish someone luck with a difficult endeavor.

ant: may the Force be without you
may the Force not be with you

ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit माया (māyā).

s.def: Magic; supernatural power as held by the gods.
The power by which the universe is made to appear; the illusion of the phenomenal world, as opposed to its true or spiritual reality.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish maya, from Yucatec Maya mayab (“flat”) or Yucatec Maya maaya, a self-designation of the northern Maya for themselves, in the form maya’ found in compounds and phrases e.g. maya’ wíinik (“Maya man”).

s.def: The Yucatec Maya language.
Any of the other various Mayan languages.

ety: From an ellipsis of Middle English it may be, equivalent to may + be. Compare mayhap.

s.def: Certainly.
ex: Maybe not the best idea.

s.def: Perhaps, possibly.
ex: A small extra effort now can maybe save you much work later.
Maybe I was imagining it, but I could swear that the dog understood what I was saying.

s.def: Perhaps that is true (expressing no commitment to a decision or a neutral viewpoint to a statement).
ex: Okay. See you later, maybe. — Maybe I’ll see you later.

s.def: Possible; uncertain.
Something that is possibly true.
An answer that shows neither agreement nor disagreement.
ex: The results of the poll were inconclusive. We got two yeses, three nos, and four maybes.

s.def: A future event that may or may not happen.
ex: About your raise: it's a big maybe.

ety: From the distress signal mayday, from French m'aider, short for Venez m'aider! (“Come to help me!”). The term was conceived in the early 1920s by Frederick Stanley Mockford, officer-in-charge of radio at Croydon Airport in England. He had been asked to think of a word that would indicate distress and would easily be understood by all pilots and ground staff in an emergency. Since much of the air traffic at the time was between Croydon and Le Bourget Airport in Paris, he proposed the term "mayda…

s.def: An international distress signal used by shipping and aircraft.
ex: "Odd that she hasn't sent out a Mayday." "That is curious. Her radio must be disabled."

ety: From May + flower.

s.def: Any of several plants that flower in May - especially the hawthorn (in Britain) and the trailing arbutus (in the US).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂sder.? Latin Maia Latin -us Latin Maiusder. Old French maibor. Middle English May English May English fly English mayfly From May (“fifth month”) + fly (“flying insect”). Compare Saterland Frisian Moaifljooge (“blowfly”).

s.def: Any of the many fragile insects of the order Ephemeroptera that develop in fresh water and live very briefly as winged adults.
ex: While some animals take months to reproduce, mayfly need just one perfect day.
[A] silver fish clooped a lazy arc downstream, not really caring that the mayfly were out of reach; […]
Mayflies are fragile, gossamer-winged insects that arise from bodies of water and often swarm in great numbers.

s.def: Characterized by a short duration; short-lived.

ety: From the phrase “it may hap”.

s.def: Maybe; perhaps; possibly; perchance.
ex: I'm one that has spoken to a King, I am: mayhap you'll never see such another […]
Then I heard the rush, the stamping and neighing, of some young mares, pasturing there, as they raced to and fro, bewildered or mayhap only in play.
"If you're after some money," said the millionaire, "move that cat out of the way." Catweazle shook his head. "Mayhap 'tis a fetch."

ety: The noun is derived from Late Middle English mayehem, maihem, a late form of maym, maim (“disfigurement, injury, mutilation; disfigured person”) (whence modern English maim (noun)), from Anglo-Norman mahaim, mahainne (“mutilation”), and Old French mehaing, meshaing (“bodily harm, loss of limb”). The verb is partly: * from Late Middle English mahaym, maheyme, a late form of maimen, maymen (“to injure seriously, mutilate, maim; to damage; to destroy; to afflict with disease; to dispossess”) (when…

s.def: Often preceded by to cause or make: great confusion, destruction, disorder, or trouble; chaos, turmoil; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: In all the mayhem, some children were separated from their parents.
What if the legendary hero Robin Hood had been born into the mayhem of the 20th century?
We terrified the mare and foal. / The fox stood still and far too bold. / So we strung him up, brush neatly folded— / Mayhem, maybe.

s.def: The criminal offence of maiming (“seriously wounding”) a person such that their ability to defend or protect themselves is weakened or completely removed; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: to commit mayhem

s.def: The criminal offence of maiming a person by depriving them of the use of any of their limbs.
Violent conduct, especially the violent infliction of injury on a person or thing.
ex: The fighting dogs created mayhem in the flower beds.

s.def: To commit the criminal offence of mayhem (noun sense 1) on (someone); to maim.
To violently inflict injury on (someone); to injure, to wound.

ety: Transliteration of Russian Майко́п (Majkóp).

s.def: The capital and largest city of Adygea, Russia.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French mayonnaise, possibly named after the city of Maó (Mahón in Spanish), Minorca, whence the recipe was brought back to France. Compare Spanish mahonesa. Alternative suggested origins include the city of Bayonne (bayonnaise); the Duke of Mayenne and the words manier (“to handle”) in French or moyeu (“eye yolk”) in Old French.

s.def: dressing
A dressing made from vegetable oil, raw egg yolks, vinegar or lemon juice, and seasoning, used on salads, with French fries, in sandwiches, etc.
ex: There are 250 foods, including mayonnaise, cheese and cocoa, that don't list ingredients at all.
The oils in store-bought mayonnaise range from olive oil to sunflower oil to safflower oil and some less desirable oils!
Most store-bought mayonnaise contains ingredients (vinegar, lemonjuice, and salt) that actually slow bacterial growth

s.def: Any cold dish with that dressing as an ingredient.
ex: We served a lobster mayonnaise as a starter.

s.def: Any cream, for example for moisturizing the face or conditioning the hair, for which the base is egg yolks and oil.
ex: hair mayonnaise
facial mayonnaise

s.def: Exaggeration.
To cover or season with mayonnaise.
ex: I thought of mayonnaising her racket handle or substituting it for sunblock, but decided against it.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s Proto-Indo-European *-yōs Proto-Indo-European *méǵyōs Proto-Italic *majjōs Latin maior Old French mairebor. Middle English maire English mayor From Middle English maire, from Old French maire (“head of a city or town government”), a substantivation of Old French maire (“greater”), from Latin maior (“bigger, greater, superior”), comparative of magnus (“big, great”). Doublet of major. Cognate with Old High German meior (“estate manager, steward, bailiff”…

s.def: leader of a city
The chief executive of the municipal government of a city, borough, etc., formerly (historical) usually appointed as a caretaker by European royal courts but now usually appointed or elected locally.
ex: The office of mayor has been the tomb of many political ambitions.
When the burdens of the Presidency seem unusually heavy, I always remind myself that it could be worse—I could be a mayor of a city instead.

s.def: Ellipsis of mayor of the palace, the royal stewards of the Frankish Empire.
Synonym of mair, various former officials in the Kingdom of Scotland.
A member of a city council.
A high justice, an important judge.
A largely ceremonial position in some municipal governments that presides over the city council while a contracted city manager holds actual executive power.
A local VIP, a muckamuck or big shot reckoned to lead some local group.
ex: In some parts the burlesque civic official was designated ‘Mayor of the Pig Market’.
The Mayor of Castro Street, that was Harvey's unofficial title.

ety: Borrowed from Persian مازندران (mâzandarân, literally “the gate or the valley of the giants”).

A land mentioned in Shahnameh and Avesta.

ety: From Middle English mase, from Middle English masen (“to perplex, bewilder”); or perhaps from Old English *mæs (“delusion, bewilderment”); akin to Old English āmasian (“to perplex, confound”), Icelandic masa (“to chatter”). More at amaze.

s.def: A labyrinth; a puzzle consisting of a complicated network of paths or passages, the aim of which is to find one's way through.
Something made up of many confused or conflicting elements; a tangle.

s.def: A confusion of thought; a state of bewilderment.
To amaze, astonish, bewilder.

s.def: To daze or stupefy.
ex: mazed […] by the eyes of the crowd
She rowed back alone, the simple soul that was in her forwandered and mazed with excess of joy.

ety: Via German Mazurka and Russian мазу́рка (mazúrka), from Polish mazurek (“dance of the Masurian”), the Masurians being the inhabitants of Mazowsze (compare Medieval Latin Mazovia), an ancient cultural region in east-central Poland.

s.def: A traditional Polish folk dance in triple time, usually moderately fast, containing a heavy accent on the third beat and occasionally the second beat.
A classical musical composition inspired by the folk dance and conforming in some respects to its form, particularly as popularized by Chopin.
A figure skating move that combines elements of the toe loop and bunny-hop.

ety: From Middle English me, from Old English mē (“me”, originally dative, but later also accusative, supplanting accusative mec), from Proto-West Germanic *miʀ, from Proto-Germanic *miz (“me”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁me- (“me”). Cognate with Scots me, North Frisian me, Saterland Frisian mie, Dutch me, mij, Low German mi, German mir (dative only), Icelandic mér (also still dative), Latin mē, Ancient Greek μέ (mé), ἐμέ (emé), Sanskrit मा (mā), all meaning “me”.

s.def: The first-person singular, as the object (of a verb, preposition, etc).
ex: Can you hear me?
He gave me this.

s.def: I, the first-person singular, as the subject.

s.def: Used in isolation or apposition, or (sometimes proscribed) as the complement of the copula (be).

Who said that? —(It was) not me.

ety: From the Latin phrase meā culpā (“through my fault”), ablative case of mea culpa (“my fault, guilt”), taken from the Confiteor, a traditional penitential prayer in Western Christianity.

ety: From Middle English mede, from Old English medu, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey; honey wine”). A meadow.

Farewel ye crystal streams, that pass Thro’ fragrant meads of verdant grass:
But any man that walks the mead, In bud, or blade, or bloom, may find, According as his humours lead, A meaning suited to his mind.

ety: From Middle English medowe, medewe, medwe (also mede > Modern English mead), from Old English mǣdwe, inflected form of mǣd (see mead), from Proto-Germanic *mēdwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂met- (“to mow, reap”), enlargement of *h₂meh₁-. s.def: Low land covered with coarse grass or rank herbage near rivers and in marshy places by the sea.

Any grass of the genus Poa.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see meadow, grass. Any grass that thrives in the moist conditions of meadows.
A standardized dialect of the Mari language used mainly in the European part of the Russian Federation.

ety: From meadow + lark.

s.def: The meadow pipit (Anthus pratensis).
Any of several songbirds of the genera Sturnella and Leistes, native to the Americas.
ex: But the meadowlark acts by instinct, not by plan.
Closing it behind me and away I do run / To the meadow where the meadowlark is singing in the trees
Your voice is like a meadowlark / But your heart is like an ocean / Mysterious and dark

ety: From meadow + rue.

ety: From Middle English megre, from Anglo-Norman megre, Old French maigre, from Latin macer, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Akin, through the Indo-European root, to Old English mæġer (“meager, lean”), West Frisian meager (“meager”), Dutch mager (“meager”), German mager, Old Norse magr whence the Icelandic magur, Norwegian Bokmål mager and Danish mager. Poor, deficient or inferior in amount, quality or extent
ex: A meager piece of cake in one bite.

Dry and harsh to the touch (e.g., as chalk).
To make lean.

ety: From Middle English mel, from Old English mǣl (“measure, time, occasion, set time, time for eating, meal”), from Proto-West Germanic *māl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlą, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognate with West Frisian miel, Dutch maal (“meal, time, occurrence”), German Mal (“time”), Mahl (“meal”), Norwegian Bokmål mål (“meal”), Swedish mål (“meal”); and (from Proto-Indo-European) with Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure”), Latin mensus, Russian ме́ра (méra, “measure”),…

s.def: Food that is prepared and eaten, usually at a specific time, and usually in a comparatively large quantity.
ex: Breakfast is the morning meal, lunch is the noon meal, and dinner, or supper, is the evening meal.
c1450, Secreta Secretorumː He that will cast meal upon meal is not able to have (a) long life.
c1500, The King and the Hermitː I have been there and taken deal / And have had many (a) merry meal.

s.def: The ground-up edible part of various grains, used as a basis of food or feed; either flour or a coarser blend than flour (usage varies).
Food served or eaten as a repast.
ex: This is the meal pleasantly set . . . . this is the meat and drink for natural hunger, / It is for the wicked just the same as the righteous . . . .

s.def: A break taken by a police officer in order to eat.
ex: They [tape recorders] can be turned off while officers are on meal or in the car to protect their private conversations […]
“I was on meal when I heard the call on the radio and recognized the address. What the hell?”

s.def: A time or an occasion.
ex: Ye wolde wepe at every mele; But for my sone wepe ye never a dele. You would weep at every meal, but for my son you never weep a deal.

a1450, Henry Lovelich, Merlinː Also soon as the dragons together feal, betwixt them shall begin a sorry meal.

s.def: Any of various similarly granular materials prepared from other sources, such as bones or wood.
Any of various other granular or powdery materials, either ground by humans or occurring in nature, named figuratively after a resemblance to grain meal.
To yield or be plentiful in meal.
A speck or spot.
A part; a fragment; a portion.
Someone or something that provides income or livelihood, especially as an exploited source.
ex: I don't enjoy this job, but it is my meal ticket.

s.def: A ticket or voucher that can be exchanged for food.
ex: Volunteers are provided with a meal ticket for every four hours of service.

ety: From Middle English meeltime, from Old English mǣltīma (“mealtime”), equivalent to meal + time. Compare mealtide, Old English mǣltīd (“mealtime”), Dutch maaltijd (“meal”), German Mahlzeit (“meal, mealtime”), Danish måltid (“meal, mealtime”), Icelandic máltíð (“meal”), Icelandic matmálstími (“mealtime”).

s.def: The appointed time at which a meal is served or eaten.
ex: My youngest son has a special cry for mealtimes.

ety: From meal + worm.

s.def: The larval stage of the mealworm beetle (Tenebrio molitor), a species of darkling beetle.
ex: We buy mealworms to supplement our chickens' feed ration, and they do some scratching in the yard to find other bugs too.

s.def: This or any other larva that looks similar and is found in similar circumstances (i.e., in meal, in flour, in food, in the pantry, in feed, in the feedroom), such as the larva of a mealmoth (flour moth).
ex: Near-synonym: waxworm
They'd seen a few mealmoths and mealworms in recent days, and then they figured out that the cornflakes in the pantry were the source of the problem.

ety: From meal + worm + beetle.

s.def: A darkling beetle (or darkening beetle) of species Tenebrio molitor, in the family Tenebrionidae, whose larvae (mealworms) are typically used as a food source for reptile, fish, and avian pets.

ety: From meal + -y. Cognate with German mehlig.

s.def: Resembling meal (the foodstuff).
ex: Below the hole the mice made in the woodwork was a pile of mealy sawdust.

s.def: Of the pale yellow color of a canary.
A canary of a pale yellow color.
Alternative form of mealy-mouthed.

ety: From Middle English menen (“to intend; remember; lament; comfort”), from Old English mǣnan (“to mean, complain”), Proto-West Germanic *mainijan, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; complain”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyn- (“to think”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meyno-, extended form of Proto-Indo-European *mey-. Germanic cognates include West Frisian miene (“to deem, think”) (Old Frisian mēna (“to signify”)), Dutch menen (“to believe, think, mean”) (Middle Dutch menen…

s.def: To intend.
ex: I didn't mean to knock your tooth out.
I mean to go to Arévalo in Spain this summer; I’ve been meaning to tell you for weeks, but I’ve just found the time.
I meant to take the car in for a smog check, but it slipped my mind.

s.def: To convey (a meaning).
ex: The sky is red this morning—does that mean we're in for a storm?

s.def: To have conviction in (something said or expressed); to be sincere in (what one says).
ex: Does she really mean what she said to him last night?
Say what you mean and mean what you say.

s.def: To cause or produce (a given result); to bring about (a given result).
ex: One faltering step means certain death.
This breakthrough will mean that we spend less on electricity bills.

s.def: to intend; plan on doing
Ungenerous; stingy; tight-fisted.
ex: He's so mean. I've never seen him spend so much as five pounds on presents for his children.

s.def: A method or course of action used to achieve some result.
ex: To say truth, it is a meane full of uncertainty and danger.
You may be able, by this mean, to review your own scientific acquirements.
Philosophical doubt is not an end, but a mean.

s.def: To be of some level of importance.
ex: That little dog meant everything to me.
Formality and titles mean nothing in their circle.

s.def: To lament.
ex: All the tyme of his sickness he never said, “Alace!” or meaned any pain, whilk was marvellous. Never man died in greater peace of mind or body.
“ If you should die for me, sir knight, “ There’s few for you will mane, “ For many a better has died for me, “ Whose graves are growing green.

s.def: Hearty; spicy.

ety: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

s.def: One of the turns of a winding, crooked, or involved course.
ex: the meanders of an old river, or of the veins and arteries in the body

s.def: One of a series of regular sinuous curves, bends, loops, turns, or windings in the channel of a river, stream, or other watercourse
A tortuous or winding journey.
Synonym of Greek key, a decorative border; fretwork.
ex: The scales are conceived of as meander fretwork; but I do not know whether, for this reason, this fish is associated with thunder.

s.def: A self-avoiding closed curve which intersects a line a number of times.

To wind or turn in a course or passage
ex: The stream meandered through the valley.

s.def: To be intricate.
ex: His speech meandered through various topics.

s.def: To wind, turn, or twist; to make flexuous.
ex: Her labyrinth-like ţurns, and mad meander'd trace[…]

ety: From Middle English mening, menyng, equivalent to mean + -ing. Cognate with Scots mening (“intent, purpose, sense, meaning”), West Frisian miening (“opinion, mind”), Dutch mening (“view, opinion, judgement”), German Meinung (“opinion, view, mind, idea”), Danish and Swedish mening (“meaning, sense, sentence, opinion”), Icelandic meining (“meaning”).

s.def: symbolic value of something
significance of a thing, as "the meaning of life"
The denotation, referent, or idea connected with a word, expression, or symbol.
The connotation associated with a word, expression, or symbol.
The purpose, value, or significance (of something) beyond the fact of that thing's existence.
ex: Near-synonyms: meaningfulness, point, purpose, significance, use
the meaning of life

s.def: Intention.
ex: It was their meaning to take what they needed by strong hand.

s.def: present participle and gerund of mean

Proto-Italic *keiwis Latin ceivis Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Proto-Italic *-tāts Latin -tās Latin ceivitās Late Latin cīvitātem (city) Old French citetbor. Middle English cite English city English megacity From mega- + city.

s.def: A very large city; a megalopolis, typically one with population over 10 million.
ex: Why, for instance, do water users in a megacity like Lagos not pay an extra charge to get cesspits pumped out?

ety: PIE word *méǵh₂s From mega- (prefix meaning ‘very large, great’) + -lith (suffix meaning ‘stone’), a back-formation from megalithic probably modelled after monolith. from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”)

s.def: A large stone slab making up a prehistoric monument, or part of such a monument.
A prehistoric monument made up of one or more large stones.
A large stone or block of stone used in the construction of a modern structure.

ety: From megalo- + -cephaly.

s.def: Synonym of macrencephaly

ety: Borrowed from French mégalomanie; equivalent to megalo- + -mania.

s.def: A psychopathological condition characterized by delusional fantasies of wealth, power, or omnipotence.
Narcissistic personality disorder.
An obsession with grandiose or extravagant things or actions.

ety: By surface analysis, megalomania + -ac, or, by surface analysis, megalo- + -maniac.

s.def: One affected with or exhibiting megalomania.
Of, exhibiting, or affected with megalomania.

ety: From megalo- (“great”) + -polis (“city”).

s.def: A large conurbation, where two or more large cities have sprawled outward to meet, forming something larger than a normal metropolis.
ex: The Eastern Seaboard megalopolis extends from New Hampshire to Alexandria, VA.

ety: From megalo- + -saur.

s.def: A carnivorous dinosaur of the family Megalosauridae.
A rare species of deepwater shark, Megachasma pelagios, a filter-feeder, swimming with its large mouth wide open to capture plankton and jellyfish.

ety: From mega- + -phone.

s.def: A portable, usually hand-held, funnel-shaped device that is used to amplify a person’s natural voice toward a targeted direction.
Mouthpiece or promoter; one who speaks for or publicizes on behalf of another.
ex: If Pack does become head of the BBG, critics fear that he will turn Voice of America and the other BBG networks into a megaphone for Trump.

s.def: To use a megaphone; to speak through a megaphone.
A cytotoxic neolignan obtained from the laurel Aniba megaphylla.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s Proto-Hellenic *mégas Ancient Greek μέγᾰς (mégăs)der. English mega- English pixel English megapixel From mega- + pixel.

s.def: One million pixels, used as a unit of resolution of digital cameras.
ex: This camera has a resolution of three megapixels.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μέγαρα (Mégara).

s.def: A city west of Athens in Attica, Greece.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s Proto-Hellenic *mégas Ancient Greek μέγᾰς (mégăs)der. English mega- English ton English megaton From mega- + ton.

s.def: A measure of the strength of an explosion or a bomb based on how many million tons of TNT would be needed to produce the same energy. (A derived unit for TNT equivalent.)
ex: Holonyms: gigaton < teraton < petaton < exaton (rare) < zettaton (rare) < yottaton (rare)
Meronyms: ton of TNT < kiloton

s.def: One million tons.
ex: Holonym: gigaton
Meronym: kiloton

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s Proto-Hellenic *mégas Ancient Greek μέγᾰς (mégăs)der. English mega- English watt English megawatt From mega- + watt.

s.def: Exceptionally powerful, intense, or enormous in impact.
ex: I also love the way you always greet me with a megawatt smile.
It has been nearly 30 years since Warren's first major hit, Laura Branigan's “Solitaire,” and her mega-watt success has seldom dimmed.

s.def: Chiefly preceded by the: depression, low spirits, unhappiness.

Any of various diseases of animals, especially horses, marked by a disturbance of equilibrium and abnormal gait and behaviour such as staggers or a sudden vertigo, sometimes followed by unconsciousness; the staggers.
plural of megrim

ety: From Ancient Greek μείωσις (meíōsis, “a lessening”), from μειόω (meióō, “I lessen”), from μείων (meíōn, “less”). The biological sense was coined by British biologists John Bretland Farmer and John Edmund Sharrock Moore in 1905 as maiosis in a paper in the Quarterly Journal of Microscopic Science, with the spelling corrected on etymological grounds later that year. Doublet of miosis.

s.def: Cell division of a diploid cell into four haploid cells, which develop to produce gametes.
A figure of speech in which something is presented as smaller or less significant than it actually appears.

ety: From Meitner + -ium; named for Lise Meitner.

s.def: A transuranic chemical element (symbol Mt) with atomic number 109.
The capital city of Tigray, Ethiopia.

ety: Ultimately from German Melamin.

s.def: A strong aromatic heterocyclic base, triaminotriazine, used in combination with formaldehyde to manufacture melamine resins; any such resin, such as Formica
ex: The interior melamine panels were designed to be easily removable for repair or future refurbishment, and the linoleum floor was for easy cleaning.

ety: From Late Latin melancholia, which was in turn borrowed from the Ancient Greek medical term μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency. Doublet of melancholy.

s.def: Deep sadness or gloom; melancholy
depression, characterised by irrational fears, guilt and apathy

ety: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, melancholy + -ic.

s.def: Filled with or affected by melancholy—great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
ex: Just as the melancholic eye / Sees fleets and armies in the sky.

s.def: Pertaining to black bile (melancholy).
Pertaining to the melancholic temperament or its associated personality traits.

ety: From Middle English malencolie, from Old French melancolie, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “atrabiliousness”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency. Compare the Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”). The adjectival use is a Middle English innovation, perhaps influenced by the suffixes -y, -ly. Doublet of melancholia.

s.def: Great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
ex: My mind was troubled with deep melancholy.
"The ancients referred melancholy to the mind, the moderns make it matter of digestion—to either case my plan applies," said Lady Mandeville.

s.def: Black bile, formerly thought to be one of the four "cardinal humours" of animal bodies.
Affected with great sadness or depression.
ex: Melancholy people don't talk much.
[…] he is melancholy without cause, and merry against the hair: […]

s.def: Suggestive of wistfulness or subdued emotion.
ex: It was the same old song / With a melancholy sound.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-der. Proto-Indo-European *mélh₂ns Proto-Hellenic *mélans Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas)lbor. Ancient Greek νῆσος (nêsos)lbor. Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Old French -ie Middle French -ie French -ie French Mélanésiebor. English Melanesia From French Mélanésie (coined by Jules Dumont d'Urville), from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “dark”) + νῆσος (nêsos, “island”), referring to the skin…

s.def: A continental region of Oceania, consisting of New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago, the Solomon Islands, New Caledonia, Vanuatu and Fiji.
ex: My job, then, is that of a cultural and religious broker of sorts, co-opting Melanesia to serve as a stimulus to thought in Le Moyne classrooms.

ety: From French mélange, from Middle French mélange, meslange, from Old French meslance, meslinges (“set of diverse elements”), derived from mescler (“to mingle, mix up”) (modern French mêler), from Vulgar Latin *misculāre, from Latin misceō (“mix”) + -inges, a suffix from Frankish *-ingo (“-ing”). More at mix, -ing.

s.def: A mixture of different things; a disordered mixture.
ex: The room was a melange of comic books and posters.

s.def: A Viennese coffee speciality, half steamed milk and half coffee.
A large-scale breccia formed in the accretionary wedge over a subductional environment.

ety: From French mélanisme; by surface analysis, melan(o)- + -ism.

s.def: Congenital abundance or excess of melanin pigmentation in the skin, hair, feathers and/or eyes, more than is typical for the species.

ety: From melano- + -oma.

s.def: A dark-pigmented, usually malignant tumor arising from a melanocyte and occurring most commonly in the skin.

ety: From melano- + -osis.

s.def: The morbid deposition of black matter, often of a malignant character, causing pigmented tumours.
A pigmentation of tissue.
Synonym of nigredo.

ety: From mela- + tone + -in, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black, dark”).

s.def: A hormone, related to serotonin, that is secreted by the pineal gland, and stimulates colour change in the skin of reptiles, and is involved in the sleep and wake and reproductive cycles in mammals.
ex: How exactly melatonin relates to sleep is still not understood.
Melatonin production can be delayed or arrested by even brief flashes of bright light entering the eye, research has shown.

s.def: Any material similar in its chemistry and effect to the natural hormone.

ety: From Hebrew מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (malkî-ṣed̠eq). The name literally means “righteousness is my king”.

s.def: A king and priest mentioned in the book of Genesis; contemporary of Abraham.
ex: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.

ety: The verb is probably derived: * from a blend of melt + weld; or * from melled (“blended; mingled”), the past participle of mell. The noun is derived from the verb. Compare also melting pot.

s.def: To combine (multiple things) together; to blend, to fuse.
ex: One can meld copper and zinc together to form brass.

s.def: To combine, to blend, to fuse.
The result of multiple things being combined together; a blend.
Especially in games of the rummy family:
Especially in games of the rummy family: a combination of playing cards which is announced or played to score points.
ex: The realization that Istra was in the room made him forget most of his melds at pinochle; […]

ety: Borrowed from French mêlée, from Old French meslee, feminine past participle of mesler (“to mix”), derived from Latin misceō (“mix”). Doublet of medley.

s.def: A battle fought at close range, (especially) one not involving ranged weapons; hand-to-hand combat; brawling.
A loud, confused or tumultuous fight, argument or scrap.
Any confused, disorganised, disordered or chaotic situation.
Lively contention or debate, skirmish.
A cavalry exercise in which two groups of riders try to cut paper plumes off the helmets of their opponents, the contest continuing until no member of one group retains his plume.
Small cut and polished gemstones sold in lots.
To physically hit in close quarters, as opposed to shooting, blowing up, or other ranged means of damage. Often refers to the usage of a hand-to-hand weapon.
Of a weapon: used in close-range combat, e.g. a sword. Compare with ranged.
ex: A melee weapon is used to attack a target within 5 feet of you, whereas a ranged weapon is used to attack a target at a distance.

s.def: Of a character, using melee weapons.

ety: From Latin melilōtos, from Ancient Greek μελίλωτος (melílōtos), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + λωτός (lōtós, “lotus”); later reinforced by Old French mellilote.

s.def: A fragrant plant of the genus Melilotus, often having small yellow or white flowers.

ety: Borrowed from French mélinite, from Ancient Greek μήλινος (mḗlinos, “quince-yellow”).

s.def: A yellow clay mineral from Bavaria.
An explosive containing picric acid and guncotton.
An infectious disease caused by the bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic to some areas of Southeast Asia and northern Australia.
ex: Twenty-seven proteins distinctively reacted with human plasma following environmental exposure or clinical melioidosis.
Melioidosis is the etiological designation of a spectrum of clinical manifestations caused by the gram-negative bacillus Burkholderia pseudomallei.

ety: First attested in 1542; borrowed from Late Latin meliorātus, perfect passive participle of meliorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from melior (“better”).

s.def: To make better; to improve; to solve a problem.
ex: They offered some compromises in an effort to meliorate the disagreement.
Nature by art we nobly meliorate.
June 8, 1783, George Washington, Circular to the States […] and the pure and benign light of revelation have had a meliorating influence on mankind.

s.def: To become better.

ety: From Latin melior (“better”) + -ism. Reportedly coined by British author George Eliot in her letters, published in 1877.

s.def: The view or doctrine that the world can be improved through human effort (often understood as an intermediate outlook between optimism and pessimism).
ex: At the convention, the official mood was traditional Methodist meliorism.
Enclaves of meritocratic and virtuous sociability, the lodges exuded […] a thoroughgoing meliorism.

ety: From Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa, “bee, honey, or honeybee”). In Ireland it is sometimes used as a feminine form of the Gaelic male name Maol Íosa (literally “servant of Jesus”).

s.def: A female given name from Ancient Greek, popular in the latter half of the 20th century.
ex: And her owne handmayd, that Melissa hight / Appointed to attend her dewly day and night
Miss Melissa Wackles was the eldest daughter, Miss Sophy the next, and Miss Jane the youngest.

s.def: Bee-nymph in Greek mythology.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mélit Proto-Italic *meli Latin mel Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *bʰorós Proto-Italic *-foros Latin -fer Latin melliferlbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English melliferous PIE word *mélit Learned borrowing fro…

s.def: Of a plant or its parts: bearing any substance (such as nectar or pollen) which is collected by bees to produce honey.
Producing honey.
Honeyed, sweet.
ex: melliferous music
The souimangas live on insects, to which they add the melliferous juice of flowers.

ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English melowe, melwe (“ripe, mellow; juicy; sweet”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain, possibly: * from an attributive use of melow, melowe, melewe, mele (“meal from ground grain or legumes; flour; kernel of barley or lentils”) [and other forms], from Old English melo, melu (“meal (edible part of a grain or pulse); flour”), from Proto-Germanic *melwą (“ground corn; meal; flour”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to crush; to grind”); or…

s.def: Soft or tender by reason of ripeness; having a tender pulp.
ex: a mellow apple
A little longer, yet a little longer, / And Nature drops him down, without your Sin, / Like mellow Fruit, without a Winter Storm.
Ay, how fine they be in their liveries, and each of 'em as full of meat as an egg, and as sleek and as round about as a mellow codlin.

s.def: Matured and smooth, and not acidic, harsh, or sharp.
ex: [H]e was ready and willing to hear what I might have to say: his spirit was of vintage too mellow and generous to sour in one thunder-clap.

s.def: Soft and easily penetrated or worked; not hard or rigid; loamy.
ex: [I]f your soil was pretty mellow it would do, but if there came wet, wet, wet to make it all of a mummy, why then—

s.def: Mature; of crops: ready to be harvested; ripe.
Fruitful and warm.
ex: And mellow Autumn, charged with bounteous fruit, / Where is she imaged? in what favoured clime / Her lavish pomp, and ripe magnificence?

s.def: Not coarse, brash, harsh, or rough; delicate, rich, soft, subdued.
ex: [F]rom the neighbouring water, hear at morn / The hound, the horses' tread, and mellow horn; […]
Larger constellations burning, mellow moons and happy skies, / Breadths of tropic shade and palms in cluster, knots of Paradise.
It was a low house, with smooth grey thatch and buff walls, looking pleasant and mellow in the evening light.

s.def: Senses relating to a person or their qualities.
ex: Late that night, everyone was sprawled on the sofas and bean bags in the lounge room, mellow because they'd smoked a couple of joints of hash.

s.def: Pleasing in some way; excellent, fantastic, great.
The property of being mellow; mellowness.
A comfortable or relaxed mood.

ety: From French mélodium, with change of ending.

s.def: A type of reed organ with a single keyboard.
An accordion where the melody-side keyboard is limited to the notes of diatonic scales in a small number of keys.
A music hall.

ety: Borrowed from French mélodique. By surface analysis, melody + -ic.

s.def: Of, relating to, or having melody.
ex: Debussy's melody is fractional, fragmentary. But at the core all his music is melodic and melody is its main motive force.

s.def: Melodious, tuneful.

ety: Possibly a blend of melodeon + harmonica.

s.def: A free-reed keyboard wind instrument, often played with a flexible plastic tube connected to the mouthpiece.
ex: On “Seven by Seven” it was the reedy blend of two melodicas, played by Mr. Apfelbaum and Mr. Valera over a haunting drone.

ety: Inherited from Middle English melodious, from Middle French melodieus, melodieux. By surface analysis, melod(i) + -ous.

s.def: Having a pleasant melody or sound; tuneful.
ex: Patinkin’s melodious voice is a natural fit for animation, and he breathes just the right type of upper-crust life into Hugh in 22 short minutes.

ety: From melody + -ize.

s.def: To compose or play melodies.
To make melodious; to write a melody for (existing text).

ety: From French mélodrame, the second element refashioned by analogy with drama; ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”, “member”, “song”, “tune”, “melody”) + δρᾶμα (drâma, “deed”, “theatrical act”). Compare melodrame. Cognate to German Melodram and Spanish melodrama.

s.def: A drama abounding in romantic sentiment and agonizing situations, with a musical accompaniment only in parts which are especially thrilling or pathetic.
A kind of drama having a musical accompaniment to intensify the effect of certain scenes.
A passage in which the orchestra plays a somewhat descriptive accompaniment, while the actor speaks.
ex: The grave-digging scene in Beethoven's “Fidelio” has much melodrama.

s.def: Any situation or action which is blown out of proportion.

ety: From melodrama + -tic. Modelled after dramatic.

s.def: Of or pertaining to melodrama; like or suitable to a melodrama; unnatural in situation or action.
Exaggeratedly emotional or sentimental.
ex: She wrote him a melodramatic letter, threatening to kill herself.

ety: From Middle English melodie, melodye, from Old French melodie, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).

s.def: A sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase.
ex: Alyssa likes to sing melodies while playing the drums.
There is a melody upon the Earth as though ten thousand streams all sang together for their homes that they had forsaken in the hills.

ety: From Middle English meloun, melon, from Old French melon, from Late Latin melonem, from Latin melopeponem, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).

s.def: The large, round to ovoid fruits that have rinds and are of such plants.
A light pinkish orange color, like that of some melon flesh.
The breasts.
ex: She indicated her left melon, underneath which lay the heart. “Because you stuck with me, and whether you ever said it or not, that is love.”
“Wait a minute.” I said. “James with another woman? Mommy, that doesn't even sound right?” “It's true. I caught him squeezing her melons.”

s.def: Some of the plants of the family Cucurbitaceae grown for food, generally not including the cucumber.
The head, the brain.
ex: Think! Use your melon!

s.def: A member of the Green Party, or similar environmental group.
A mass of adipose tissue found in the forehead of all toothed whales, used to focus and modulate vocalizations.
Of a light pinkish orange color, like that of melon flesh.
Alternative form of mellon.

ety: From Middle English melten, from a merger of Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both meaning “to melt, digest,” from Proto-West Germanic *meltan and *maltijan, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną and *maltijaną, both from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“melt”). Cognate with Icelandic melta (“to digest”).

s.def: To change (or to be changed) from a solid state to a liquid state, usually by a gradual heat.
ex: I melted butter to make a cake.
When the weather is warm, the snowman will disappear; he will melt.

s.def: To dissolve, disperse, vanish.
ex: His troubles melted away.

s.def: To soften, as by a warming or kindly influence; to relax; to render gentle or susceptible to mild influences; sometimes, in a bad sense, to take away the firmness of; to weaken.
ex: For pity melts the mind to love.
The traveller hears me now and then, ⁠And sometimes harshly will he speak: ⁠‘This fellow would make weakness weak, And melt the waxen hearts of men.’

s.def: To be discouraged.
To be emotionally softened or touched.
ex: She melted when she saw the romantic message in the Valentine's Day card.
My heart melted when I first heard the song.

s.def: To be very hot and sweat profusely.
ex: I need shade! I'm melting!

s.def: Molten material, the product of melting.
ex: The crust (a mere 1% of the Earth's volume) is made of lighter melt products from the mantle.

s.def: The transition of matter from a solid state to a liquid state.
The springtime snow runoff in mountain regions.
A melt sandwich.
ex: I recently asked a group of people whether they had eaten tuna melts as a kid. Everyone remembered a version of this dish.

der: butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth

ety: From melt (verb) + down (adverb), a deverbal from melt down (verb).

s.def: An act or process of melting.
A mass of melted material.
Chiefly preceded by a descriptive word: uncontrolled disorder which often has disastrous consequences; (countable) a situation involving this; a crisis.
ex: Channel 4 switchboards went into meltdown this week when viewers called to complain about a Brass Eye programme on child sex.

s.def: (Sudden) loss of control over one's behaviour, emotions, etc.; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: After the huntsman raced across my windscreen, I had an arachnophobic meltdown on the side of the road.

s.def: The process of changing the state of a substance from solid to liquid by heating it past its melting point.
The act of softening or mitigating.
The temperature at which the solid and liquid phases of a substance are in equilibrium; it is relatively insensitive to changes in pressure.
The point at which things go wrong or become dangerous; a crisis or meltdown.

ety: From Middle English membre, from Old French membre, from Latin membrum (“limb, body part”), from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Akin to Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌼𐌶 (mimz, “meat, flesh”), Crimean Gothic menus. Coexists with native limb, from Old English lim (“limb, joint, main branch”). Mostly displaced lith (“limb, joint, member”), from Old English liþ (“limb, member, join, tip”), which still survives in British dialect.

s.def: One who belongs to a group.
Part of an animal capable of performing a distinct office; an organ; a limb.
ex: For as we haue many members in one body, and all members haue not the same office:

s.def: The penis.
ex: If your wife is old and your member is exhausted, eat onions in plenty.

s.def: A part of a whole.
ex: The I-beams were to become structural members of a pedestrian bridge.
The member intertongues and grades laterally with the lower sandstone member of the Pocahontas Formation of Early Pennslyvanian age

s.def: One of the propositions making up a syllogism.
An element of a set.
the judge or adjudicator in a consumer court.
A part of a discourse or of a period, sentence, or verse; a clause.
Either of the two parts of an algebraic equation, connected by the equality sign.
A file stored within an archive file.
ex: The zip file holding the source code of this application has 245 members.

s.def: A representative elected by the voters of an electoral district to a house of a parliament.

ety: Etymology tree English member Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English membership From member + -ship.

s.def: The fact of being a member of a set.
The state of being a member of a group or organization.
ex: The terms of membership agreement were vague.
He has memberships in clubs in three cities.

s.def: The body of members of an organization.
ex: The memberships of the state chapters elect delegates to the national convention.

ety: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin membrāna (“skin or membrane that covers parts of the body”), from membrum (“a limb or member of the body”) + -āna. Doublet of membrana.

s.def: A flexible enclosing or separating tissue forming a plane or film and separating two environments.
A piece of parchment forming part of a roll.

ety: Clipping of mimeme, equivalent to mime + -eme. Coined by British biologist Richard Dawkins in 1976 in his book The Selfish Gene. Shortened (after gene) from mimeme (compare English phoneme), anglicized as if from a noun derived from Ancient Greek μῑμέομαι (mīméomai) with the deverbal suffix -μα (-ma), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitation, copy”). The concept was later applied to the Internet by Mike Godwin.

s.def: Any unit of (originally cultural) information, such as a practice or idea, that is transmitted verbally or by repeated action from one mind to another in a comparable way to the transmission of genes.
ex: Examples of memes are tunes, ideas, catch-phrases, clothes fashions, ways of making pots or of building arches.
Related memes tend to form mutually supporting meme-complexes such as religions, political ideologies, scientific theories, and New Age dogmas.
The original Hobson and Jobson stock comic characters have died out as a meme, as has the application of their names to the Muharram in India.

s.def: Media, usually humorous, which is copied and circulated online with slight adaptations, such as basic pictures, video templates, etc.
ex: He posted a meme that went viral within a few hours on social media.
He stuck memes on the wall to campaign for the position of President.
I do...but my journal is a mess. It's mostly filled with memes and my bitching about a house I am building.

s.def: A specific instance of a meme, such as an image macro or a video, often with humorous superimposed text.
ex: This meme generator lets you make your own memes by adding a caption to existing images, or by uploading your own image.
I'm always posting memes on the groupchat.

s.def: Something which is deceptive; a trick, a ruse.
ex: It's a meme degree, you know. Good luck getting a job from that.

ety: From metric + system, from French métrique. See also meter.

ety: Blend of metropolitan + heterosexual, equivalent to metro- + -sexual. Coined by British writer Mark Simpson in 1994, it enjoyed a brief popularity in the early 2000s.

ety: From figurative use of metal (since 16th century). The two spellings were originally interchangeable variants, but came to be distinguished by sense in the 18th century.

ety: From Middle English mewe, mowe, meau, from Old English mǣw (“seagull”), from Proto-West Germanic *maiwī, from Proto-Germanic *mai(h)waz (“seagull”). ety: From 1599 or earlier (1530 in a Scottish document), apparently from Shakespeare with this spelling. Perhaps from Middle English mewen (“to whimper”) + -le (frequentative suffix).

My father started rubbing and rubbing on Mittens, scruffying her fur the wrong way, and she mewled her protests.
The neighbours’ cats stroll into my garden, mewling and hoping for a little bit of in flagrante. Honey bees brazenly assault the cherry blossom.

s.def: A soft cry or whimper; an act of mewling.
ex: I let out another moaning mewl, biting my lip as I awaited whatever he planned.
The scratching stopped, and there was another piteous mewl from behind the door.

ety: From Middle English mydwaye, mydweye, from Old English midweġ (“midway”), equivalent to mid- + way. Cognate with Dutch midweg (“midway”), Middle Low German midwech (“midway”).

s.def: The middle; the midst.

ety: From Middle English midwif, corresponding to mid (“with”) + wif (“woman, wife, female”). It appears not to be entirely clear whether the original understanding was “with-woman” in the sense of “attending/assisting woman”, or “they who are with the woman” (namely the mother).

ety: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin migrātus, perfect passive participle of migrō (“to migrate, change, transport”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
