This set the pattern for four years, as the two monarchs minueted around the vast Commonwealth, never again to face each other personally in battle.

ety: From Middle English mynus, from Latin minus, neuter form of minor, comparative form of parvus (“small, little”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *mey- (“few, small”).

s.def: Made less or reduced by (followed by an expression of number or quantity).
ex: Seven minus two is five.

s.def: Without; deprived of.
ex: I walked out minus my coat.

s.def: The minus sign (−).
A negative quantity.
A downside or disadvantage.
Being a negative quantity; pertaining to a deficit or reduction.
ex: a minus number

s.def: That is below zero by (a specified amount) on a scale.
ex: minus seven degrees
Arriving during late spring in the satellite's southern hemisphere, Voyager found the coldest body in the solar system, minus 235°C (-391°F).

s.def: Worse off than before; out of pocket.
Ranking just below (a designated rating).
ex: He got a grade of B minus for his essay.

s.def: To subtract.
ex: Four plus one is 5 and you go down because it's minusing, […]

s.def: The symbol −, used to denote the operation of subtraction or to indicate that a number is negative.

ety: From French minuscule, from Latin minuscula, feminine of minusculus (“rather less, rather small”), from minus (“less, smaller”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

s.def: A lowercase letter.
Either of the two medieval handwriting styles minuscule cursive and Caroline minuscule.
ex: By the eighth century, Irish scribes had refined everyday cursive writing in minuscule to allow its use for the production of quality vellum books.

s.def: A letter in these styles.
Written in minuscules, lowercase.
Written in minuscule handwriting style.
Very small; tiny.
ex: a minuscule dot

ety: From Middle English mynute, minute, mynet, from Old French minute, from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”). Doublet of menu and menudo.

s.def: A unit of time which is one sixtieth of an hour (sixty seconds).
ex: You have twenty minutes to complete the test.

s.def: A point in time; a moment.
ex: I conked out the minute I got home.
Tell her, that I some Certainty may bring; / I go this minute to attend the king.

s.def: A while or a long unspecified period of time.
ex: Oh, I ain't heard that song in a minute!
“Man, I haven’t seen you in a minute,” he says, smiling still. “Maybe like two, three years ago?”
I seen Too$hort up there. Me and $hort ain't talked in a minute.

s.def: minute of use of telephone network
A short but unspecified time period.
ex: give me a minute
Wait a minute, I’m not ready yet!

s.def: A unit of angle equal to one-sixtieth of a degree.
ex: We need to be sure these maps are accurate to within one minute of arc.

s.def: A (usually formal) written record of a meeting or a part of a meeting.
ex: Let’s look at the minutes of last week’s meeting.

s.def: A unit of purchase on a telephone or other similar network, especially a cell phone network, roughly equivalent in gross form to sixty seconds' use of the network.
ex: If you buy this model, you’ll get 100 free minutes.

s.def: A nautical or a geographic mile.
An old coin, a half farthing.

der: a sucker is born every minute

s.def: The hand of a clock or watch face that revolves once each hour and indicates the minutes.
Alternative form of minute man.
The official notes kept during a meeting.

ety: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

s.def: plural of minutia

ety: PIE word *ǵʰmṓ The origin of the noun is uncertain. The following possible derivations have been suggested: * A variation of minikin (“(obsolete) young person, especially a young woman; small or insignificant person, thing, or amount”) + a variation of -s (suffix forming hypocoristic nouns (nicknames)) (compare minckins, a variant of minikin). * From Dutch mens, mensch (“human being, person; (derogatory, informal) woman”) (obsolete), Middle Dutch minsc, minsce, minsch; or from German Low German…

s.def: A flirtatious, impudent, or pert young woman.
ex: Single, and generally on the make, she was alternatively an angel, a devil and a minx.
We're quite a powerful group, us wrinkly teenagers, us pre-menopausal minxes.
Both girls [in Joseph Haydn's Le pescatrici] reveal themselves as minxes.

s.def: A promiscuous woman; also, a mistress (“the other woman in an extramarital relationship”) or a prostitute.
ex: They are a couple of alluring wanton Minxes.
There wasn't an Archimandrite of Dane's Island and the townlands nor a minx from the Isle of Woman […] would come next or nigh him, […]

s.def: A pet dog.
Used transitively when followed by it: to behave like a minx, that is, in a flirtatious and impudent manner.
ex: Alison might have, if she hadn't minxed herself out of a job.
It's just a late date. It's like I'm Carrie Bradshaw, minxing it around Manhattan.
Moonface minxed and flashed her red nails like a dancer, chameleon that she was.

s.def: To make (someone) like a minx; (intransitive) to become like a minx.
Obsolete spelling of mink (“any of various semi-aquatic, carnivorous mammals in the Mustelinae subfamily”).
ex: Many of these birds are destroyed by Weasels and Minxes.
2d. Carnivora, or flesh eaters. Of these we have […] the New York ermine, or ermine weasel; the mink, or minx otter; the common otter; […]

ety: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Doublet of milagro and miraculum. Partially displaced native wonder, from Old English wundor (“miracle, wonder”).

s.def: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.
ex: Many religious beliefs are based on miracles.
An example of a miracle associated with Muhammad is the splitting of the moon.

s.def: A fortunate outcome that prevails despite overwhelming odds against it.
An awesome and exceptional example of something.
ex: economic miracle
engineering miracle
miracle of engineering

s.def: To affect by a miracle; to work a miracle upon.
ex: Deleuze and Guattari are right in miracling fleas into the bestiary, but it is already rich enough to do without them.
They think I've miracled the dogs, as the Eucharist miracled my mother. That I, Bonne, am pulsing with holy spirit.

ety: From Middle French miraculeux. Displaced native Old English wundorlīċ.

s.def: By supernatural or uncommon causes, e.g. by a god; that cannot be explained in terms of normal events.
Very surprising; amazing.

ety: An unadapted borrowing from French mirage c. 1812.

s.def: An optical phenomenon in which light is refracted through a layer of hot air close to the ground, often giving the illusion of a body of water.
An illusion.
To cause to appear as or like a mirage.
ex: All that had been in his mind seemed suddenly miraged before him—the removal of Hunterleys, his own wife's failing health.
The vision of a salon was miraged before her, with herself in the middle deftly manipulating the destinies of a nation.

ety: From Middle English mire, a borrowing from Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzijō, whence also Swedish myr, Norwegian myr, Icelandic mýri, Dutch *mier (in placenames, for example Mierlo). Related to Proto-Germanic *meusą, whence Old English mēos, and Proto-Germanic *musą, whence Old English mos (English moss).

s.def: Deep mud; moist, spongy earth.
ex: Sow ran and squall'd, While Jack he bawl'd, And Jill join'd in the choir, Dog Ball being near, Bit sow by the ear, And threw Jack into the mire.
His laden feet sand and stuck in mire; he was bedaubed with the blue-gray clay from head to foot; but he had escaped the deadly river!

s.def: An undesirable situation; a predicament.
A bog or fen; (in wetland science, specifically) a peatland which is actively forming peat, such as an active bog or fen.
To cause or permit to become stuck in mud; to plunge or fix in mud.
ex: to mire a horse or wagon

s.def: To sink into mud.
To weigh down.
To soil with mud or foul matter.
An ant.
ex: Wen I lay down behine dat log I plunk masef right een one dem aunty mire nest an bout 10 million of dem leetle devil begin to heat me.

ety: From Hebrew מִרְיָם (Miryam), possibly from Aramaic מרים (Maryām, “bitter”), from a root מר (m-r) meaning "to be bitter". The meaning of this name which is the Old Testament equivalent of Mary has been debated for centuries. Some other explanations are mutiny / rebellion / disobedience from a root מרי (m-r-y).

s.def: The sister of Moses and Aaron and the daughter of Amram and Jochebed.
ex: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.

s.def: A female given name from Hebrew.
Synonym of Mary, mother of Jesus, chiefly in contexts emphasizing her historical or Jewish identity.

ety: From Middle English mirour, from Old French mireor (“mirror”, literally “looker, watcher”), from mirer (“look at”), from Latin mīror (“wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, to be glad”). Displaced native Middle English schewere, schawere, from Old English sċēawere (“mirror”, literally “watcher”), which was also the word for "spy".

s.def: A smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light so as to give an image of what is in front of it.
ex: I had a look in the mirror to see if the blood had come off my face.
He broke the mirror with the pickaxe.
We could see the lorry in the mirror, so decided to change lanes.

s.def: A website or server that contains replicated data from another site.
ex: Although the content had been deleted from his blog, it was still found on some mirrors.

s.def: An object, person, or event that reflects or gives a picture of another.
ex: His story is a mirror into the life of orphans growing up.
O goddess, heavenly bright, / Mirror of grace and majesty divine.

s.def: A mirror carp.
An ethical-didactic treatise that details exemplary conduct through models, advising kings, princes, clergy, etc. on how to behave.
Of an event, activity, behavior, to be identical to; to be a copy of; to imitate closely.
ex: He tried to mirror Elvis's life by copying his fashion and mannerisms.
“Does he mirror?” one therapist, who came to our home, asked. “What is mirroring?” I asked back. “Does he mimic what you do, like Simon Says?”

s.def: To reflect, as in a mirror.
To act as a reflection of, either by being identical to, or by being identical but reversed.
ex: The placement of the paintings mirrored the positions of the windows on the opposite wall.

s.def: To create something identical to (a website, etc.).

ety: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Middle Dutch merchte (“pleasure, joy, delight”).

s.def: The emotion usually following humor and accompanied by laughter.
ex: But sorrow that is couch'd in seeming gladness Is like that mirth fate turns to sudden sadness.
And he began to laugh again, and that so heartily, that, though I did not see the joke as he did, I was again obliged to join him in his mirth.

s.def: That which causes merriment.
ex: Phantasmal mirth, folded away: muskperfumed.

ety: From Middle English myry, equivalent to mire + -y.

s.def: Resembling or characteristic of a mire; swampy, boggy.
ex: Only these marishes and myrie bogs, / In which the fearefull ewftes do build their bowres, / Yeeld me an hostry mongst the croking frogs […].
summer was long over, and cold and frost and miry ways kept them much indoors […]
Beyond the bazaar one could see the huge, miry river."

ety: From Persian میرزا (mirzâ).

s.def: An educated man in India or Iran (Persia); an official, a clerk.
ex: The same success attended the other mirzas and emirs in their excursions.
This he presented to the Khan of Puhra, who called upon his mirza, or clerk, to read it aloud.

ety: From Persian میرزا (mirzâ), from earlier میرزاد (mirzâd), composed of میر (mir, “commander”) (from Arabic title أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander, prince”)) and the suffix ـزاد، ـزاده (-zâd, -zâde, “child of, son of”), from زادن (zâdan). Akin to Amir, amir, emir and admiral.

s.def: A surname.

ety: From Middle English misaventure, from Old French mesaventure, from mes- (“mis-”) + aventure (“adventure”). Equivalent to mis- + adventure. Compare disadventure.

s.def: Synonym of misfortune, bad luck or mishap, an instance of bad luck.
ex: All under the sun are subject at times to misery and misadventure.

s.def: Synonym of mistake, a misguided and/or failed enterprise, a risky action that turns out badly.
ex: yet another American military misadventure

s.def: A fatal mishap, especially one voluntarily risked by the victim, bad luck causing an accidental death without attaching any liability to any other involved parties.

ety: From Middle English misavisen, and also from mis- + advise.

s.def: To give bad advice
ex: Expel from your confidence, men who have never ceased to misadvise you!

ety: From mis- + alliance, partly after French mésalliance.

s.def: An unsuitable alliance, especially an unsuitable marriage.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English ally English misally From mis- + ally.

s.def: To wrongly join together; to wrongly ally with or to.
ex: 'Tis my beliefwhen, things are misallied, The sooner they part company the better.

s.def: To marry badly; to marry an inferior

ety: Formed in the late 19th century as mis- (“hatred”) + -andry (“men”) by analogy with misogyny; compare the Ancient Greek μισανδρία (misandría), from μισέω (miséō, “hate”) + ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”).

s.def: Hatred of, contempt for, or prejudice against men.
ex: The are cases of rabid misogyny as of rabid misandry

ety: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”); compare miser.

s.def: One who has a negative view of the entire human race.
Someone who distrusts or avoids other people.

ety: From Ancient Greek μισανθρωπία (misanthrōpía), from μισάνθρωπος (misánthrōpos), from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”). The word is analysable as miso- + -anthropy.

s.def: A negative view or hatred of the human race.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- Latin applicō Old French applierbor. Middle English aplien English apply English misapply From mis- + apply.

s.def: To apply incorrectly; to misuse.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English appropriate English misappropriate From mis- + appropriate.

s.def: To take something for wrong or illegal purposes.
To embezzle.
ex: The accountant was found to have misappropriated funds over a period of three years.

ety: From Arabic مِسْبَحَة (misbaḥa) from سَبَّحَ (sabbaḥa, “to praise, to glorify”).

s.def: A set of Islamic prayer beads.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English begotten English misbegotten From mis- + begotten.

s.def: Born out of wedlock; illegitimate.
Ill-conceived.
Bad; worthless.
past participle of misbeget
One born illegitimately (i.e., out of wedlock); a bastard.
A person born into infelicitous circumstances.

ety: From Middle English misbehaven, equivalent to mis- + behave.

s.def: To act or behave in an inappropriate, improper, incorrect, or unexpected manner.
ex: He doesn't mean to misbehave; he just doesn't know better.

ety: From Middle English misbelieven, misbileven, equivalent to mis- + believe. Compare earlier misbelief.

s.def: To believe incorrectly; hold to a false belief.
To disbelieve; doubt.
Abbreviation of miscellaneous.

ety: From Middle English miscallen, equivalent to mis- + call.

s.def: To call (someone) bad names; to insult, abuse.
To call (someone or something) incorrectly or by the wrong title or name.
ex: ‘In this country, peasants miscall it “Cowslip,” though of course the true Cowslip, Primula veris, is a different plant altogether.’

s.def: To make a wrong call (prediction or announcement).
An incorrect call.
Archaic form of miskal.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English carriage English miscarriage From mis- + carriage.

s.def: The spontaneous natural termination of a pregnancy, especially before it is viable; the fatal expulsion of a foetus from the womb before term.
ex: Susan Billig had suffered four miscarriages before giving birth to her firstborn daughter, Amy[…] .

s.def: A failure; a mistake or error.
ex: for feare least blame / Of her miscarriage should in her be fond, / She wist not how t'amend, nor how it to withstond.

ety: From Middle English miscarien. By surface analysis, mis- + carry.

s.def: To have an unfortunate accident of some kind; to be killed, or come to harm.
To go astray; to do something wrong.
To have a miscarriage; to involuntarily abort a foetus.
To fail to achieve some purpose; to be unsuccessful, to go wrong (of a business, project etc.).
ex: Pluto observing, since the Peace, The Burial Article decrease; And, vext to see Affairs miscarry, Declar'd in Council, Death must marry […]

s.def: Of a letter etc.: to fail to reach its intended recipient.
ex: It likewise alluded to several letters, which, as it appeared to me, must have miscarried or have been intercepted,[…].

ety: From Middle English miscasten, equivalent to mis- + cast.

s.def: To cast or reckon incorrectly.
To cast or direct erroneously or improperly.
ex: to miscast a glance

s.def: To cast an actor in an inappropriate role.
To make an error when casting a vote.
An erroneous cast or reckoning.
Erroneously cast

ety: Blend of Latin miscēre (“mix”) + Latin genus (“race”) + -ation. Coined by American journalist David Goodman Croly in 1864 and first used in an anonymous pamphlet he coauthored, which claimed to be written by a person who believed in the inherent unity of all racial groups, that marriage between blacks and whites would create a better race, and that the American Civil War was a fight for the latter idea. Later, it was exposed that the pretext of the pamphlet was false and that it had actually be…

s.def: The mixing or blending of race in marriage or breeding, interracial marriage.
A mixing or blending, especially one which is considered to be inappropriate.
ex: as is clear in the works of Nathaniel Hawthorne, it has a horror of any spiritual miscegenation between the human and the natural.
... if a miscegenation of Latin and Sanskrit may be permitted.
...'true English' before it was bastardised in its miscegenation with the Norman French.

ety: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“mix”).

s.def: Consisting of a variety of ingredients or parts.
ex: A miscellaneous pile of clothing, buttons, tools and other junk.

s.def: Having diverse characteristics, abilities or appearances.
Not in any other category.

ety: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

s.def: An assortment of miscellaneous items.
A collection of writings on various subjects or topics; an anthology.
ex: a monthly miscellany of literature

s.def: The condition of being miscellaneous, of being a hodgepodge.

ety: From Anglo-Norman meschance, Old French meschance, meschaunce.

s.def: Bad luck, misfortune.
ex: But let this same be presently perform'd / Even when men's minds are wild, lest more mischance / On plots and errors happen.
I write gaily enough, for there is no use in bewailing such a hopeless mischance.

s.def: A mishap, an unlucky circumstance.
To undergo (a misfortune); to suffer (something unfortunate).

ety: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).

s.def: Harm or injury:
ex: She had mischief in her heart.
Sooner or later he'll succeed in doing some serious mischief.
Vanity working on a weak head, produces every sort of mischief.

s.def: A cause or agent of annoyance, harm or injury, especially a person who causes mischief.
ex: Epimetheus was scatter-brained and a mischief to men for having taken the woman [Pandora] that Zeus had formed.

s.def: Conduct that playfully causes petty annoyance.
ex: Drink led to mischief.

s.def: A playfully annoying action.
ex: John's mischief, tying his shoelaces together, irked George at first.

s.def: A nest or pack of mice or rats.
ex: Meet a mischief of mice that is not nibbling away at the foundation of an old building.
A group of rats is not a herd or a gaggle, but a pack or a mischief of rats. Rats in general are omnivorous, meaning they will eat almost anything.
This was only the latest internet-based catastrophe caused by a mischief of rats (yes, that's what a group of rats is called).

s.def: A criminal offence defined in various ways in various jurisdictions, sometimes including causing damage to another's property.
The Devil; used as an expletive.
ex: What the mischief are you? and how the mischief did you get here, and where in thunder did you come from?

s.def: Casual and/or flirtatious sexual acts.
To do a mischief to; to harm.
ex: "Not now, Smee," Hook said darkly. "He is only one, and I want to mischief all the seven. Scatter and look for them."

s.def: To slander.

ety: From Middle English myschevous, mischevous, from Anglo-Norman meschevous, from Old French meschever, from mes- (“mis-”) + chever (“come to an end”) (from chef (“head”)). By surface analysis, mischief + -ous.

s.def: Causing mischief; injurious.

Troublesome, cheeky, badly behaved, impish, naughty, disobedient; showing a fondness for causing trouble in a playful way and liking to have fun by playing harmless tricks on people or doing things they are not supposed to do.
ex: Matthew had a twin brother called Edward, who was always mischievous and badly behaved.

ety: From Middle English mischeosen, mischesen, equivalent to mis- + choose.

s.def: To choose incorrectly or badly; to make a wrong choice.
ex: Up to a certain point he was a free agent , he could choose his path ; he mischose it , and he was in the toils of necessity

ety: From Middle English miscible, from Late Latin miscibilis (“that can be mixed”), from Latin miscēre (“to mix”).

s.def: Able to be mixed together in all proportions.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English communication English miscommunication From mis- + communication.

s.def: An interaction between two parties in which information is/was not communicated as desired.

ety: From mis- + conduct (noun sense).

s.def: Behavior that is considered to be unacceptable.
ex: The student was banned from using the university's computing resources for two weeks due to gross misconduct on the Internet.

s.def: A penalty or write-up for improper behavior.
ex: There is definitely an indication of retaliation in this case. I have never received a misconduct for possessing or using drugs.

s.def: To mismanage.
To behave inappropriately, to misbehave.
ex: It had been pointed out […] that in the past enemy aliens misconducting themselves had been returned to the internment camp.

s.def: To act improperly.
ex: The quartermasters have misconducted, and the government should bear the loss resulting from that misconduct.
It seems no answer for the recipient to allege that he was incompetent and misconducted, but that the acts were committed outside the jurisdiction.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English construction English misconstruction From mis- + construction.

s.def: Mistaken or faulty construction; an instance of it.
ex: a misconstruction of the law

ety: From Middle English misconstruen, equivalent to mis- + construe.

s.def: To interpret erroneously, to understand incorrectly; to misunderstand.
ex: His words were misconstrued as an insult.
It’s easy to misconstrue her silence as agreement.
misconstrue the meaning

ety: From Middle English miscounten, equivalent to mis- + count.

s.def: To count incorrectly.
An incorrect counting.

ety: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

s.def: Lacking in conscience or moral principles; unscrupulous.
ex: How do we get fair treatment when confronting miscreant workers sometimes means no care at all?

s.def: Holding an incorrect religious belief.
One who holds a false religious belief; a misbeliever.
One who has behaved badly, or illegally.
ex: The teacher sent the miscreants to see the school principal.

s.def: One not restrained by moral principles; an unscrupulous villain.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English create English miscreate From mis- + create.

s.def: To create wrongly or poorly.
Miscreated; illegitimate; forged.
ex: miscreate titles
With opening titles miscreate, whose right / Suits not in native colours with the truth;

ety: From mis- + cue.

s.def: In a cue sport, an error in hitting the ball with the cue.
The act of missing one's cue or of responding to a cue intended for another actor.
A miss of the object one intended to hit.
To give an incorrect cue.
to mishit, strike incorrectly.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English date English misdate From mis- + date.

s.def: A wrong date.
To date incorrectly; to mark with the wrong date.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-? Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-der. Proto-Germanic *missaz Proto-Germanic *missa- Proto-West Germanic *missa- Old English mis- Middle English mys- English mis- English deal English misdeal From mis- + deal.

s.def: To deal or distribute wrongly.
ex: Bill, you have misdealt two hands of poker already.

s.def: Incorrect dealing or distribution.

s.def: Any of many minute arachnids which, along with the ticks, comprise subclass Acari (syn. Acarina).
A small coin formerly circulated in England, rated at about a third of a farthing.
ex: One mite wrung from the lab'rer's hands Shall buy and sell the miser's lands;

s.def: A lepton, a small coin used in Judea in the time of Christ.
A small weight; one twentieth of a grain.
Anything very small; a minute object; a very little quantity or particle.
ex: Those trousers are a mite too big, but you'll soon grow into them.

s.def: A small or naughty person, or one people take pity on; rascal.
ex: “Tom told me that, but twasn't your fault, the little mite just couldn't wait to be born that's all.” A small smile played on Leah's lips.

s.def: Eye dialect spelling of might.
Alternative form of mitre (“to unite at an angle of 45°”).
Alternative form of mitre.
A joint between two members at an angle to each other; each member is cut at an angle equal to half the angle of the junction and usually joint at right angles to each other.

ety: From Middle English mitridate and methridat, from Old French mithridat, from Late Latin mithridatum and mithridatium, from Latin Mithridātīus (“of or related to Mithridates”), from Mithridātēs + -ius, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridatium, mithridatum, and mithridaticon.

s.def: Any of various historical medicines, typically an electuary compounded with various poison, believed to derive from Mithridates VI and to serve as a universal antidote.
ex: Auicen saythe; There be certeyne medicins... which wyl not suffre poyson to approche nere the harte, as triacle and Metridate.
Fools may talk of Mythridate, Cordials, Elixers...
What he wanted, in effect, was a universal antidote, which medical science has for years referred to as a mithridate.

s.def: Ellipsis of mithridate mustard.

ety: From Latin Mithridātēs, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), from Old Persian *Miθradātah.

s.def: ancient male given name
a male given name popularized in Achaemenid and post-Achaemenid Persia

ety: From Middle English mitigaten (“to relieve pain, soothe; (swelling) to abate; (hemorrhoids) to relieve; (the mind) to placate, appease; to end, check; to stop, cease”), from mitigat(e) (“mitigated, alleviated, relived”, also used as the past participle of mitigaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin mītigātus, the perfect passive participle of mītigō (“to make soft, ripe; to tame, pacify”), from mītis (“gentle, mild, ripe”) + -igō (“to do, make”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps…

s.def: To reduce, lessen, or decrease and thereby to make less severe or easier to bear.
ex: But in yielding to it the retaliation has been mitigated as much as possible, both in its extent and in its character...
Then they tell us that vaccination will mitigate the disease that it will make it milder.
Then I discovered the brilliance of the landscape around was mitigated by blue spectacles.

s.def: To downplay.
To give force or effect toward preventing a problem.
ex: We've mitigated against the chance of flooding.

s.def: Mitigated, alleviated.

ety: From German Mitochondrium, coined by Carl Benda in 1898, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + χονδρίον (khondríon), diminutive of χόνδρος (khóndros, “grain, morsel”).

s.def: A spherical or ovoid organelle found in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells and containing genetic material separate from that of the host; it is responsible for the conversion of food to usable energy in the form of ATP.

ety: From German Mitose, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + -osis, probably in reference to the thread-like chromatin seen during mitosis.

s.def: The division of a cell nucleus in which the genome is copied and separated into two identical halves. It is normally followed by cell division.
ex: Meronyms: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey-der.? Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos)der. English mito- English -some English mitosome From mito- + -some.

s.def: An organelle found within certain unicellular eukaryotes which lack mitochondria.

ety: From French mitrailleuse, from mitrailler (“to fire grapeshot”).

s.def: A breech-loading machine gun consisting of a number of barrels fitted together, so arranged that the barrels can be fired simultaneously, or successively, and rapidly.

ety: From Middle English mytre, from Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”). Its use in reference to a counterfeit coin derived from the bishop's mitre stamped upon it. Doublet of Mithras, Mithra, Mitra, and Mehr.

s.def: A covering for the head, worn on solemn occasions by church dignitaries, which has been made in many reincarnations, most recently as a tall cap with two points or peaks.
The surface forming the bevelled end or edge of a piece where a miter joint is made; also, a joint formed or a junction affected by two bevelled ends or edges; a mitral joint.
A 13th-century coin minted in Europe which circulated in Ireland as a debased counterfeit sterling penny, outlawed under Edward I.
A cap or cowl for a chimney or ventilation pipe.
A gusset in sewing, etc.
A square with one triangular quarter missing from the outside.
A mitre shell
A power saw that is a bench circular saw that is used to make accurate crosscuts and miters in a workpiece by positioning a mounted blade onto a board, that can be positioned at a variety of angles.

ety: Clipping of mitten.

s.def: A mitten
An oversized, protective glove such as an oven mitt or a baseball mitt.
A hand.
ex: Hey, get your cotton-picking mitts off my sandwich!
"Give us yer mitts, mate," said Alf. I held my hands out toward him.

ety: From Middle English myteyne, from Old French mitaine (Modern French mitaine), of unclear origin; possibly from mite, miste (“playful name for cat”) + -aine. Alternatively, mitaine may be from Old High German mittamo (“half”), superlative of mitti (“midpoint”), from Proto-Germanic *midjô, *midją (“middle, center”), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between, in the middle, center”). Compare Catalan mitana, Medieval Latin mitta, mitana, and Occitan mitana.

s.def: A boxing glove.
A type of glove or garment that covers a hand with a separate sheath for the thumb, but not for other fingers, which are either enclosed in a single section or left uncovered.
The paw of a cat or dog that is of a different color from the main body.
A romantic rejection; dismissal of a lover.
ex: to give someone the mitten; to get the mitten

s.def: To dress in mittens; to put a mitten on.
ex: He mittened his hand and beat it violently for a minute before exposing it to the frost to strike a match.

ety: From Latin mittimus (the opening word of such a document), first-person plural of mittō (“send”).

s.def: A warrant issued for someone to be taken into custody.
ex: Away George, away, raise the watch at Ludgate, and bring a Mittimus from the Iustice for this desperate villaine.
But she pertinaciously refused to make any response. So that he was about to make her mittimus to Bridewell when I departed.

s.def: A writ for moving records from one court to another.
A formal dismissal from a situation.

ety: Borrowed from Hebrew מצווה (mitsvá, “a commandment”).

s.def: An act of kindness, a good deed.
ex: ‘You heard about them pulling my license. That was indirectly Joel. Who, without meaning to, did me such a mitzvah.’

s.def: Any of the 613 commandments of Jewish law.
ex: She called Penansky regularly to remind her to observe the mitzvahs.

s.def: A Jewish celebration, but particularly a clipping of bar mitzvah and/or bat mitzvah.

ety: From Middle English mixen (attested in past tense as mixed, myxyd), from Old English *mixian, miscian, from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan, from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European *miḱ-sḱé-ti, from *meyǵ-, *meyḱ- (“to mix”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian miskje (“to mix, blend”), Middle Dutch mischen (“to mix”), Low German misken, mischen (“to mix”), Old High German miskian, miskēn (“to mix”) (German mischen), Welsh mysgu (“to mix”), Latin misceō (“mix”), Ancient…

s.def: To stir together.
ex: Mix the eggs and milk with the flour until the consistency is smooth.
In a medium bowl, mix together the leeks, lemon zest, the remaining ¼ teaspoon salt, and the remaining 1½ tablespoons oil.

s.def: To combine (items from two or more sources normally kept separate).
ex: to mix business with pleasure
Don't mix the meat recipes with the dairy recipes.
What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

s.def: To form by mingling; to produce by the stirring together of ingredients; to concoct from different parts.
ex: Yellow and blue paint mix to make green.
Therefore J haue chosen an Argument, mixt of Religious and Ciuill Considerations; And likewise mixt between Contemplatiue, and Actiue.

s.def: To blend by the use of a mixer (machine).
ex: Mix the egg whites until they are stiff.

s.def: To combine (several tracks).
ex: I'll mix the rhythm tracks down to a single track.

s.def: To produce a finished version of (a recording).
ex: I'm almost done mixing this song.

s.def: To unite with in company; to join; to associate.
ex: The mention of the six knots of elderwood is curious, for that tree mixes largely in folk lore.

s.def: The result of mixing two or more substances; a mixture.
ex: Now add the raisins to the mix.

s.def: The result of combining items normally kept separate.
ex: My recipe file was now a mix of meat and dairy.
The combination of classical music and hip hop is a surprisingly good mix.

s.def: A preparation, usually in the form of a powder, into which other ingredients can be mixed to prepare a specified foodstuff.
ex: Cake mix. Pancake mix. Hot chocolate mix.

ety: Deverbal from mix up.

s.def: A confusion, mistake, muddle or misunderstanding.

ety: From mix, equivalent to mix + -ed. Compare Middle English mixid (“mixed”, past participle), Old English miscode (“mixed”, preterite). More at mix. In adjectival use, reinforced by French mixte and/or Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“mix”), from the same Indo-European root as mix.

s.def: simple past and past participle of mix
Having two or more separate aspects.
ex: I get a very mixed feeling from this puzzling painting.
The various studies produced mixed results.

s.def: Not completely pure, tainted or adulterated.
ex: My joy was somewhat mixed when my partner said she was pregnant: it's a lot of responsibility.

s.def: Including both male(s) and female(s).
ex: The tennis match was mixed, with a boy and a girl on each side.
My son attends a mixed school, my daughter an all-girl grammar school.
We were the first paper to involve large numbers of gay men and lesbians: today, we remain the only truly mixed periodical in our community.

s.def: Stemming from two or more races or breeds.
ex: The benefit dog show has both mixed and single-breed competitions.
Mixed blood can surprisingly produce inherited properties which neither parent showed

s.def: Polarizing; including both positive and negative feedback.
ex: The movie has received mixed reviews from movie critics.

s.def: Marriage between people of different socially-distinguished groups, such as different races, cultures or religions.
A king and a queen of different suits as a starting hand in Texas hold 'em (see marriage (poker slang)).

ety: From mixed + martial arts.

s.def: A style of combat sport allowing a wide range of combat techniques such as striking and grappling.
ex: Mixed martial arts is essentially about making the opponent tire out before you do so you are at an advantage in dealing devastating moves.

ety: Etymology tree English mix Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English mixer From mix + -er.

s.def: A machine outfitted with (typically blunt) blades with which it mixes or beats ingredients in a bowl below.
One who, or a device that, mixes or merges things together.
One who mixes or socializes.
ex: Bad mixer as he was, he preferred to be "out of it" in a crowd than out of it altogether.

s.def: A nonalcoholic drink (such as lemonade, Coca-Cola or fruit juice) that is added to spirits to make cocktails.
ex: Do we have any mixers? I don't want to drink this vodka neat.

s.def: A mixing console.
ex: I have such a quiet bong that I literally have to put my mixer in my lap and turn both knobs all the way up just to get it to pick up the bubbles.

s.def: A dance or other social event meant to foster new acquaintances, as at the beginning of a school year.
Any of various social dances involving frequent changes of partners.
A device for combining hot and cold water before it emerges from a single spout or shower head.
A nonlinear electrical circuit that creates new frequencies from two signals applied to it.
A chiropractor who uses other treatments in addition to spinal adjustment.

ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.

s.def: The act of mixing.
ex: The mixture of sulphuric acid and water produces heat.

s.def: Something produced by mixing.
ex: An alloy is a mixture of two metals.

s.def: Something that consists of diverse elements.
ex: The day was a mixture of sunshine and showers.

s.def: A medicinal compound, typically a suspension of a solid in a solution
ex: A teaspoonful of the mixture to be taken three times daily after meals

s.def: A compound organ stop.
A cloth of variegated colouring.
A mix of different dry foods as a snack, especially chevda or Bombay mix.

ety: From Japanese 宮古島 (miyako-jima).

s.def: The Miyako language of the island, one of several Ryūkyūan languages.
A group of islands in Okinawa Prefecture, Japan. It lies a few hundred kilometres east of Taipei, Taiwan.

ety: From Japanese 宮脇 + English forest. Named after Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki.

s.def: A forest planted using the Miyawaki method invented by Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki.

ety: Borrowed from Japanese 宮崎(みやざき) (Miyazaki).

s.def: The capital city of Miyazaki Prefecture, Japan.
A prefecture of Japan.
A surname from Japanese.

ety: From Middle English mesan, meseyn, myson, from Middle French misaine, modified from Old French migenne (through influence from Italian mezzana), from Old Catalan mitjana, feminine of mitjan, ultimately from Latin medianus. Doublet of mean and median.

s.def: Mizzenmast.
Mizzensail.
Hindmost; nearest the stern.
ex: the mizzen shrouds, sails, etc.

ety: From mizzen + mast.

s.def: The aftmost mast on a ship having three masts; the third-tallest mast on a full-rigged ship.
The third-foremost mast on a ship having more than three masts.
The second mast of a ship having two masts where the second one is shorter, such as a ketch or yawl.

ety: From mizzen + sail.

s.def: A fore-and-aft sail set on a mizzenmast.
ex: Six of the Krabben's massive tentacles had wrapped themselves around the mizzensail.

s.def: Initialism of Multiple Launch Rocket System.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Mνημονῐκός (Mnēmonĭkós) is derived from μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives); while μνήμων (mnḗmōn) is from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μω…

s.def: Of or relating to mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).
Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
Of or relating to memory.
Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
The human-readable, textual form of an assembly language instruction, not including operands.
Synonym of mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).

ety: Borrowed from Māori moa, from Proto-Polynesian *moa (“fowl”).

s.def: Any of several species of large, extinct, flightless birds of the family Dinornithidae that were native to New Zealand; until its extinction, one species was the largest bird in the world.
ex: For instance, the little bush moa fed nearly exclusively on forest vegetation, whereas the heavy-footed moa was a grazer in open vegetation habitats.

s.def: An extremely tall individual.

ety: From Middle English mone, mane, mān, (also as mene), from Old English *mān, *mǣn (“complaint; lamentation”), from Proto-West Germanic *mainu, from Proto-Germanic *mainō (“opinion; mind”). Cognate with Old Frisian mēne (“opinion”), Old High German meina (“opinion”). Old English *mān, *mǣn is inferred from Old English mǣnan (“to complain over; grieve; mourn”). More at mean.

s.def: A low, mournful cry of pain, sorrow or pleasure.
ex: let out a deep moan
We heard the distant moan of a stag in pain.

s.def: A lament or sorrow.
ex: to make one's moan

s.def: To make a moan or similar sound.
ex: She moaned with pleasure and squirmed with delight from receiving oral sex.
They shared a common dread that he would begin moaning.

s.def: To complain about; to bemoan, to bewail; to mourn.
ex: Much did the Craven seeme to mone his case […].
1708, Matthew Prior, the Turtle and the Sparrow Ye floods, ye woods, ye echoes, moan / My dear Columbo, dead and gone.

s.def: To grieve.
To say in a moan, or with a moaning voice.
ex: ‘Please don't leave me,’ he moaned.

s.def: To complain; to grumble.
To distress (someone); to sadden.
ex: which infinitely moans me

s.def: Of or pertaining to a moa.

ety: From Middle English mote, from Old French mote (“mound, embankment”); compared also to Old French motte (“hillock, lump, clod, turf”), from Medieval Latin mota (“a mound, hill”), of Germanic origin, perhaps via Frankish *mot, *motta (“mud, peat, bog, turf”), from Proto-Germanic *mutô, *mudraz, *muþraz (“dirt, filth, mud, swamp”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mut- (“dark, dirty”). Cognate with Alemannic German Mott, Mutte (“peat, turf”), Bavarian Mott (“peat, turf”), dialectal Dutch mot (“dust,…

s.def: A deep, wide defensive ditch, normally filled with water, surrounding a fortified habitation.
A characteristic of a business that enhances its resilience against competitive pressures, arising from the inherent nature of its products, services, brand, or other structural advantages.
A circular lowland between a resurgent dome and the walls of the caldera surrounding it.
A clear ring outside the eyewall of a tropical cyclone.
A hill or mound.
To surround with a moat.

ety: From Middle English mob, short for mobile, from Latin mōbile (vulgus) (“fickle (crowd)”).

s.def: A large or disorderly group of people; especially one bent on riotous or destructive action.
ex: Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.
See also: Mob (the masses)

s.def: The lower classes of a community; the rabble.
ex: A cluster of mob, who were making themselves merry with their betters.

s.def: A group of animals of any kind.
ex: Well behind the fire were the pack-saddles and a dark mob of feeding horses[.]

s.def: A mafia: a group that engages in organized crime.
ex: What if it is a mob killing? They can’t hurt me, but …
See also: Mob, Mafia (proper noun senses for specific ones)

s.def: A group of Aboriginal people associated with an extended family group, clan group or wider community group, from a particular place or country.
To crowd around (someone), sometimes with hostility.
ex: The fans mobbed a well-dressed couple who resembled their idols.

s.def: To crowd into or around a place.
ex: The shoppers mobbed the store on the first day of the sale.

s.def: A promiscuous woman; a harlot or wench; a prostitute.
A mob cap.
ex: c. 1773-1774, Oliver Goldsmith, letter to Mrs Bunbury cover their faces with mobs

s.def: To wrap up in, or cover with, a cowl.

ety: From Classical Persian موبَد (mōbad).

s.def: A Zoroastrian cleric of a particular rank, qualified to serve as celebrant priest at the Yasna ceremony and to train other priests.
Group bullying.
The aggressive behaviour of a group of animals on another individual (especially a predator).
Mob programming.

ety: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”). The video-gaming sense was coined by Richard Bartle to describe NPCs or creatures capable of moving "under their own power" in the 1978 video game Multi-User Dungeon. Bartle retracted an earlier claim of his that it was from the kinetic sculpture sense of mobile (for the "unpredictable but limited" motion of the hanging ornaments).

s.def: Capable of being moved, especially on wheels.
ex: mobile home; mobile library

s.def: decoration
Able to move freely or easily.
ex: She's mobile again after her skiing accident.

s.def: Easily moved in feeling, purpose, or direction; excitable; changeable; fickle.
ex: the quick and mobile curiosity of her disposition

s.def: Pertaining to or by agency of mobile phones.
ex: mobile number
mobile internet

s.def: Characterized by an extreme degree of fluidity; moving or flowing with great freedom.
ex: Mercury is a mobile liquid.

s.def: Changing in appearance and expression under the influence of the mind.
ex: mobile features
a mobile face

s.def: Capable of being moved, aroused, or excited; capable of spontaneous movement.
The internet accessed via mobile devices; the version of a product seen on mobile devices.
ex: There are many business opportunities in mobile.
The bug affects mobile, but not desktop.

s.def: One who moves or can move (e.g. to travel).
An electronic game played using a cellular phone.

ety: From mobile + phone.

s.def: A portable (handheld) telephone that connects with the cellular telephone network.
A portable telephone (for example, one installed in a car) that connects with the telephone network, typically by means of radio transmissions.

ety: From Middle French mobilité, and its source, Latin mōbilitās (“mobility”).

s.def: The ability to move; capacity for movement.
ex: I find the enduring existence of high heels both a frustrating mystery and a testament to the triumph of women’s neuroses over their mobility.

s.def: A tendency to sudden change; mutability, changeableness.
The ability of a military unit to move or be transported to a new position.
The degree to which particles of a liquid or gas are in movement.
The ability of people to move between different social levels or professional occupations.

ety: From French mobilisation or mobilize + -ation.

s.def: The marshalling and organizing of troops and national resources in preparation for war, bringing them to a state of readiness for an action.
ex: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed into law a key piece of legislation overhauling the country’s mobilization rules.

s.def: The act of mobilizing.
ex: a national mobilization to fight climate change

s.def: The softening of rock such that geochemical migration can take place.
The transport of a copy of a gene from one chromosome, or one organism to another.

ety: From French mobiliser.

s.def: To make something mobile.
To assemble troops and their equipment in a coordinated fashion so as to be ready for war.
To get ready for war.
Subject to mobilization

ety: From mob + -o- + -cracy.

s.def: Rule or control by the mob (or by the mass of ordinary people); a mob as a politically powerful force.
ex: That this ultrareactionary mobocracy was composed mainly of people with brown skins ought to have made no difference.

ety: From Powhatan makasin, mockasin, mawhcasuns (plural), from Proto-Algonquian *maxkeseni. The word is cognate with Massachusett mohkisson, mokussin, Mi'kmaq mksɨn, Munsee mahkusin, Ojibwe makizin. First appears c. 1612 in the writings of John Smith. It has been suggested that sense 4 (“North American snake”) may be derived from a different Native American word.

s.def: A modern shoe with either a low or no heel resembling a traditional Native American moccasin in that the leather forming the sides of the shoe is stitched at the top.
ex: Walking moccasin of gray chrome tanned leather. Waterproof. Flexible elk sole.
The men's shoe, a classic, low-heeled moccasin, was called Model 175. A classier women's version soon followed.

s.def: A traditional Native North American shoe, usually without a heel or sole, made of a piece of deerskin or other soft leather turned up at the edges which are either stitched together at the top of the shoe, or sewn to a vamp (a piece covering the top of the foot).
ex: The captive wore the moccasins gratefully.

s.def: A light beige colour, like that of a moccasin.
ex: He came in a primitive, rickety buggy, drawn by an old, moccasin-colored horse, which, it is to be hoped, had seen better days.
I prefer the Culprit brand in the moccasin color, the red shad color and the black with blue tail.

s.def: Any of several North American snakes of the genus Agkistrodon, particularly the copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) and the cottonmouth or water moccasin (Agkistrodon piscivorus).

ety: From Mocha, Yemen, a port on the Red Sea, from Arabic اَلْمُخَا (al-muḵā), for its role as a major marketplace for coffee during Ottoman rule. The beans often had a chocolaty flavor, hence by extension came to refer to any coffee with a chocolate flavor, or any mixture of coffee and chocolate flavors, notably coffee with chocolate syrup added.

s.def: A coffee drink with chocolate syrup added, or a serving thereof.
ex: "Can you hear the kitchen door being opened at this moment or detect the exact aroma of our host's mocha?" he demanded.

s.def: A flavour that combines coffee and chocolate.
ex: mocha brownies

s.def: A dark brown colour, like that of mocha coffee.
A strong Arabian coffee.
Any of a number of species of moths in the geometrid subfamily Sterrhinae, many European species having dark brown coloration.
An Abyssinian weight, equivalent to a Troy grain.
Of a dark brown colour, like that of mocha coffee.
A city in Taiz Governorate, Yemen.
A village in Gujarat, India.
A village in Madhya Pradesh, India.
A city in Tungurahua Province, Ecuador.
A female given name.
A surname.
The name originally proposed for JavaScript.

ety: From Middle English mokken, from Old French mocquer, moquier (“to deride, jeer”), from Middle Dutch mocken (“to mumble”) or Middle Low German mucken (“to grumble, talk with the mouth half-opened”), both from Proto-West Germanic *mokkijan, *mukkijan (“to low, bellow; mumble”), from Proto-Germanic *mukkijaną, *mūhaną (“to low, bellow, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūg-, *mūk- (“to low, mumble”). ex: Is tortured thirst itself too sweet a cup? Gall, and more bitter mocks, shall make it up.

s.def: Mockery; the act of mocking.
Ellipsis of mock examination.
ex: He got a B in his History mock, but improved to an A in the exam.

s.def: A mockup or prototype; particularly, ellipsis of mock object, as used in unit testing.
ex: Mocks replace the objects with which your methods under test collaborate, thus offering a layer of isolation.

s.def: To mimic, to simulate.
ex: To see the life as lively mocked as ever / Still sleep mocked death.
Mocking marriage with a dame of France.

s.def: To create an artistic representation of.
ex: [I]ts sculptor well those passions read / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things, / The hand that mocked them and the heart that fed: […]

s.def: To make fun of, especially by mimicking; to taunt.
ex: Let not ambition mock their useful toil.

s.def: To tantalise, and disappoint the hopes of.
ex: The wind is mocking my efforts to light a fire!
Why do I overlive? / Why am I mocked with death, and lengthened out / to deathless pain?
He will not […] / Mock us with his blest sight, then snatch him hence.

ex: mock leather
mock turtle-soup

Any of several similar but not closely related plants.

ety: First use appears c. 1915–1920, deverbal from mock up (verb), by imitation of French maquette.

ety: From mock + -er.

ety: From Middle English mokkery, from Anglo-Norman mokerie, mokery and Middle French mocquerie, moquerie, from moquer, moker (“to mock”) + -erie (“-ery”), perhaps from Byzantine Greek μωκός (mōkós, “mocker”), perhaps from Arabic مَكْر (makr, “scheme, plot”). Equivalent to mock + -ery.

Something so lacking in necessary qualities as to inspire ridicule; a laughing-stock.
Something insultingly imitative; an offensively futile action, gesture etc.
Mimicry, imitation, now usually in a derogatory sense; a travesty, a ridiculous simulacrum.
ex: The defendant wasn't allowed to speak at his own trial - it was a mockery of justice.

ety: From mocking + bird, from the ability of the birds to mimic sounds and, in some cases, hum as a wake-up call.

s.def: Any of various long-tailed American songbirds of the genera Mimus and Melanotis, noted for their ability to mimic calls of other birds.
Synonym of tui (“a species of honeyeater, Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae, a bird which is endemic to New Zealand”).

Clipping of modification.

Moderations: university examinations generally taken in the first year.

ety: From Middle French modal, from Medieval Latin modālis (“pertaining to a mode”), from Latin modus (“mode”). Compare to French, Spanish, and Portuguese modal and Italian modale. By surface analysis, mod(e) + -al.

A modal (etymology 1, adjective sense 2) form, notably a modal auxiliary.
Of, relating to, or describing the mood of a clause.
Of, relating to, or composed in the musical modi by which an octave is divided, associated with emotional moods in Ancient — and in medieval ecclesiastical — music.
Of, or relating to the modality between propositions.
Relating to the statistical mode.
Requiring immediate user interaction and thus presented so that it cannot be closed or interacted behind until a decision is made.
ex: a modal dialog; a modal window

s.def: Relating to the form of a thing rather to any of its attributes.
Having separate modes in which user input has different effects.
A modal (etymology 1, adjective sense 4) proposition.

In lace-making, a small decorative piece inserted into a pattern.
Style or fashion; popular trend.
ex: Her wardrobe is always in mode.
The dress she wore was no longer a cheap blue serge but a handsome tricolette, richly trimmed according to the prevailing mode.

A malleable substance used in building models and sculpting.

ety: From Middle English moderat(e) (“moderate, temperate”), borrowed from Latin moderātus, perfect active participle of moderor (“to regulate, to restrain, to moderate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from moder-, modes-, a stem appearing also in modestus (“moderate, discreet, modest”), from modus (“a measure”); see mode and modest. Doublet of moderato. Displaced native Old English ġemetlīċ (“moderate”) and metegian (“to moderate”). Cognate with French modéré.

ex: moderate language
a moderate Calvinist
travelling at a moderate speed

Mediocre.
Average or middling, for example in price.
Not violent or rigorous; temperate; mild; gentle.
ex: a moderate winter

One who holds an intermediate position between extremes, as in politics.
ex: While the moderates usually propose political compromise, it's often only achieved when the extremists allow them so
The moderates are the natural advocates of ecumenism against the fanatics of their churches.

To reduce the excessiveness of (something).
ex: to moderate rage, action, desires, etc.
By its astringent Quality, it moderates the relaxing quality of warm Water.

s.def: To become less excessive.
ex: He used to be an extremist but moderated later in life.

Mr. Chairman, at this moment I stand astonished at my own moderation!
America is a model of force and freedom and moderation - with all the coarseness and rudeness of its people.

ex: With the quick moderation of the weather some buying has appeared that had been held up because of the extremely cold weather […].

s.def: The process of moderating a discussion.

An examiner at Oxford and Cambridge universities.
At the University of Dublin, either the first (senior) or second (junior) in rank in an examination for the degree of Bachelor of Arts.
Someone who supervises and monitors the setting and marking of examinations by different people to ensure consistency of standards.
A mechanical arrangement for regulating motion in a machine, or producing equality of effect.
A kind of lamp in which the flow of the oil to the wick is regulated.

ety: From Middle French moderne, from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, "just now". See also mode.

Even though we moderns can never crawl inside the skin of the ancient and think and feel as he did […] we must as historians make the attempt.

ety: From Middle English modicum, from Latin modicum (“a little, a small amount”), a noun use of the neuter form of modicus (“moderate; restrained, temperate; reasonable”) + -cum (suffix forming neuter nouns). Modicus is derived from modus (“a measure; a bound, limit”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”)) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). The plural form modica is derived from Latin modica.

s.def: A modest, small, or trifling amount.
ex: Unable to garner even a modicum of support for his plan, he conceded to follow the others.
I have learned from experience that a modicum of snuff can be most efficacious.
He drinks iced lemonade through a long straw, without moving, without even shifting his head, and thereby gains a modicum of inner coolness.

ety: From Middle English modificatioune, from Middle French modification and its etymon Latin modificātiō (“a measuring”), from modificāre (“to limit, control, modify”); see modify. By surface analysis, modify + -ication.

ety: Uncertain; may be a compound term of Somali words "muuq" (appearance) + "disho", present subjunctive form of dil (beat / kill). ety: Figurative use of Moghul, which originally meant Mongol, or person of Mongolian descent. In this context, it refers to the Mughal Empire (Mughal being Persian or Arabic for "Mongol") of the Indian subcontinent that existed between 1526 and 1857: the early Mughal emperors claimed a heritage dating back to the Mongol ruler Genghis Khan. ety: From Old French monarchie, from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”). By surface analysis, mon- (“one, single”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

s.def: A government in which sovereignty is embodied within a single, today usually hereditary head of state (whether as a figurehead or as a powerful ruler).
ex: An absolute monarchy is a monarchy where the monarch is legally the ultimate authority in all temporal matters.

s.def: The territory ruled over by a monarch; a kingdom.
ex: What scourge for perjury / Can this dark monarchy afford false Clarence?

s.def: A form of government where sovereignty is embodied by a single ruler in a state and his high aristocracy representing their separate divided lands within the state and their low aristocracy representing their separate divided fiefs.

ety: From Middle English monasterie, from Old French monastere, from Medieval Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermitage, monastery”), from μοναστήριος (monastḗrios, “alone, made alone”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium”, suffix forming place names), from μονάζω (monázō, “to be alone”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”) + -άζω (-ázō, verb-forming suffix). ety: From Middle French monastique, from Late Latin monasticus.

s.def: To render moral; to correct the morals of; to give the appearance of morality to.

s.def: To apply to a moral purpose; to explain in a moral sense; to draw a moral from.

ety: From Dutch moeras (“marsh, swamp”), an alteration (with influence from Dutch moer (“moor”)) of a direct descendant of Middle Dutch marasch (“marsh”).
