s.def: Dishonest, shady.

ety: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).

s.def: A muttered complaint or protest; the expression of dissatisfaction in a low muttering voice; any expression of complaint or discontent.
ex: In fear of disease and in the interest of his health man will be muzzled and masked like a vicious dog, and that without any murmur of complaint.

s.def: low sounds or speech
Any low, indistinct sound, like that of running water.
ex: The delightful murmur of water running over pebbles is heard a few yards off
1979: A translation of the Eclogues by Paul Alpers The windy murmur of the breeze subsides.

s.def: Soft indistinct speech.
ex: A murmur arose from the audience.
She howl'd aloud, “I am on fire within. / There comes no murmur of reply. / What is it that will take away my sin, / And save me lest I die?”
The moment had come for the honeyed word. I lowered my voice to a confidential murmur, but on her inquiring if I had laryngitis raised it again.

s.def: The sound made by any condition which produces a noisy, or turbulent, flow of blood through the heart.
To grumble; to complain in a low, muttering voice, or express discontent at or against someone or something.
ex: The Iewes then murmured at him because he sayde: I am that breed which is come doune from heaven.

s.def: To speak or make low, indistinguishable noise; to mumble, mutter.
ex: I couldn't hear the words; he just murmured a lot.
The bees murmured in the forest. The waves murmured on the shore.
“Oh yes,” he murmured in a tone of obligatory surprise, as he proceeded to make the kind of 2 which he attributed to Margaret's style of chirography.

s.def: To say (something) indistinctly, to mutter.
ex: Gabriel murmured a confused reply, and hastened on.
With a husky voice she murmured that he was the very dearest grandfather anyone ever had.
“[…] Don’t look now,” he murmured, lowering his eyes demurely, “but the most handsome man in Brookfield, Connecticut, has just walked in the room.”

ety: From the common Irish name Murphy. Compare Donovan (“a potato”).

s.def: An Irish or white potato.

ety: Named after Edward A. Murphy Jr. (1918–1990), a development engineer who worked for a brief time on the rocket-sled experiments of the United States Air Force in 1948.

s.def: An adage which states that if anything can go wrong, then it will.
ex: I ran into the perfect exemplification of “Murphy's law” at one university, where everything that could go wrong did!

ety: The noun is derived from Late Middle English morein, morine, moreyn (“(widespread) death; widespread sickness, plague; fatal disease; carnage; carrion”), from Anglo-Norman morine, mourine, moreyn (“death; widespread sickness, plague; carrion; cattle disease”), Middle French morine, and Old French morine, mourine, murine (“widespread sickness, plague; animal which has died from a disease”), from Late Latin morina (“plague”), probably from Latin morior (“to die; to decay, wither”). The adjective…

s.def: Infectious disease; pestilence, plague; (countable) sometimes used in curses such as a murrain on someone: an outbreak of such a disease; a plague.
ex: VVhat the Murrion care I vvho you are, hold off your Fingers, or Ile cut them vvith this Diamond.
But vvhat the murrain have they to do vvith Quality, vvhy don't their Husbands make 'em mind their Shops?
[A]t last, with a murrain to her, she cast her bewitching eye upon me.

s.def: A widespread affliction, calamity, or destructive influx, especially when seen as divine retribution; a plague.
ex: Usura [a personification of usury] is a murrain, usura / blunteth the needle in the maid’s hand / and stoppeth the spinner’s cunning.

s.def: Any of several highly infectious diseases of cattle or other livestock, such as anthrax, babesiosis, or rinderpest; or a particular epizootic thereof; also, an infectious disease affecting other animals, such as poultry.
ex: water murrain

s.def: An infectious disease affecting plants.
ex: potato murrain

s.def: A poor-quality green-salted animal hide.
Death, especially from an infectious disease.
ex: Moreyn dethe mortalité […] mourine […]

s.def: Rotting flesh, especially of an animal which has died from a disease; carrion.
Disgusting or offensive, as if having an infectious disease; contemptible, despicable, loathsome, plaguey.
ex: No, ich know thars not within this land / A muryner Cat than Gyb is, betwixt the tems [Thames] and Tyne, […]

s.def: Used as an intensifier: to a great extent; extreme, intense.
Used as an intensifier: extremely, very.

ety: Transliteration of Arabic مُوسَى (mūsā), Persian موسی (Musâ), and Turkish Musa; ultimately from Biblical Hebrew. Doublet of Moses.

s.def: A male given name from Arabic, equivalent to English Moses.
Moses, a rasul in Islam.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic مُصَلًّى (muṣallan), from صَلَّى (ṣallā, “to pray”).

s.def: A place for praying (e.g. outside a mosque); a praying room.

ety: Borrowed from French muscat.

s.def: A white grape variety; used as table grapes and for making raisins and sweet wine.
ex: Among Turks, pills consisting of hemp buds, muscat nuts, saffron, and honey were a popular aphrodisiac.

s.def: The muscatel wine made from these grapes.
The vine bearing this fruit.

ety: From Middle English muscle, muscule, muskylle, and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (“mouse”). Doublet of mussel. More at mouse.

s.def: contractile tissue
A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.
ex: Muscle consists largely of actin and myosin filaments.

s.def: An organ composed of muscle tissue.
ex: You, Boxer, the very day that those great muscles of yours lose their power, Jones will sell you to the knacker […]

s.def: A well-developed physique, in which the muscles are enlarged from exercise.
Strength, force.
ex: The lesson to be drawn from the events of 1914, to Roosevelt's mind, was that civilization needed muscle to defend it, not just solemn words.
It was going to take muscle to pluck Miss Agnes out of the canal.

s.def: Hired strongmen or bodyguards.
ex: It was easy enough to dodge him, let him crash into the floorboards. Peltroc knew that his priority was the leader, not the hired muscle.

s.def: To use force to make progress, especially physical force.
ex: He muscled his way through the crowd.
Hensel and Wilson hit a series of leg shots simultaneously as Christian muscles between them with Quinn right on his heels.
Nothing the Nebraskans ever again recorded managed to muscle more than minimal attention.

s.def: To move forcefully or with great strength.
ex: She muscled through the ruins.

s.def: A disorder in which a person becomes obsessed with the idea that they are not muscular enough.

ety: PIE word *múHs From muscle + memory. First attested in 1892.

s.def: The ability to reproduce a particular movement using subconscious neuromuscular control which is acquired as a result of the physiological adaptation of the body to repetition of the movement.
ex: I said that one can move a muscle only if one has an inherent muscle memory which has been stored in the brain at some previous time.
My shadow / Change is coming / Now is my time / Listen to my muscle memory / Contemplate what I've been clinging to / Forty six and two ahead of me

s.def: The ability to regain lost muscle size and strength much faster than initially building it, due to retained muscle nuclei.

ety: Corrupted from Spanish mascabado or Portuguese mascavado, from the verb mascavar, a corrupted form of menoscabar (“to despise”).

s.def: An unrefined brown sugar with a strong flavour of molasses.

ety: In 1850 from Muscovy glass + -ite, from the province Muscovy in Russia. Named by James Dwight Dana.

s.def: A pale brown mineral of the mica group, being a basic potassium aluminosilicate with the chemical formula KAl₂(Si₃Al)O₁₀(OH,F)₂; used as an electrical insulator etc.

ety: 1535. From Latin Moscovita (“resident of Moscow or Muscovy, Russian”), also Muscovita, Moschovita, from Moscovia or Muscovia (“Muscovy”) + -ita.

s.def: An inhabitant or native of Muscovy or Moscow.
A Russian.
Of or relating to Muscovy or Moscow, or the people of these places.
Russian.
Muscovy duck

ety: Late 17th century; from muscle (Latin mūsculus) + -ar. Compare French musculaire.

s.def: Having large, well-developed muscles.
Of, relating to, or connected with muscles.
Brawny, thewy, having strength.
Robust, strong.
ex: Future prime ministers may struggle to replicate the sort of muscular countrywide support that [Narendra] Modi was able to earn.
Playing out now, with Florida leading, is one of the most muscular policing movements in modern times.

s.def: Full-bodied
ex: muscular wine

ety: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

s.def: Of a person: a source of inspiration.
ex: Yoko Ono was John Lennon's wife, lover, and muse.

s.def: A poet; a bard.
ex: So may some gentle Muse With lucky words favour my destined urn

s.def: To become lost in thought, to ponder.
To say (something) with due consideration or thought.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:muse.

s.def: To think on; to meditate on.
ex: Come, then, expressive Silence, muse his praise.

s.def: To wonder at.
ex: Muse not that I thus suddenly proceed; for what I will, I will, and there an end.

s.def: An act of musing; a period of thoughtfulness.
ex: still he sate long time astonished / As in great muse, ne word to creature spake.
And with this Alan fell into a muse, and for a long time sate^([sic]) very sad and silent.
He fell into a muse and pulled his upper lip.

s.def: A gap or hole in a hedge, fence, etc. through which a wild animal is accustomed to pass; a muset.
ex: Find a hare without a muse. (old proverb)

ety: From Middle English Muse, from Latin Musa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

s.def: One of the nine Ancient Greek deities of the arts.

ety: From museum + -ology.

s.def: The design, organization, and management of museums.

ety: From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of mosaic.

s.def: A building or institution dedicated to the acquisition, conservation, study, exhibition, and educational interpretation of objects having scientific, historical, cultural or artistic value.
ex: visit the history museum
They're opening a new coin exhibition at the local museum.

s.def: To place in a museum.
ex: I use daily those books that for others are museumed. The glass case approach depresses me, makes books into porcelain, guts them of what they are.

s.def: To visit museums.
ex: I told her I'd do just one visit to start; I don't really have time to do a lot of museuming.

ety: Probably a variant of mash, or from a dialectal variant of Middle English mos (“mush, pulp, porridge”); compare Middle English appelmos (“applesauce”), from Old English mōs (“food, victuals, porridge, mush”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōs, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“porridge, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“wet, fat, dripping”). Cognate with Scots moosh (“mush”), Dutch moes (“pulp, mush, porridge”), German Mus (“jam, puree, mush”), Swedish mos (“pulp, mash, mush”).

s.def: A somewhat liquid mess, often of food; a soft or semisolid substance.
A mixture of noise produced by the harmonics of continuous-wave stations.
The foam of a breaker.
A magmatic body containing a significant proportion of crystals suspended in the liquid phase or melt.
A gun.
ex: Do you want me to back out the mush, bruv?

s.def: To squish so as to break into smaller pieces or to combine with something else.
ex: He mushed the ingredients together.
One must compartmentalize one's life and not let different facets/experiences mush over into one another.

s.def: A food comprising cracked or rolled grains cooked in water or milk; porridge.
Cornmeal cooked in water and served as a porridge or as a thick sidedish like grits or mashed potatoes.
ex: However, they did make and sometimes even bake cornmeal mushes that could be either sweetened or fortified with fat.

s.def: A directive given (usually to dogs or a horse) to start moving, or to move faster.
A walk, especially across the snow with dogs.

ety: Borrowed from Armenian Մուշ (Muš).

s.def: A historically Armenian city in the Turuberan province of Greater Armenia, now in eastern Turkey.
A province of Turkey.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Arabic مُشْرِك (mušrik).

s.def: A person who rejects tawhid; an idolater, a polytheist.
ex: And do not marry mushrik women until they believe, for a believing bondmaid is better than a mushrik woman, even though you may admire her.

ety: From Middle English muscheron, musseron, from Anglo-Norman musherum, moscheron, from Old French moisseron, of obscure origin: probably derived from Old French mosse, moise ("moss"; whence also French mousse), as the use first applied to a type of fungus which grows in moss, from Frankish *mosu (“moss”) or Old Dutch *mosa (“moss”), akin to Old High German mosa (“moor, swamp”), Old High German mos (“moss, bog”), Old High German mios (“moss, mire”), Old English mēos (“moss”), Old English mōs (“bog…

s.def: A fungus producing such fruiting bodies.
Ellipsis of mushroom cloud.
To gather mushrooms.
ex: We used to go mushrooming in the forest every weekend.

s.def: Any of the fleshy fruiting bodies of fungi typically produced above ground on soil or on their food sources (such as decaying wood).
ex: Some mushrooms are edible whereas others are poisonous, and sometimes they are difficult to tell apart.
Arabs consider the eating of mushrooms as an aphrodisiac aid.

s.def: Champignon or Agaricus bisporus, the mushroom species most commonly used in cooking.
Any of the mushroom-shaped pegs in bar billiards.
A concrete column with a thickened portion at the top, used to support a slab.
Something that grows very quickly or seems to appear suddenly.
One who rises suddenly from a low condition in life; an upstart.
ex: upstarts […]call in reproach mushrooms

s.def: Having characteristics like those of a mushroom, for example in shape or appearance, speed of growth, or texture.
ex: mushroom cloud

ety: Etymology tree English mush Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English mushy From mush + -y.

s.def: Resembling or having the consistency of mush; semiliquid, pasty, or granular.
ex: I don't especially like mushy oatmeal.
Today, some seafood experts say, the cheaper (though mushier) roe feeds 60 percent of the market.

s.def: Soft; squishy.
ex: The brake pedal is mushy sometimes when I step on it.
Compared with the excellent scroll wheels on the Basilisk V3 and G502 X, the G203’s scroll wheel feels less defined and mushier in its ratcheting.

s.def: Overly sappy, corny, or cheesy; sentimental, especially in a romantic way; maudlin.
ex: Skip the mushy, romantic scenes and get to the action.
The day before she left for college, she and Vicki said goodbye. They exchanged mushy cards and promised to write frequently.

ety: From Middle English musik, musike, borrowed from Anglo-Norman musik, musike, Old French musique, and their source Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ), from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”), an Ancient Greek deity of the arts. By surface analysis, muse + -ic (“pertaining to”). In this sense, displaced native Old English drēam (“music”), whence Modern English dream. Fully displaced Old English sweġl.

s.def: A series of sounds organized in time, usually employing some combination of harmony, melody, rhythm, tempo, timbre, sound design, lyrics, etc., often to convey a mood.
ex: I keep listening to this music because it’s a masterpiece.
Music lessons in early childhood lead to changes in the brain that could improve its performance far into adulthood, researchers say.

s.def: Any interesting or pleasing sounds.
ex: Wilson's definite genius for rapid, witty dialogue which becomes a kind of conversational music at times.

s.def: An art form, created by organizing pitch, rhythm, and sounds made using musical instruments and/or singing.
A guide to playing or singing a particular tune; sheet music.
Electronic signal jamming.
Heated argument.
Fun; amusement.
To seduce or entice with music.
Musical.

ety: From music + box.

s.def: A box that generates or plays music, particularly one using mechanical means rather than electronic, generally using a cylinder or disk containing the music.
A school whose main objective is teaching music.
A short film integrating a song and imagery, produced for promotional or artistic purposes.

ety: From Middle English musical, from Old French [Term?], from Medieval Latin mūsicālis, from Latin mūsica (“music”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives); equivalent to music + -al.

s.def: Of, belonging or relating to music, or to its performance or notation.
ex: musical proportion
musical instruments

s.def: Pleasing to the ear; sounding agreeably; having the qualities of music; melodious; harmonious.
ex: She had a musical voice.

s.def: Fond of music; discriminating with regard to music; gifted or skilled in music.
ex: having a musical ear
The child is musical.

s.def: Pertaining to a class of games in which players move while music plays, but have to take a fixed position when it stops; by extension, any situation where people repeatedly change positions.
ex: Musical beds is the faculty sport around here.
Musical seats upon an airplane is not a game I recommend.
“Sounds like y'all are playing musical houses. How did you convince your mama to move to Austin?”

s.def: A stage performance, show or film that involves singing, dancing and musical numbers performed by the cast as well as acting.
ex: It is unthinkable for a straight play to enjoy a life span like those of the blockbuster musicals or to earn such astronomical grosses.

s.def: A meeting or a party for a musical entertainment; a musicale.

A children's game in which players circle a group of chairs. There is one chair fewer than the number of players. When someone who is not watching stops playing music, everybody sits down, and the player left without a chair is eliminated.
Any activity which results in repeated, pointless shuffling of people or objects.
ex: O’Donnell sounded world-weary as he recollected trying to sustain strategies for big issues through games of ministerial musical chairs.

ety: From Middle English musical instrumentis pl, musicalle instrumentes pl.

s.def: A device, object, contrivance or machine used to produce musical notes or sounds.

ety: From the French soirée musicale.

s.def: A musical entertainment, usually private and typically involving classical music
ex: Mr. and Mrs. Hugh Dillman entertained two hundred guests this evening with a musicale at Playa Rienta, their ocean front home.

ety: From Middle English musician, musicien, from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to musike + -ien. By surface analysis, music + -ician.

s.def: A composer, conductor, or performer of music; specifically, a person who sings and/or plays a musical instrument as a hobby, occupation, or profession.
ex: Jenny is a talented musician, playing the cello, saxophone, piano and guitar.

s.def: One who studies musicology.

ety: Etymology tree English music Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *lóǵos Proto-Hellenic *lógos Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) Ancient Greek -λογῐ́ᾱ (-logĭ́ā)bor. Latin -logialbor. French -logiebor. English -logy English musicology From music + -logy.

s.def: The scholarly or scientific study of music, as in historical research, music theory, or the physical nature of sound.

ety: From Middle English muske, borrowed from Old French musc, from Late Latin muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠muʃk⁠/) whence Persian مشک (mošk). Ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland of animals secreting the substance being compared to human testicles, a diminutive of मूष् (mūṣ, “mouse”), the shape of human testicles being compared to mice, from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s (“mouse”). Cognate with mouse.

s.def: A greasy secretion with a powerful odour, produced in a glandular sac of the male musk deer and used in the manufacture of perfumes.
ex: An old medical record relates that by means of musk the genital power of a man in his eightieth year was resuscitated.

s.def: A similar secretion produced by the otter and the civet.
A synthetic organic compound used as a substitute for the above.
The odour of musk.
Body odor, especially when aroused or unwashed.
ex: I was so excited I could smell my own musk.

s.def: A musk deer (genus Moschus).
A muskflower (Erythranthe moschata).
A plant of the genus Erodium (Erodium moschatum); the musky heronsbill.
A plant of the genus Muscari; grape hyacinth.
A small tree or tall shrub, Olearia argophylla, of south-eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania, with leaves that produce a musky aroma.
ex: [W]here the gullies are fringed with blackwoods, wattle, myrtles, musks and sassafras[.]

ety: So called because of the strong odour, or musk, emitted by the males during the rutting season.

s.def: An Arctic mammal, Ovibos moschatus of the Caprinae subfamily of the family Bovidae, having a thick coat and long curved horns.

ety: First attested in 1633; named for the scent of its immature flower heads.

s.def: A biennial herb of species Carduus nutans, in the sunflower family Asteraceae with a large drooping purple flower head, native to parts of Eurasia and North Africa and a common invasive species elsewhere.

ety: From Cree ᒪᐢᑫᐠ (maskek).

s.def: A terrain composed of peat bog with tussocky meadow and woody vegetation including spruce.

ety: First attested around 1210 as a surname, and later in the 1400s as a word for the sparrowhawk (Middle English forms: musket, muskett, muskete (“sparrow hawk”)), from Middle French mousquet, from Old Italian moschetto (a diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca) used to refer initially to a sparrowhawk (given its small size or speckled appearance) and then a crossbow arrow. The name was subsequently adopted for a heavier, shoulder-fired version of an arquebus, adhering to a pattern of namin…

s.def: A kind of firearm formerly carried by the infantry of an army, originally fired by means of a match, or matchlock, for which several mechanical appliances (including the flintlock, and finally the percussion lock) were successively substituted; ultimately superseded by the rifle.
ex: Soldier, soldier, won't you marry me, with your musket, fife and drum.

s.def: A male Eurasian sparrowhawk (Accipiter nisus).

ety: From musk + melon.

s.def: A true melon (Cucumis melo): such a plant or its fruit, especially one with sweet flesh.

ety: Perhaps so called for its musky odour and because it resembles a rat, or perhaps called by an Algonquian name like the Abenaki moskwas, with the spelling altered under the influence of the English words musk and rat.

s.def: A semiaquatic rodent of the tribe Ondatrini.
Any of several shrews in the family Soricidae, especially an Asian house shrew (Suncus murinus).
A bandicoot rat.

ety: Etymology tree English musk Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English musky From musk + -y.

s.def: Resembling or characteristic of musk, especially in scent.
muskellunge

ety: Borrowed around 1615 from Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim, “one who submits”), the active participle of أَسْلَمَ (ʔaslama, “he submitted”), verb form IV from the triliteral root س ل م (s l m), "to be whole, intact". The verbal noun إسْلام (ʔislām) means literally "submission". In a religious sense, الْإِسْلَام (al-ʔislām) translates to "faith, piety", and مُسْلِم (muslim) to "one who has (religious) faith or piety".

s.def: An adherent of Islam.
ex: Muslims invented the concept of zero, which is a foundation for the numbering system used throughout the world.
“At the end of the day, Jews and Muslims are cousins,” Alhomsi said.

s.def: A person who internalizes the Islamic cultural tradition, or way of thinking, as a frame of reference.
ex: Unfortunately, unlike “secular Jew” or “cultural Jew”, the term “cultural Muslim” isn’t widely understood.

s.def: A member of a predominantly Muslim South Slavic ethnic group (usually a Bosniak), irrespective of actual religious beliefs (used historically in Yugoslavia but persisting to some degree in some former Yugoslav states).
Being or relating to a believer of Islam.

ety: From French mousseline, from Italian mussolina, from Mussolo (“Mosul”), that is Mosul in northern Iraq (compare 1875 Knight, Edward H., Knight's American Mechanical Dictionary, V2 p1502: "Muslins are so called from Moussol in India."). Doublet of mousseline.

s.def: Any of several varieties of thin cotton cloth.
ex: A bleached or unbleached thin white cotton cloth, unprinted and undyed. [Nineteen varieties are thereafter listed.]

s.def: Fabric made of cotton, flax (linen), hemp, or silk, finely or coarsely woven.
ex: Other very different styles of fabric are now indifferently called muslins, and the term is used differently on the respective sides of the Atlantic.

s.def: Any of a wide variety of tightly-woven thin fabrics, especially those used for bedlinen.
Woven cotton or linen fabrics, especially when used for items other than garments.
A mock-up of a garment pattern made of inexpensive fabric for the purpose of optimizing its fit on the wearer, before the garment is produced in more expensive fabric.
ex: Fitting this pattern is tricky, so we recommend you make a muslin first.

s.def: Any of several different moths, especially the muslin moth, Diaphora mendica.
Woman as sex object; prostitute, as in a bit of muslin.
ex: "That was a pretty bit of muslin hanging on your arm—who was she?” asked the fascinating student.

ety: Related to mess (“disorder”).

s.def: To rumple, tousle or make (something) untidy.
ex: The old man affectionately mussed his grandson's hair.

s.def: A mess (disagreeable mixture or confusion of things; disorder).
A scramble, as when small objects are thrown down, to be taken by those who can seize them; a confused struggle.
ex: Gods so! a muss, a muss, a muss, a muss.

s.def: A term of endearment.

ety: From Middle English muscle (“mussel”), from Old English muscle, from Proto-West Germanic *muskulā, from Late Latin muscula, from Latin mūsculus (“mussel, muscle”, literally “little mouse”). Doublet of muscle.

s.def: Any of several groups of bivalve shellfish with elongated, asymmetrical shells.

ety: From Middle English moste ("must", literally, "had to", the past tense of Middle English moten (“to have to”)), from Old English mōste (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of mōtan (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną. Cognate with Dutch moest (“had to”), German musste (“had to”), Swedish måste (“must, have to, be obliged to”). More at mote.

s.def: To do as a requirement; indicates that the sentence subject is required as an imperative or directive to execute the sentence predicate, with failure to do so resulting in a failure or negative consequence.
ex: You must arrive in class on time.
This door handle must be rotated fully.
Everybody told me I must stop worrying, but I couldn't, because I knew that somehow there was still something wrong about the situation.

s.def: To do with certainty; indicates that the speaker is certain that the subject will have executed the predicate.
ex: If it has rained all day, it must be very wet outside.
Where would you have put the keyring? You couldn’t have lost it again! - I must have, because it's nowhere to be found.
I said it must be pretty late and I really must go.

s.def: Used to indicate that something is very likely, probable, or certain to be true.
ex: The children must be asleep by now.
There's the doorbell. It must be Dad.

s.def: Something that is mandatory, required or recommended.
ex: If you're trekking all day, a map is a must.
"There are no musts in my life - I'm free, white, and twenty-one."

s.def: Fruit juice that will ferment or has fermented, usually from grapes.
ex: No sweet grape lies hidden here in the shade of its vine-leaves, No fermenting must fills and o'erflows the deep vats.

s.def: The property of being stale or musty.
Something that exhibits the property of being stale or musty.
To make musty.
To become musty.
Alternative spelling of musth.

every dog must have his day
every dog must have its day

ety: From must + have.

s.def: Essential to own.
ex: The must-have toy is the apotheosis of the marketing of toys as fashion accessories.

s.def: US standard spelling of moustache.
ex: The fly, named “Daptolestes leei,” has markings on its face reminiscent of Lee’s characteristic sunglasses and white mustache.

ety: From Arabic مُصْطَفَى (muṣṭafā, “the chosen one”).

s.def: A male given name from Arabic used by Muslims.

ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish mestengo, from Old Spanish mesteño (“feral animal”) or mestengo (“feral animal”).

s.def: A small, hardy, naturalized (feral) horse of the North American west.
ex: Having ridden a distance of two or three miles, Garey slackened his pace, and put the mustang to a slow walk.

s.def: A merchant marine who joined the U.S. Navy as a commissioned officer during the American Civil War.
ex: He is a product of the merchant marine and is one of the officers called "Mustangs" who entered the navy during the Civil War.

s.def: A commissioned officer who started military service as an enlisted person.
ex: […] and the chief engineer is a "mustang" — that is, an officer who has risen from the ranks of enlisted men.
Mustang— Officer who came up through the ranks. None better.

s.def: To hunt mustangs (wild horses), either for military use or for slaughter as pet food.

ety: From Middle English mustard, from Old French moustarde (French moutarde), from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum. Compare Saterland Frisian Muster (“mustard”), Dutch mosterd (“mustard”), German Low German Musterd (“mustard”), Icelandic mustarður (“mustard”). Displaced Middle English senep, from Old English senep, from Latin sināpi (“mustard”). Sometimes mistakenly thought to come from Latin mustum ardens, but such a Latin phrase is not attested, and it is well understood that that the final -ar…

s.def: Dark yellow colour, the colour of mustard.
The tomalley of a crab, which resembles the condiment.
plant
A plant of certain species of the genus Brassica, or of related genera (especially Sinapis alba, in the family Brassicaceae, with yellow flowers, and linear seed pods).
Powder or paste made from seeds of the mustard plant, and used as a condiment or a spice.
ex: When the waitress brought the food, I asked whether she had any Dijon mustard.
He loved having mustard and toast for breakfast.

s.def: The leaves of the mustard plant, used as a salad.
ex: Mustard and cress sandwiches.

s.def: One of a family of vesicants containing one or more 2-chloroethyl (C₂H₄Cl) groups, commonly used in chemical warfare and cancer chemotherapy.
Ellipsis of mustard gas.
Energy, power (when throwing a baseball).
Of a dark yellow colour.

ety: Calque of German Senfgas.

s.def: A highly cytotoxic vesicant, C₄H₈Cl₂S, used in World War I that is known to cause skin burns, blisters, inflammation, edema, and potentially other respiratory effects.

s.def: The essential oil allyl isothiocyanate, also obtained from mustard seeds.
The hot pungent oil expressed from mustard seeds; used sparingly as a food dressing.
Any carnivorous mammal of the diverse weasel family Mustelidae, which also includes badgers, otters, martens, mink and wolverines.
ex: Mustelid diversity is well reflected in the Neogene fossil record, in spite of the fact that mustelids are among the rarest of fossil carnivores.
The mustelid head has a low, flat skull and short face with small ears and eyes.

ety: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”). Cognate with French montrer (“to show”), Italian mostrare (“to show”), Spanish mostrar (“to show”). See also monster.

s.def: A gathering.
ex: She seems to hear the Repetition of his Mens Names with Admiration; and waits only to answer him with as false a Muster of Lovers.
Of the temporal grandees of the realm, and of their wives and daughters, the muster was great and splendid.

s.def: Showing.
ex: And when you find your women's favour fail, / 'Tis ten to one you'll know yourself, and seek me, / Upon a better muster of your manners.

s.def: To show, exhibit.
To be gathered together for parade, inspection, exercise, or the like (especially of a military force); to come together as parts of a force or body.
ex: The whole male population, men and boys, mustered on the top of the hill.

s.def: To collect, call or assemble together, such as troops or a group for inspection, orders, display etc.
To enroll (into service).
To gather or round up livestock.
To look within oneself to summon (a particular positive quality, such as strength, energy or courage); see: muster up.
ex: I couldn't muster the courage to tell him.
That which Walter Raleigh had not courage to tell, not one of these men could muster the courage to ask.
She musters a smile for his nostalgic tale

s.def: Synonym of mustee.

ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi मस्त (mast) / Urdu مَسْت (mast, “drunk, intoxicated; lustful”); and also from Middle Hindi مَسْت (mst /⁠mast⁠/)), and from its etymon Classical Persian مَسْت (mast, “(adjective) drunk, intoxicated; (literary) in rut; of an elephant: in musth; (noun) drunkard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to be wet; to become wet”).

s.def: Chiefly preceded by in or on: the state each year during which a male animal (usually a camel or an elephant) exhibits increased aggressiveness and sexual activity due to a high level of testosterone.
ex: No animal in the world is so dangerous as an elephant in must.
I couldn't see the driver, and across my mind it rushed / That the Commissariat elephant had suddenly gone musth.

s.def: An instance of this.

ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English musty; further origin uncertain, possibly from one of the following: * From Anglo-Norman muste, moste, variants of moiste, muiste (“moist”), from Old French moiste (“clammy, damp, moist, wet”) (modern French moite (“muggy; sticky, sweaty”)), from a blend of Vulgar Latin *mucidus (from Latin mūcidus (“mouldy, musty”), from Old Latin mūceō (“to be mouldy or musty”) + -idus (suffix meaning ‘tending to’, forming adjectives)) + Latin mustum (“unferme…

s.def: Affected by dampness or mould; damp, mildewed, mouldy.
ex: Bradley assenting, went with him into an early public-house, haunted by unsavoury smells of musty hay and stale straw, […]
It was a thin book bound in faded morocco, with a copper-plate engraving as a frontispiece; the pages were musty with age and stained with mould.

s.def: Having an odour or taste of mould; also (generally), having a stale or unfresh odour or taste.
ex: musty food musty furniture a musty odour
It was a close, musty, ill-ventilated place, since its inmate seldom left it.

s.def: Characteristic of or relating to mould or mouldiness.
Of attitudes, ideas, writing, or other abstract things: no longer fresh or interesting; outdated, stale.
Of a person: boring and unadventurous; also, old-fashioned, stuck in the past.
ex: My friend the doctor was a thorough antiquary: a little rusty, musty old fellow, always groping among ruins.

s.def: Bad-tempered, grumpy, irritable.
A type of snuff with a musty flavour (adjective sense 2).
To turn musty (adjective sense 1 or 2); to must.
Of a male animal such as a camel or an elephant: in musth.

ety: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.

s.def: Changeable, dynamic, evolutive; inclined to change, evolve, mutate.
Having a value that is changeable during program execution.
Being one of the signs Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces, associated with adaptability, flexibility and sympathy.
Something mutable; a variable or value that can change.

ety: From Latin mūtāns, present participle of mūtō. By surface analysis, muta- + -ant.

ex: Furthermore, it is possible that there occasionally arises what may be called a mutant of very desirable character from a eugenic point of view.

s.def: Someone or something that seems strange, abnormal, or bizarre.
ex: Your neighbor seems to be a mutant; he’s so cringy!

s.def: Synonym of mutex.
A changed version of a program, developed as part of mutation testing.
Of, relating to, undergoing (i.e. mutating), or resulting from change or mutation; that has undergone mutation.
ex: Scientists have created a mutant enzyme that breaks down plastic drinks bottles—by accident.

ety: From Ottoman Turkish متصرف (mutasarrıf, “governor of a sanjak”) (modern Turkish mutasarrıf), from Arabic مُتَصَرِّف (mutaṣarrif, “autonomous one, governor of a province”), from تَصَرَّفَ (taṣarrafa, “to act, to act independently”).

s.def: The governor of a province in some Muslim contexts, particularly (historical) in the Ottoman Empire.

ety: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.

Any alteration or change.
A mutant.
An alteration in a particular sound of a word, especially the initial consonant, which is triggered by the word's morphological or syntactic context and not by its phonological context.
The transfer of title of an asset in a register.
A group of thrushes.
ex: Birdwatchers would enjoy a host of sparrows, a herd of swans, a descent of woodpeckers, a herd of wrens, and mutation of thrushes.
Names for a group: A flute or mutation of thrushes.
A Mutation of Thrushes The authors of the books of venery were not predicting Darwin with this term, but taking a cue from a common fable of the time.

ety: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.

Silent; not making a sound.
Not uttered; unpronounced; silent; also, produced by complete closure of the mouth organs which interrupt the passage of breath; said of certain letters.
Not giving a ringing sound when struck; said of a metal.
A stopped consonant; a stop.

A person who does not have the power of speech.

s.def: An object for dulling the sound of an instrument, especially a brass instrument, or damper for pianoforte; a sordine.

ety: So called because it is not very vocal (though not entirely mute).

ety: From Arabic المُثَنَّى (al-muṯannā).

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin mutilātus, the perfect passive participle of mutilō (“to mutilate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), itself from mutilus (“maimed”).

ety: Originally a trademark, from Latin mutare (“to change”), and -scope.

s.def: A motion-picture device of the late nineteenth century, to be viewed by one person at a time through a peephole.

ety: From Middle English muteren, moteren, of imitative origin. Compare Low German mustern, musseln (“to whisper”), German muttern (“to mutter; whisper”), Old Norse muðla (“to murmur”). Compare also Latin muttīre, mutīre.

ety: A pun on "assured destruction" ("a highly reliable ability to inflict unacceptable damage ... even after absorbing a surprise first strike"), a term used in discussions of American nuclear strategy in the 1960s. ety: From earlier muzle, musle, mousle, mussel, mozell, from Middle English mosel, from Old French musel, museau, muzeau (modern French museau), from Late Latin mūsus (“snout”), probably expressive of the shape of protruded lips and/or influenced by Latin mūgīre (“to moo, bellow”). A person's mouth.

The Sino-Tibetan official language of the country of Myanmar.
The script in which the Myanmar language is written.

ety: From Ukrainian Микола́їв (Mykolájiv), from Микола́й (Mykoláj, “Nicholas”). The city near the Dniester was founded under the Polish name Mikołajów, named for its founder and first owner, Mikołaj Tarło. The city on the Southern Buh was founded under the Russian name Никола́ев (Nikolájev), named by the city’s founder, H.S.H. Prince Grigory Potemkin, for Никола́й Чудотво́рец (Nikoláj Čudotvórec, St Nicholas the Wonderworker), on whose feast day (the 6th of December) in 1788 (reckoned according to t…

s.def: city in Mykolaiv, Mykolaiv, Mykolaiv, Ukraine
A village in Bobrovytsia urban hromada, Nizhyn Raion, Chernihiv Oblast, Ukraine, founded in 1587.
A village in Chornyi Ostriv settlement hromada, Khmelnytskyi Raion, Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Ukraine, founded in 1555.
A village in Lopatyn settlement hromada, Chervonohrad Raion, Lviv Oblast, Ukraine, founded before 1772.
A village in Davydiv rural hromada, Lviv Raion, Lviv Oblast, Ukraine, first mentioned in 1670.
A city, the administrative centre of Mykolaiv urban hromada, Stryi Raion, Lviv Oblast, Ukraine, founded in 1570 near the River Dniester.
A city, the administrative centre of Mykolaiv urban hromada, Mykolaiv Raion, Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine, founded in 1789 at the confluence of the Inhul and the Southern Buh.
ex: Coordinate term: Mykolaiv and Sevastopol Military Governorate (predecessor administrative division [1805–1864])

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μύκονος (Múkonos).

s.def: An island of the Cyclades, Greece.

ety: From Dutch mynheer, mijnheer.

s.def: Sir, as a polite form of address to a Dutchman or Afrikaner.
ex: But trifling apart, there is one thing certain, mynheeren, and that is, that some extraordinary event is taking place on board the Dutchman.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *múHs Proto-Hellenic *mū́s Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs)der. English myo- From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse; muscle”).

s.def: Muscle.

ety: Etymology tree English myocard(ium) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English myocarditis From myocard(ium) + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the myocardium.

ety: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (kardíā, “heart”).

s.def: The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *múHs Proto-Hellenic *mū́s Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs)der. English myo- English fibril English myofibril From myo- + fibril.

s.def: Any of the cylindrical organelles, found within muscle cells, that are the contractile unit of muscles.

ety: From Japanese 茗荷 (myōga).

s.def: A Japanese type of ginger, Zingiber mioga, of which only the shoots and flower buds are used in cooking.
A small globular protein, containing a heme group, that carries oxygen to muscles.

ety: From myo- + -logy.

s.def: The physiological study of muscles.
ex: Examination of the myology of the Comephoridae, an endemic fish family in Lake Baikal, has revealed their morphological peculiarities.
He greets me as if I'd been waiting all my life to learn the secrets of Bovine Myology and Muscle Profiling.

ety: From myo- + -oma.

s.def: A tumor composed of muscle tissue, usually benign and commonly occurring in the uterus and the esophagus.
One who has myopia.

ety: Etymology tree English myopia Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English myopic From myopia + -ic.

s.def: Near-sighted; unable to see distant objects unaided.
ex: Corrective lenses compensate for the excessive positive diopters of the myopic eye.
A stronger prescription for myopic night drivers is often needed.
She yanked the paper from her motherʼs hands, bringing it very close to her myopic eyes.

s.def: Shortsighted; improvident.
ex: His postwar roles, full of myopic obsession, stalkerish derangement, and a desire for vengeance, don't seem like ground Hanks is willing to cover.

s.def: Narrow-minded.
ex: Scientific advances can draw us outside of our myopic comfort zone.
Will you come testify in the court of myopic opinion / Or will you settle for oblivion?

ety: From myo- (“relating to muscle”), and Ancient Greek μυός (muós), genitive of μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + -in.

s.def: Any of a large family of motor proteins found in eukaryotic tissues, allowing mobility in muscles.
An albuminous body present in dead muscle formed in the process of coagulation which takes place in rigor mortis.

ety: Borrowed from Latin myosōtis, from Koine Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, literally “ears of a mouse”), from genitive of μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) and nominative plural of οὖς (oûs, “ear”).

s.def: Any plant of the genus Myosotis, the forget-me-nots.
ex: Cut all the myosotis there is.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek μῡρῐ́ος (mūrĭ́os) Ancient Greek -ᾰ́ς (-ắs) Ancient Greek μῡρῐᾰ́ς (mūrĭắs)bor. Late Latin mȳriasbor. French myriade English myriad From French myriade, from Late Latin mȳriadem (accusative of mȳrias), from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (muríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”). By surface analysis, myria- + -ad.

s.def: A countless number or multitude (of specified things)
ex: Earth hosts a myriad of animals.

s.def: ten thousand — see also ten thousand
Ten thousand; 10,000
Multifaceted, having innumerable elements.
ex: "As a clinician, it's a difficult symptom to treat," Cornelius said. "The end symptom may be the same, but what's causing it may be myriad."

s.def: Great in number; innumerable, multitudinous.
ex: Earth hosts myriad animals.

ety: From taxonomic name Myriapoda.

s.def: Any arthropod (such as centipedes and millipedes) of the subphylum Myriapoda.

ety: From Myrmidon, from Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes).

s.def: A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes orders of a superior without protest or pity (sometimes applied to bailiffs, constables, etc).
ex: Tobias (to Jonas Fogg, manager of a madhouse): "I will die ere I submit to you or your vile myrmidons."
He cared no more for the Devil and all his myrmidons, for he kenned brawly he was damned.

ety: From Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus (“ben nut”), from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos), from μύρον (múron, “perfume”) + βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

s.def: A plum-like fruit from various trees of the genus Terminalia, formerly used in medicine and now in the dyeing industry; also, the tree itself.
ex: turbith, agaric, myrobolanes, hermodactyls, from the East Indies, tobacco from the West […].
Myrrh, sweet marjoram, and the plum-like myrobalan fruit were likewise usual ingredients of aromatic preparations.

ety: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic. Compare Arabic مُرّ (murr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”), Hebrew מור / מֹר (mōr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”). Compare מרור : maror.

s.def: A red-brown resinous material, the dried sap of a tree of the genus Commiphora, especially Commiphora myrrha, used as perfume, incense or medicine.
ex: A compound of eggs boiled with myrrh, pepper, and cinnamon, taken on several successive days, is recommended by Arabs for strengthening amorous vigor.

s.def: Synonym of chrism.
The herb chervil.

ety: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

s.def: An evergreen shrub or small tree of the genus Myrtus, native to southern Europe and north Africa.
ex: In the Middle Ages pulverized myrtle leaves were applied to the body as a sexual stimulation.

s.def: A small tree or tall shrub, Cyrilla racemiflora, native to temperate and tropical regions of the Americas.
A tall evergreen Australian tree, Nothofagus cunninghamii, native to Victoria and Tasmania.
ex: [W]here the gullies are fringed with blackwoods, wattle, myrtles, musks and sassafras[.]

s.def: A dark green shade that resembles the color of Myrtus leaves.

ety: From Middle English myself, meself, from Old English mē selfum and similar phrases, equivalent to me + self, later partly reinterpreted as my + self / -self. Cognate with Scots mysel, mysell (“myself”), West Frisian mysels (“myself”), Dutch mijzelf (“myself”), German mich selbst, mir selbst (“myself”), Norwegian Bokmål meg selv (“myself”).

s.def: Personally, for my part; used in apposition to I, sometimes for simple emphasis and sometimes with implicit exclusion of any others performing the activity described.
ex: I myself have witnessed the event.

s.def: Me, as the object of a verb or preposition without a reflexive trigger. Sometimes used for intensifying the pronoun of oneself.
ex: Give the ball to John or myself.

s.def: Me, as direct or indirect object the speaker as the object of a verb or preposition, when the speaker is also the subject.
ex: I taught myself.
(I) don’t think much of your new car, myself.

s.def: In my normal state of body or mind.
ex: I feel like myself.

s.def: my name is...
ex: Myself John.

s.def: I (as the subject of a verb).
ex: My wife and myself want to go on vacation.
Myself am confident that an ointment of it is one of the best remedies for a scabby head that is.

ety: From Latin mystagōgus, Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós). By surface analysis, mystic + -agogue.

s.def: A person who prepares an initiate for entry into a mystery cult, or who teaches mystical doctrines.

ety: From Middle English *misterius (implied in misteriusly), probably partly from Middle French mystérieux and partly from Latin mystērium + -ous. By surface analysis, mystery + -ous.

s.def: Of unknown origin.
ex: He received a mysterious phone call this morning.

s.def: Having unknown qualities.
ex: Our boss is a mysterious man who hardly ever meets with us.

s.def: Difficult to understand.
ex: Why he left without saying goodbye is quite mysterious.
Buttressed by clothes, walls and objects, there was the bourgeois family, the most mysterious institution of the age.

s.def: Deliberately evasive or enigmatic.
ex: Stop being mysterious and just tell me what you want.

der: the Lord works in mysterious ways

ety: From Middle English mysterie, from Anglo-Norman misterie (Old French mistere), from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”). Displaced native Old English ġerȳne.

s.def: Something secret or unexplainable; an unknown.
ex: The truth behind the events remains a mystery.

s.def: Someone or something with an obscure or puzzling nature.
ex: That man is a mystery.

s.def: An account, story, book, film, or play, often with the theme of crime or murder, with a surprise ending that explains all the strange events that have occurred.
A mystery play.
A secret or mystical meaning.
ex: […] and, not knowing the meaning or misterie of her pollicie, forgat no termes of reproche or rigorous rebuke against his chast doughter.

s.def: A religious truth not understandable by the application of human reason alone (without divine aid).
A sacrament.
A secret religious celebration, admission to which was usually through initiation.
ex: the Eleusinian mysteries
the Mysteries of Mithras
There’s no initiation either into such mysteries.

s.def: A particular event or series of events in the life of Christ.
ex: The second decade of the Rosary concerns the Sorrowful mysteries, such as the crucifixion and the crowning with thorns.

s.def: A craft, art or trade; specifically a guild of craftsmen.
ex: The trades, the crafts, the mysteries, would all be losers.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mewH- Proto-Indo-European *mewH-ye-der. Ancient Greek μῡ́ω (mū́ō) Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *-eyéti Proto-Indo-European *-esyéti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Ancient Greek -έω (-éō) Ancient Greek μῠέω (mŭéō) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs) Ancient Greek μῠ́στης (mŭ́stēs) Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Hell…

s.def: Of, or relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries; mystical.
ex: a mystic dance

s.def: Mysterious and strange; arcane, obscure or enigmatic.
ex: Tho’ truths in manhood darkly join, ⁠Deep-seated in our mystic frame, ⁠We yield all blessing to the name Of Him that made them current coin; […]

s.def: Someone who practices mysticism.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mewH- Proto-Indo-European *mewH-ye-der. Ancient Greek μῡ́ω (mū́ō) Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *-eyéti Proto-Indo-European *-esyéti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Ancient Greek -έω (-éō) Ancient Greek μῠέω (mŭéō) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs) Ancient Greek μῠ́στης (mŭ́stēs) Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Hell…

s.def: Relating to mystics or mysticism.
Having a spiritual or magical significance that transcends human understanding.
Inspiring a sense of spiritual mystery, awe, and fascination.

ety: From mystic + -ism, from Old French mistique (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin mysticus (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated, initiate”) from μῡ́ω (mū́ō, “to close one's lips or eyes; initiate into the mysteries”). Compare Asturian misticismu, Catalan misticisme, French mysticisme, German Mystizismus, Italian misticismo, Portuguese misticismo, Sicilian misticisimu, Spanish mist…

s.def: The beliefs, ideas, or thoughts of mystics.
A doctrine of direct communication or spiritual intuition of divine truth.
A transcendental union of soul or mind with the divine reality or divinity.
Obscure thoughts and speculations.

ety: From French mystifier, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”) + Latin -ficare.

s.def: To thoroughly confuse, befuddle, or bewilder.
ex: Solar eclipses continued to mystify ancient humans for thousands of years.

ety: Borrowed from French mystique (“a mystic”), from Latin mysticus. See also the doublet mystic.

s.def: An aura of heightened interest, meaning or mystery surrounding a person or thing.
A town in southern Greece.

ety: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”). Attested in English since 1830. Doublet of mythos.

s.def: divine story

A traditional story which embodies a belief regarding some fact or phenomenon of experience, and in which often the forces of nature and of the soul are personified; a sacred narrative regarding a god, a hero, the origin of the world or of a people, etc.
ex: Jacobsen's theory about the empty storehouse is still valid, for a myth never has one meaning only; a myth is a polyphonic fugue of many voices.

s.def: Such stories as a genre.
ex: Myth was the product of man's emotion and imagination, acted upon by his surroundings. (E. Clodd, Myths & Dreams (1885), 7, cited after OED)

s.def: A commonly-held but false belief, a common misconception; a fictitious or imaginary person or thing; a popular conception about a real person or event which exaggerates or idealizes reality.
ex: Scientists debunk the myth that gum stays in the human stomach for seven years.

s.def: A person or thing held in excessive or quasi-religious awe or admiration based on popular legend
ex: Father Flanagan was legendary, his institution an American myth. (Tucson (Arizona) Citizen, 20 September 1979, 5A/3, cited after OED)

s.def: A person or thing existing only in imagination, or whose actual existence is not verifiable.
ex: As for Mrs. Primmins's bones, they had been myths these twenty years.

s.def: An invented story, theory, or concept.
ex: His story is a pure myth.

ety: From mytho- + -genic.

s.def: Producing or capable of producing myths.

ety: From mythology + -ical.

s.def: Of, or relating to myths or mythology.
ex: In short—to be mythological in my conclusion—the quiver of Cupid hangs at the girdle of Fate together with her spindle and scissors.

s.def: Legendary.
Imaginary.

ety: First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mȳthologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”). By surface analysis, myth + -ology or mytho- + -logy.

s.def: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A similar body of myths concerning an event, person or institution.
The systematic collection and study of myths.
Pervasive elements of a fictional universe that resemble a mythological universe.
ex: This tongue-in-cheek episode is especially fun for people who don’t take their “X-Files” mythology seriously.

s.def: The set of misconceptions and false attitudes that are held about something and contribute to its perception.

ety: From mytho- + -mania. Compare French mythomanie f.

s.def: A compulsion to tell lies and exaggerate the truth.

ety: From Hellenistic Ancient Greek μυθοποιία (muthopoiía, “mythopoeia”) + -ic.

s.def: Giving rise to myths; pertaining to the creation of myth.
ex: No other fully historical hero has furnished such a perfect opportunity for the mythopoeic faculty.
If we study myth in a scientific way, we miss the experience of moving into a mythopoeic mode of consciousness.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”). Doublet of myth. The plural form mythoi is from Ancient Greek μῦθοι (mûthoi), and the form mythoses from mythos + -es.

s.def: Anything transmitted by word of mouth, such as a fable, legend, narrative, story, or tale (especially a poetic tale).
A story or set of stories relevant to or having a significant truth or meaning for a particular culture, religion, society, or other group; a myth, a mythology.
ex: The term cobber [...] is still a part of our linguistic culture, and mateship is still a part of our cultural mythos.
Most of the bad broncos, if mythos is peppered with a slight shake of practicality, were more-likely-as-not just a cavvyard of crow-hoppers.

s.def: A set of assumptions or beliefs about something.
A recurring theme; a motif.
ex: In addition to mythoi drawn from myths and fairy tales, romances also employ mythoi derived from chivalric romances.
